lead: Today's two readings belong together: both speak of priests. Hebrews says that no one takes the priestly office for himself; he is called by God, “just as Aaron was”. Luke opens his Gospel inside the temple, with a priest named Zechariah, his wife Elizabeth, who is “a descendant of Aaron”, and a whole people praying outside while the incense burns. The Panchangam remembers Aaron on this first day of July, and the readings show what a priest is: someone called, set apart to offer gifts and sacrifices on behalf of the people, and himself in need of mercy. The key words are called and righteous.

r.h: Called by God, just as Aaron was
set: The Letter to the Hebrews is a long sermon, written by an author the Church does not name. It was received early as part of the Pauline tradition, though almost all scholars agree that its style and thought differ from Paul's; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. It is addressed to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to lose heart, and it shows that everything good in the worship of Israel finds its fulfilment in Christ.

Chapter 4 ended by calling Jesus the great high priest who has passed through the heavens and can sympathise with our weakness (4:14–16). Chapter 5 now explains what any high priest is, so that the author can show how Jesus is one, and more than one (5:5–10). Today's four verses are a portrait of the high priest of Israel, of whom Aaron, the brother of Moses, was the first.
str: v. 1: the high priest is taken from among human beings and appointed to act for them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins.
vv. 2–3: he can be gentle with the ignorant and the wayward because he shares their weakness, and so he offers also for his own sins.
v. 4: no one takes the honour for himself; he is called by God, as Aaron was.
¶ Three marks of a priest: he is one of us, he stands before God for us, and he is called.
kw: A rare Greek verb, meaning to bear with feelings that are measured and gentle, neither hard nor careless. The priest can be patient with sinners because he knows his own weakness. The same letter says of Jesus that he “has been tested as we are, yet without sin” (4:15).
Priesthood is not a career chosen from within; it is a vocation received from outside. In the Old Testament God summoned Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1).
A pair of words for all that Israel offered: grain and first-fruits on one side, animals on the other. The priest carries the offerings of the people to God.
vv: Every high priest chosen from among mortals is put in charge of things pertaining to God on their behalf, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.
A priest does not stand above the people; he is “chosen from among mortals”. He is one of them, and he is appointed for them.
He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is subject to weakness;
The priest's own weakness is meant to make him merciful, not harsh. A priest who forgets that he is a sinner forgets his work.
and because of this he must offer sacrifice for his own sins as well as for those of the people.

On the Day of Atonement Aaron had first to offer a bull for himself and his household, and only then the goat for the people (Leviticus 16:6, 11, 15). This is the very point where Jesus differs: he has no sin of his own to atone for (Hebrews 7:27).
And one does not presume to take this honor, but takes it only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
Aaron did not seek the office; God chose him and his sons, and Moses consecrated them (Exodus 28–29). The call comes first, and the ordination confirms it.
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on the priesthood with the Old Testament: God made Israel a priestly kingdom (Exodus 19:6), set apart the tribe of Levi for the liturgy, and appointed priests to act for the people before God and to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, recalling this very verse (CCC 1539). All that the priesthood of the old covenant prefigured is fulfilled in Christ, the one mediator between God and human beings (CCC 1544). The Church also applies verse 4 to every vocation to Holy Orders: no one has a right to ordination, and no one claims the office for himself; he is called by God (CCC 1578).

r.h: A priest, his wife and the praying people
set: Luke begins his Gospel with a short preface (1:1–4) and then, at once, goes to Jerusalem. The first scene is not in Bethlehem or Nazareth but in the temple, at the hour of the incense offering. The Gospel will end in the same place: after the Ascension the disciples “were continually in the temple blessing God” (24:53).

The priests of Israel were divided into twenty-four sections, which served in the temple in turn for a week at a time (1 Chronicles 24:1–19); the section of Abijah was the eighth (24:10). Zechariah was a priest of that section. The time is “the days of King Herod”, so the story is set before Herod's death, about 4 BC. Zechariah and Elizabeth are the opening figures of the new beginning that God is about to make.
str: vv. 5–7: the couple: a priest of the section of Abijah and his wife, a descendant of Aaron; both righteous and without children.
vv. 8–9: Zechariah is chosen by lot to enter the sanctuary and offer incense.
v. 10: the whole assembly is praying outside.
¶ The story continues after today's verses with the angel at the altar of incense (1:11–20).
kw: Right with God. The word is used of Joseph (Matthew 1:19) and of Simeon (Luke 2:25). Luke wants us to see that the Saviour is born into a world where faithful people have been waiting.
Without reproach. It does not mean sinless, but wholehearted in keeping “all the commandments and regulations of the Lord”.

The incense offered morning and evening on the golden altar before the veil of the sanctuary (Exodus 30:7–8). Its rising smoke is, in Scripture, the picture of prayer going up to God (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 8:3–4).
vv: His wife was a descendant of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
Elizabeth is from the priestly family of Aaron, the very man whom the Epistle recalls today. In Hebrew her name is Elisheba, the name of Aaron's own wife (Exodus 6:23).
Both of them were righteous before God, living blamelessly according to all the commandments and regulations of the Lord.
Luke honours the faith of Israel. The new covenant does not begin by despising the old; it begins with two faithful servants of the Law.
But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were getting on in years.
Like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah before her, Elizabeth is childless. In Scripture, whenever God gives a child to such a woman, he is about to do something new.
he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the sanctuary of the Lord and offer incense.

The lot was cast, and according to later Jewish tradition a priest might receive this honour only once in his life. God's choice comes through what looks like chance, as it did when Matthias was chosen (Acts 1:26).
Now at the time of the incense offering, the whole assembly of the people was praying outside.
The people do not watch; they pray. The first sound of the New Testament is the prayer of the people of God, joined to the offering of the priest.
ch: The Church sees in Zechariah and Elizabeth the last of the righteous of the old covenant, and in the birth of their son John the end of the long waiting: the Catechism says that John surpasses all the prophets, of whom he is the last, and is the immediate forerunner of the Lord (CCC 523). The Church also sees in the incense and the praying assembly the pattern of her own worship, where the priest offers and the people pray with him. The Syriac tradition, with its great use of incense in the Qurbono, has always loved this picture.

qa: Why does Hebrews say that a priest must offer sacrifice for his own sins?

Because every priest of the old covenant was a sinner. On the Day of Atonement Aaron had to bring a sin offering for himself before he could offer for the people (Leviticus 16:6). The author uses this to show what is new in Jesus: he is the priest who needs no offering for himself, because he is without sin (Hebrews 4:15; 7:27). A priest of the Church today, who is a sinner, still comes to confession and prays humbly at every Qurbono, and he does so because his priesthood is a sharing in the priesthood of Christ, not a power of his own.
rite: The Panchangam remembers Aaron the High Priest today, on the first day of July, which the Syriac calendar calls Tammuz. The memory is a reminder that the priesthood by which the Holy Qurbono is celebrated has its roots in the call of Aaron, and is fulfilled in Christ, the one High Priest. The Malankara faithful pray for their bishops and priests at every Qurbono; today's readings invite them to pray that those who are called will be faithful, gentle and merciful.
study: The high priest is “chosen from among mortals” and can be gentle because he knows his own weakness. How can I be patient with someone else's failings, remembering my own?
Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous, yet childless and old. What waiting in my life is God asking me to bring to prayer?
The people were praying outside while the priest offered incense. How do I take part in the prayer of the Church at the Holy Qurbono, and not only watch?

lead: Both readings ask what proves that something comes from God. In Corinthians the proof is a gift: the poor churches of Macedonia, in their affliction, “gave themselves first to the Lord”, and their giving overflowed. In John, when Jesus is accused of blasphemy, he points to his works: if they are the Father's works, believe them, “so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.” In both, what is real shows itself in what is done. The key words are grace and works.

r.h: They gave themselves first to the Lord
set: Paul is raising a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem, called “the saints” (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; Galatians 2:10). It is a sign of the unity of the Church: Gentile believers share their goods with the mother Church from which the gospel came. In 2 Corinthians 8–9 he writes to Corinth, which had begun the collection a year earlier (8:10), to help them finish it.

He writes from Macedonia, probably in AD 55–56. The churches of Macedonia, at Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea, were themselves poor and persecuted. Paul holds them up as an example, not to shame the Corinthians but to move them.
str: vv. 1–2: God's grace in Macedonia: joy and poverty overflow in generosity.
vv. 3–5: they gave willingly, beyond their means, and begged to take part; first they gave themselves.
v. 6: Titus is asked to complete the work at Corinth.
v. 7: Paul asks the Corinthians, who excel in everything else, to excel in this too.
kw: Paul begins by calling the Macedonians' gift “the grace of God” given to them. In his eyes generosity is not first a human achievement but a gift of God working in people. The same word runs through chapters 8 and 9, meaning grace, gift, favour and thanks.

The collection is called a “sharing” (communion) and a “service”. These are words of the Church's life, used also of the Eucharist and of the ministry of deacons. Giving to the poor is a part of the life of the Body of Christ, not an extra.
The word has the sense of a single, undivided heart: open-handed and without calculation. It is Paul's word for the gift that comes from a simple and wholehearted giver.
vv: their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
Joy and poverty together should not produce wealth, but here they do. The Macedonians are poor in money and rich in heart, a reversal Paul sees again and again in the Gospel.
they voluntarily gave according to their means, and even beyond their means,
The measure of giving is not only what is left over. Paul never forces the gift; he appeals to love and to a willing heart (8:8).
they gave themselves first to the Lord and, by the will of God, to us,
The order is the heart of the passage: first the person, then the gift. Money given without the giver is only money; money given with the giver is love.
so we want you to excel also in this generous undertaking.
Paul lists the Corinthians' gifts: faith, speech, knowledge, eagerness, love. To these he adds one more: generosity to those in need.
ch: From the very beginning, the Catechism recalls, Christians have brought with the bread and wine of the Eucharist gifts to share with those in need, and the collection of the Church continues Paul's custom (CCC 1351). Giving to the poor is part of the Church's worship and not only her charity. Because the gift in this passage begins with the grace of God, the Church can teach that she is called to love the poor with a love that comes from Christ.

set: The scene takes place in Jerusalem at the Feast of the Dedication (10:22), a winter feast that recalls the cleansing and rededication of the temple under Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). Jesus is walking in the portico of Solomon. The people there press him: if he is the Messiah, let him say so plainly (10:24). He answers that his works testify for him, and he says, “The Father and I are one” (10:30). Today's verses follow at once.

In John “the Jews” in these scenes means those among the leaders and the crowd in Jerusalem who opposed him. Jesus, his mother and his disciples were all Jews, and Jesus turns to the Law and the Psalms of his own people to answer them.
str: vv. 31–33: they take up stones; Jesus asks for which good work; they answer: blasphemy, because he makes himself God.
vv. 34–36: Jesus answers from Scripture: if the word of God calls human beings “gods”, can the one sanctified and sent by the Father be accused of blasphemy?
vv. 37–38: believe the works, so that you may know that the Father is in him and he in the Father.
v. 39: they try to arrest him, but he escapes.
kw: In John the “works” of Jesus are his miracles seen as signs and, more deeply, everything the Father gives him to do (5:36; 14:10–11). They are not only wonders; they show the Father at work.

To make holy, to set apart for God. It is a word used in the Greek Old Testament for consecrating the temple and its vessels, and Jesus speaks it at the feast of the Dedication. Jesus is the one consecrated by the Father and sent into the world, the true temple.
In John, to know is not only to understand a fact but to enter into a relationship. Jesus wants them to know the Father through the Son.
vv: I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these are you going to stone me?
Jesus does not argue first; he asks. His good works, the healing of the blind man, the giving of life, speak before any claim.
Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods’?

Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6. In the psalm God addresses the judges of Israel, to whom the word of God was entrusted, and calls them “gods”, a title of dignity. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: if the Scripture can use that name of those who received the word, how much more of him whom the Father sent.
and the scripture cannot be annulled
A strong statement about Scripture: it cannot be set aside. Jesus treats the Scriptures of Israel as the word of God.
the one whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world
Jesus does not weaken his claim; he deepens it. He is the Son whom the Father set apart and sent, and the word “sent” runs through the whole Gospel.
believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.
The works lead to faith in the Father and the Son, who dwell in each other. This is why the Church calls the miracles of Jesus signs.
Then they tried to arrest him again, but he escaped from their hands.
His hour has not yet come (7:30; 8:20). When it comes, he will lay down his life of his own accord (10:17–18).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the signs worked by Jesus testify that the Father sent him; they invite faith in him, and they bear witness that he is the Son of God (CCC 548, in substance). The Church reads this passage as a revelation of the unity of the Father and the Son, and therefore of the divinity of Christ, which the Council of Nicaea later set out in the word “one in being with the Father”. At the same time, the Church notes how Jesus himself honours the Scriptures: he argues from the Psalms, and says that the Scripture cannot be annulled.

study: The Macedonians gave themselves first to the Lord, and then their money. What would it mean for me to give myself, and not only something I own, to a person or a cause in need?
Jesus asks, “For which of these are you going to stone me?” When others misjudge me, do I let my good works speak, or do I argue back?

lead: Today the Church remembers St Thomas, the apostle who, according to tradition, brought the gospel to India. The Panchangam lists eight readings. The Evening Gospel (John 14:1–6) holds Thomas's own question: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”, and the answer, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” Four Old Testament readings walk the same road. In Genesis 12:1–9 Abram sets out for “the land that I will show you”. Proverbs 4:10–18 says that the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn. In Job 23:1–7 the sufferer longs to find God. In Isaiah 52 a messenger comes over the mountains with good news. The Catholic Epistle (1 Peter 2:15–17) asks believers to live as servants of God and honour everyone.

We study three readings more closely. Isaiah 52 gives the missionary's picture: the feet of the messenger who announces peace, and “all the ends of the earth” seeing the salvation of God. In 1 Corinthians 4 Paul says, “in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel”, the words of an apostle who is also a father in faith. In John 20 the doubter becomes the one who makes the Gospel's fullest confession of faith: “My Lord and my God!” The key words are the way, sent and believe.

r.h: How beautiful are the feet of the messenger
set: These verses come from the second part of the Book of Isaiah (chapters 40–55), addressed to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC. Many scholars attribute these chapters to a prophet of the exile, whom they call Second Isaiah; the Church receives the whole book as the word of God. The tone is comfort: the exile will end, and the Lord himself will bring his people home.

In today's reading Zion, Jerusalem, is told to wake and put on her beautiful clothes (v. 1). The Lord reminds his people that they were sold “for nothing” and will be redeemed (v. 3). Then comes the cry of the herald on the mountains (v. 7), the watchmen who sing (vv. 8–9), and the call to leave Babylon in procession, a new exodus (vv. 11–12). The reading ends with the opening of the Servant's song (vv. 13–15), which continues in chapter 53.
str: vv. 1–6: wake, Zion; sold for nothing, redeemed without money; the Lord will make his name known.
vv. 7–10: the messenger on the mountains, the watchmen's song, the Lord bares his arm for all the nations to see.
vv. 11–12: leave Babylon; the Lord goes before you and guards your rear.
vv. 13–15: the opening of the Servant's song: he will be lifted up, though his appearance was marred; nations will see what they had not been told.
¶ The movement is from captivity to release, from news to a procession, and from Israel to all the nations.
kw: From the verb meaning to bring news, above all good news. The Greek Old Testament renders it with the verb euangelizomai, which gives us the word “gospel”. Paul quotes this verse of the apostles' preaching in Romans 10:15.
The herald's whole message is these words. The Lord is king; the powers that held his people are not. It is the heart of the later preaching of “the kingdom of God”.
A word from the family: the kinsman who buys back a relative who has been sold. God acts as the close relative of Israel and pays the price himself (compare Isaiah 43:1).
vv: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money.
The people sold themselves into exile by their sins, and no price was received. The Lord will buy them back, and he will ask no payment. Redemption is his gift.
How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace,

The herald runs over the hills with the good news, and the prophet looks at his feet. It is the news that is beautiful, and so the one who carries it. This verse became the apostles' own picture of themselves.
all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.
The salvation of Zion is not hers alone. The ends of the earth will see it. In the New Testament this is the world to which the apostles are sent (Acts 1:8).
the Lord will go before you,
This is the new exodus. At the first exodus the Lord went before his people in a pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21). The one who sends his messengers also goes ahead of them.
my servant shall prosper; he shall be exalted and lifted up,

With these words the Servant's song begins. The Church has always seen here Christ, whose lifting up on the cross is his exaltation (John 12:32). Many Jewish readers have understood the Servant as Israel, and the New Testament itself reads the song in more than one way; Christians read it in the light of Jesus.
that which had not been told them they shall see,
Those who have not heard will see. Paul quotes this verse when he says that he wants to preach Christ where he has not yet been named (Romans 15:21).
ch: Paul quotes verse 7 in Romans 10:15 when he asks, “And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent?” The Church takes the verse as the picture of every missionary, and her mission to all nations is part of her very being: the Council teaches that the pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature (Ad Gentes 2; compare CCC 849). In the Servant's song that opens at verse 13, the Catechism sees the divine plan fulfilled in the death of Christ, the righteous Servant whose death is a ransom for the many (CCC 601; Isaiah 53:11). On Dukrono the Church reads this passage for the apostle sent to the ends of the earth.

r.h: I became your father through the gospel
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus around AD 54–55 to the Church he had founded in Corinth. The first four chapters deal with divisions: groups were boasting of their favourite teachers, saying “I belong to Paul” or “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). In chapter 4 he answers with irony, setting the proud Corinthians beside the apostles who are “fools for the sake of Christ” (4:8–13).

Today's verses are the end of that appeal, and the tone changes. Paul no longer speaks as a teacher in debate but as a father to his children. He does not wish to shame them; he wants to warn them as his beloved children (4:14).
str: v. 15: many guardians, but one father: Paul begot them in Christ through the gospel.
vv. 16–17: be imitators of me; Timothy is sent to remind them of his ways.
vv. 18–19: some are arrogant, thinking he will not come; he will come and test not their talk but their power.
vv. 20–21: the kingdom of God is power, not talk; will he come with a stick or with love and gentleness?
kw: In a Greek household the paidagogos was a trusted slave who led the child to school and watched over his conduct. He could correct but was not the father. Paul says the Corinthians have had many such guides, but only one father in faith.
Literally “I begot”. Paul uses the strongest image of his work: preaching the gospel is a kind of giving birth to new life in Christ. He says it of Onesimus too (Philemon 10).
Not noise or clever speech but the power of God at work. For Paul the sign of the kingdom is a changed life and works of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:4).
vv: in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
A father gives life. Paul's fatherhood does not rival God's; it is the way the gospel, through his preaching, gave the Corinthians new life in Christ.
I appeal to you, then, be imitators of me.
This is not pride. Elsewhere Paul explains: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1). A father in faith shows the way by walking it.
my beloved and faithful child in the Lord,
Timothy is Paul's own convert and companion. Faith is passed on through persons who love one another, not only through books and doctrines.
the kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power.
Words are cheap, and a community that boasts of its speakers can easily be empty. God's kingdom shows itself in what he does in people.
Am I to come to you with a stick, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
The father offers a choice, and everything in him hopes for the second. A true apostle corrects, but he wants to come in love.
ch: The Church honours the apostles as the foundation on which she is built, and Paul's words show what apostolic fatherhood is: to bring people to birth in Christ through the gospel, and to guide them with gentleness. The Catechism teaches that the Lord's own life is the model: in all his life Jesus presents himself as our model, and invites us to follow him (CCC 520, in substance). Paul asks to be imitated only as he imitates Christ. On this feast the Church thanks God for St Thomas as her father in faith, the one through whom, according to tradition, the gospel gave life to the first Christians of India.

set: The scene is the evening of Easter Sunday and then “a week later”, on the eighth day, the next Sunday. The disciples are gathered in a house in Jerusalem with the doors locked “for fear of the Jews”. In John “the Jews” in such places means the authorities in Jerusalem who had handed Jesus over; the disciples themselves were Jews, as was Jesus.

This is the end of John's story of the Resurrection, and in a sense of his whole Gospel: the next two verses (20:30–31) state the purpose of the book, “so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God”. Thomas has spoken twice before: when he says “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (11:16); when he asks the way (14:5); and now, when he refuses to believe unless he sees.
str: vv. 19–23: Jesus appears to the disciples: peace, the showing of the wounds, the sending, the breath of the Spirit, the forgiveness of sins.
vv. 24–25: Thomas was not there; he will not believe unless he sees and touches.
vv. 26–27: eight days later Jesus comes again and invites Thomas to touch his wounds.
vv. 28–29: Thomas's confession; a blessing for all who believe without seeing.
kw: In Hebrew, shalom: wholeness and the fullness of God's gifts. It is the usual greeting, but on Easter evening it is also the gift of the risen Lord, spoken three times in this passage (vv. 19, 21, 26).

This rare verb is the same one used in the Greek Old Testament for what God did in Genesis 2:7, when he “breathed” the breath of life into the first man. The risen Christ now breathes the Holy Spirit on the apostles, as a new creation.
ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou
Thomas speaks to Jesus with the divine title Lord and the word God. It is the highest confession in the four Gospels, and it comes from the one who had doubted most.
vv: Jesus came and stood among them
The locked door does not stop him. The risen body is real and yet no longer subject to the limits of this world.
As the Father has sent me, so I send you.
The mission of the apostles is a share in the Son's mission from the Father. The word “apostle” itself means one who is sent.
he breathed on them and said to them,
The Spirit is given in the Church's first sending out. The next verse links the Spirit with the forgiveness of sins.
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them;
Jesus gives the apostles his own power to forgive. This is why the Church has always taught that sins are forgiven through the ministry of those whom Christ sent.
Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands
Thomas does not ask for more than the others had been given: they had seen the hands and the side (v. 20). He wants to be sure that the risen one is the crucified one.
Do not doubt but believe.
Literally, “do not become unbelieving, but believing”. Jesus does not reject the question; he answers it with his own wounds and calls Thomas out of doubt.
My Lord and my God!

John does not say that Thomas touched the wounds; seeing the Lord is enough, and faith breaks out. The Gospel opened with “the Word was God” (1:1); here the disciple who was slowest to believe is the one who says it aloud of Jesus.
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.
This blessing is for every later generation, including ours. It does not belittle Thomas; his witness is the very thing by which we who have not seen come to believe.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the risen Jesus allowed himself to be touched and to be seen with his wounds, and that even before the Risen One the disciples doubted (CCC 644, in substance). It sees the Easter evening as the moment when Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive sins: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them” (CCC 1485; compare CCC 976). The Church also reads verse 21 as the root of apostolic mission: Jesus sent the apostles as the Father sent him (CCC 858). Thomas's cry has become a prayer of adoration for the whole Church.

qa: Did St Thomas really come to India?

The Church in India has held this for nearly two thousand years, and it has always been a tradition and not a document that proves it. According to tradition he reached the coast of Kerala in AD 52, founded Christian communities, and was martyred at Mylapore near Chennai about AD 72. The third-century Acts of Thomas tells of his mission to India, though it is legendary in many of its details. Scholars debate how much can be proved. The Church does not need to settle every detail to honour the faith that Indian Christians have kept, and Benedict XVI, in a general audience on 27 September 2006, spoke of Thomas's journey to India as part of the tradition of the Church.
Was it wrong of Thomas to doubt?

Thomas did not believe what the others told him, and Jesus calls him to believe. But Jesus does not shame him. He comes back after eight days, shows his wounds, and Thomas answers with the greatest confession of faith in the Gospels. His honest question is also what leads to our knowing that the risen Christ is the same one who was crucified. Doubt that is brought to Jesus can become faith; doubt that stays away from him cannot.
Why does the risen Jesus still have the marks of the nails?

The Church teaches that the risen body is the same body that was crucified, now glorified, and that the marks of the Passion remain (CCC 645, in substance). They are the sign that the cross was not undone but transformed: Christ keeps his wounds as the mark of his love, and they are the means by which Thomas recognises him.
rite: The Panchangam calls today the Dukrono of St Thomas the Apostle, Father in Faith of the Church in India, and gives it a Holy Qurbono for the people. “Dukrono” is the Syriac word for remembrance. According to tradition Thomas landed at Muziris, near Kodungallur, in AD 52, founded communities along the Kerala coast, and was martyred at Mylapore. The Malankara faithful, whose Church traces its beginnings to his preaching, keep this day as a feast of their whole heritage. The Syriac liturgy honours him as Mar Thoma Shleeha, Apostle. Today is also the name day of Most Rev. Joseph Mar Thomas, whom we remember in prayer.
study: Thomas asked, “How can we know the way?” and Jesus answered, “I am the way.” Which question do I most need to bring to Jesus today?
The messenger's feet are called “beautiful” on the mountains. Who brought the good news of Christ to me, and how can I thank them?
Paul calls the Corinthians his children in faith. Who has been a father or mother in faith to me, and to whom am I one?
Thomas moved from doubt to adoration in a single sentence. What would it mean for me to say “My Lord and my God” from the heart at the Holy Qurbono this week?

lead: On the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost the readings are about division and peace. In the evening Gospel (Matthew 12:30–37) Jesus says that whoever does not gather with him scatters, and that “by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” Leviticus 16:29–34 sets out the Day of Atonement, the one day in the year on which Israel's sins were cleansed. In 1 Samuel 4:18–22 the ark is taken, old Eli dies, and a newborn child is named Ichabod, “The glory has departed from Israel.” In Hosea 5:1–5 the prophet says that Israel's deeds do not permit them to return to their God. In Acts 4:23–31 the believers pray under threat, the place is shaken, and “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with boldness.”

We study three readings more closely. Isaiah 57:14–21 shows the high and holy God who dwells also with the contrite, and who says, “Peace, peace, to the far and the near.” Ephesians 2:11–22 answers that promise: Christ “is our peace”, has broken down the dividing wall, and makes of Jews and Gentiles one household of God. In Mark 3:20–30 the scribes accuse Jesus of working by Beelzebul, and he answers that a house divided against itself cannot stand. Today is also Family Day in the Church. The key words are house, peace and the Spirit.

r.h: Peace, peace, to the far and the near
set: These verses belong to the last part of the Book of Isaiah (chapters 56–66), which many scholars think was addressed to the community that had returned from exile in Babylon and found a hard life in a ruined land. The people are discouraged. There are quarrels about worship and about who belongs to God's people (chapter 56 speaks of foreigners and eunuchs welcomed to the Lord's house). The Church receives the whole book as the word of God.

Today's passage is the Lord's answer to a people who feel far from him. He opens with a cry to clear the road (v. 14), then speaks of himself: the high and holy God who lives in eternity and who dwells also with the humble (v. 15). His anger was real, but it has an end (vv. 16–17). What follows is a promise of healing and peace (vv. 18–19), and a warning that the wicked will not find peace (vv. 20–21).
str: v. 14: the call to build up the road and remove every obstruction from the people's way.
v. 15: the high and holy God who dwells with the contrite and humble.
vv. 16–17: he will not accuse for ever; the people's covetousness had brought his anger.
vv. 18–19: “I have seen their ways, but I will heal them”: peace to the far and the near.
vv. 20–21: the wicked are like a restless sea, and have no peace.
kw: In Hebrew, more than the end of war: wholeness, health and right relationship with God and one another. The prophet repeats the word, “peace, peace”, to show its fullness.

The far are those distant from God or from the land; the near are those close. Many interpreters take the far as the exiles scattered abroad and the near as the people in Jerusalem. Ephesians 2:17 reads the words of the Gentiles, who were far, and the Jews, who were near.
Literally “crushed”, from the verb meaning to crush. It describes the person whose pride has been broken and who has become open to God. God lives with such a person.
vv: prepare the way, remove every obstruction from my people’s way.
The command echoes Isaiah 40:3. The way home is to be made smooth for the people. The Church hears in this the work of the forerunner, John, who prepared the way of the Lord.
I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with those who are contrite and humble in spirit,
The most striking verse of the passage. The Lord, whom heaven cannot contain, makes his home in the broken-hearted. It is the heart of the whole of Scripture's teaching about humility.
I will not continually accuse, nor will I always be angry;
The Lord's anger is real, but it is not his last word. He recalls that he made the spirits and souls of his people and knows how frail they are (compare Psalm 103:9–14).
I have seen their ways, but I will heal them;
God sees everything, and still chooses to heal. Mercy that knows the whole truth is what the word “grace” means.
Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the Lord; and I will heal them.
Peace is God's gift to all, whether they are close to him or far away, and it is joined to healing. This is the verse Ephesians takes up.
There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked.
The passage ends with a sober warning, repeated at 48:22. Peace cannot be had apart from God, because it is his gift. The way back, however, is always open (v. 15).
ch: The Church reads the promise of peace “to the far and the near” in the light of Christ. In Ephesians 2:17 Paul applies it to the preaching of Christ to Gentiles and Jews alike. The Catechism teaches that earthly peace is the image and fruit of the peace of Christ (CCC 2305). God's closeness to the humble is also the song of the Magnificat, where Mary says that God has looked on the lowliness of his servant (Luke 1:46–55).

set: Ephesians is a letter about the Church and the unity of Jew and Gentile in Christ. It is traditionally ascribed to Paul, writing from prison (3:1; 4:1); many scholars think it was written in Paul's name by a close disciple, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself. Either way the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. Most of the readers were Gentile believers.

In the first half of chapter 2 Paul has said that God has made us alive in Christ by grace. Now he turns to the community: the Gentiles who were once far from God's people have been brought near, and the old hostility between Jews and Gentiles has been ended in the cross. The “dividing wall” of verse 14 may recall the low stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple that kept Gentiles from the inner courts, with its inscription warning them not to go further. Paul uses it as a picture of the separation that Christ has taken down.
str: vv. 11–12: remember what you once were: without Christ, strangers to the covenants of promise.

vv. 13–18: but now in Christ you are near: he is our peace; he has broken down the wall, made one new humanity, reconciled both to God through the cross, and given both access to the Father in one Spirit.
vv. 19–22: you are no longer strangers, but citizens and members of God's household, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as the cornerstone, and growing into a holy temple.
¶ The movement is from remembering to peace and then to building.
kw: The Greek words mean a partition and a fence. The barrier in question is the hostility between Jews and Gentiles. The cross puts that hostility to death (v. 16).
“He is our peace” does not mean only that Christ brings peace; he himself is the peace between God and humanity, and between those who were divided.
members of the household of God
From oikos, house. The Gentiles are not guests in the house of God; they belong to the family. A household is the place where people eat, pray and are cared for together.
vv: without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise,

Paul begins by honouring Israel. The covenants and the commonwealth of Israel are the gifts of God that the Gentiles were not yet sharing. The Church does not leave Israel behind; she is grafted in (Romans 11:17–18).
you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
The prophet's “far” and “near” (Isaiah 57:19) now have a name: the Gentiles who were far have been brought near. The nearness is not by their own effort but by the blood of Christ.
he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall
One body, one household. Christ does not make Gentiles into Jews or Jews into Gentiles; he makes of both one new humanity (v. 15).
reconcile both groups to God in one body through the cross,
Peace with one another begins with peace with God. The cross is the place where the two are reconciled, because there the hostility is put to death.
you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
Citizens and family members. Both pictures are needed: a city with its rights, and a home with its love.
with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.
The apostles and prophets are the foundation, but Christ is the stone that holds the corner together, so that the building does not fall apart.
ch: The Catechism uses this passage to describe the Church as God's building: the apostles are the foundation, Christ is the cornerstone, and the building has many names, among them the house and dwelling of God and the holy temple (CCC 756; compare Ephesians 2:19–22). The Church sees the “one new humanity” as the fruit of the cross, where Christ reconciles all things to God. At the same time the Church teaches that God's covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked (Romans 11:29; CCC 121 and 839), and that Paul speaks here not of cancelling Israel's calling but of Gentiles being welcomed into it.

set: Jesus has just named the Twelve on the mountain (3:13–19) and now comes “home”, to the house at Capernaum (2:1). The crowd presses so hard that he and his disciples cannot even eat. Mark tells the story in a typical pattern: he begins one scene (v. 21, his family), breaks in with another (vv. 22–30, the scribes), and then returns to the first (vv. 31–35, his mother and brothers). The two scenes explain each other: some who are near him do not understand him, and others who should know better call his goodness evil.

The scribes who came down from Jerusalem are experts in the Law and part of the leadership; the accusation comes from them, not from the Jewish people as a whole. The crowd, the Twelve and Jesus himself are all Jews.
str: vv. 20–21: the crowd; his family go out to restrain him, saying that he is out of his mind.
vv. 22–27: the scribes say he works by Beelzebul; Jesus answers with parables: a divided kingdom or house cannot stand; no one plunders a strong man's house unless he first binds the strong man.
vv. 28–30: every sin and blasphemy can be forgiven, but not blasphemy against the Holy Spirit; Mark explains that the scribes had said, “He has an unclean spirit.”
kw: he is out of his mind
Literally “he has stood outside himself”. People thought his zeal was madness. Mark never excuses the accusation; he wants the reader to see that those who love Jesus can fail to understand him.
Satan, who holds the world in his grip. Jesus is the stronger one who has come to bind him (compare Isaiah 49:24–25; Mark 1:7). Each exorcism is a piece of plunder taken from the strong man's house.
blasphēmia eis to pneuma to hagion
Not a single careless word, but a settled refusal to recognise the work of God as God's, calling the Spirit's work evil. Mark's own explanation is in verse 30.
vv: He has gone out of his mind.

The “family” here translates a general phrase meaning “those from beside him”: relatives and neighbours. Mark does not say that his mother shared the view; in the Church's reading her faith is never in doubt.
He has Beelzebul, and by the ruler of the demons he casts out demons.
His enemies cannot deny that the demons are driven out, so they say the power is evil. This is a fatal turn of mind: when what is good is called evil, there is nothing left to be healed.
If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.
Jesus answers with common sense. Evil does not fight itself. If the demons are being driven out, a stronger power is at work, and the kingdom of God has come.
no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his property without first tying up the strong man
This is a picture of Jesus's whole ministry: he has entered the house of the strong man and is releasing those held captive.
people will be forgiven for their sins and whatever blasphemies they utter;
The great generosity of the passage. Every sin, every blasphemy, can be forgiven. No sinner is outside God's mercy.
whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit can never have forgiveness

This is not a sin that God refuses to forgive but one that closes the heart against forgiveness. A person who says that the Spirit's work is the devil's will not ask for the very mercy that the Spirit brings. Anyone who fears he has committed it shows by his fear that he has not.
ch: The Catechism teaches that there are no limits to the mercy of God, but that anyone who deliberately refuses to accept his mercy by repenting rejects the forgiveness of his sins and the salvation offered by the Holy Spirit; such hardness of heart can lead to final impenitence (CCC 1864). The Church therefore reads verse 29 as a warning about a hardened heart and not as a sentence on those who are afraid. The strong man's house is read as the whole kingdom of Satan, which Christ has entered and is plundering through exorcisms, the forgiveness of sins and the cross (compare CCC 550). Here is the firm ground of the Church's unity: a house divided against itself cannot stand, and Jesus prays that his disciples be one (John 17:21).

qa: What is the “sin against the Holy Spirit”, and can I have committed it?

It is the sin of refusing, to the very end, the forgiveness that God offers. Mark explains it in verse 30: the scribes saw the Spirit's work in Jesus and called it unclean. The Catechism says that God's mercy has no limits, but that someone who deliberately refuses to repent shuts out forgiveness himself (CCC 1864). If you are afraid that you have committed it, that fear is a sign that your heart is still open to God. Go to the sacrament of Reconciliation and trust his mercy.
Does Ephesians say that the Jewish Law has been done away with?

No. The “law with its commandments and ordinances” in verse 15 refers to the observances that marked Israel off from the nations, which stood as a barrier to Gentiles being welcomed into God's people. Christ ends that barrier. He does not end God's covenant with Israel, which is never taken back, because “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839), nor the Law and the Prophets, which he came “not to abolish but to fulfill” (Matthew 5:17). Gentiles are welcomed into the covenant family, not into a replacement for it.
Did Jesus's family really think he was mad?

Mark reports what people were saying, and says that “those from beside him” went out to restrain him. It was a wide circle of relatives and neighbours who, like many others, did not yet understand him. Mark does not say that his mother believed it, and the Church honours her faith from the beginning. The story is a reminder that even those who love Jesus can fail to understand him at first, and that following him takes time.
rite: The Panchangam marks today as Family Day: pray for every family of the Church. Ephesians gives the Church her own name for herself: the household of God. In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost show the life of that household, gathered by the Spirit around the table of the Holy Qurbono. Before the anaphora the faithful exchange peace, and Christ's own gift, “he is our peace”, is put into their hands. The Catechism calls the Christian family a “domestic church” (CCC 2204): in every home the same Spirit is at work to make one body of those who were divided, and to make the house a place where Christ is at home.
study: Jesus says that a house divided against itself, “that house will not be able to stand”. Where is there a division in my family or parish that I could help to heal this week?
God dwells “with those who are contrite and humble in spirit”. What would it mean for me to be broken open before God, and not hardened?
Christ has broken down the dividing wall. Is there a wall of suspicion or old hurt that I keep building up?
It is Family Day. How can my family be a small household of God: at prayer, at table and in our care for one another?

lead: Both readings speak of being sent. In Luke the Lord sends out the seventy-two ahead of him, two by two, with no purse and no bag, to say “Peace to this house!” and to announce that the kingdom of God has come near. In Corinthians Paul defends the authority the Lord has given him, an authority “for building you up and not for tearing you down”. The Panchangam remembers the Seventy-two Heralds today, two days after the Dukrono of St Thomas. The key words are sent and building up.

r.h: Weapons that are not merely human
set: In chapters 10–13 of this letter Paul's tone becomes sharp. Some people in Corinth, whom he later calls “super-apostles” (11:5), were saying that he was bold on paper but weak in person. Many scholars think these chapters come from a separate letter written in a time of conflict, while others read the whole letter as a unity. Paul answers them, though with great reluctance and often with irony.
In today's verses he says that his struggle is not carried on by human means, defends the authority he has been given, and warns that he will be the same in person as he is in letters.
str: vv. 3–6: the weapons of his warfare are not merely human; they bring every thought captive to Christ.
vv. 7–8: they belong to Christ, and so does he; his authority is for building up.
vv. 9–11: his letters are strong and his presence is said to be weak; he will be the same in person.
kw: Fortified places. Paul uses the picture of a siege for the fight against false arguments and pride, which are like walls raised against the knowledge of God.
The word for building a house, used by Paul for the growth of the Church. Everything he does as an apostle is to be tested by whether it builds up or breaks down.
The mind and its plans. Paul does not want to destroy thought but to bring it to obey Christ, so that it serves the truth.
vv: the weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power to destroy strongholds.
The weapons are the truth, patience, prayer and love (compare 6:6–7; Ephesians 6:11–17). They look weak, but God's power works through them.
we take every thought captive to obey Christ.
The aim is not to win an argument but to lead the mind to Christ. Faith asks for the whole person, including the mind.
which the Lord gave for building you up and not for tearing you down,
This is the test of all authority in the Church. It is given by the Lord, for others, and for building up. He says this again at the end of the letter (13:10).
his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.
This is what his critics said. Paul does not deny that he is weak; he will say that the Lord's power is made perfect in weakness (12:9).
ch: The Church has always read these verses as a charter for her spiritual warfare. The Catechism teaches that prayer is a battle and that it needs faith, humility and perseverance (CCC 2725–2745, in substance). It also teaches that ministry in the Church is service, and the authority of those who lead is given for the good of the faithful (CCC 876, in substance).

set: Jesus has set his face towards Jerusalem (9:51). He sends messengers ahead of him to the places he will visit. Luke alone tells this mission of a larger group, after the earlier mission of the Twelve (9:1–6). The manuscripts differ on the number: some read seventy, others seventy-two. The Panchangam and the Malayalam Bible follow seventy-two. Many scholars see in either number a sign of all the nations of the world, since the list of nations in Genesis 10 has seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in many Greek witnesses.

The disciples go in pairs, to support one another and to give a trustworthy witness (compare Deuteronomy 19:15). They go ahead to the towns and places that Jesus himself intends to visit on his way to Jerusalem, to prepare for his coming. The warnings about towns that do not welcome them use the old language of the prophets, to show the seriousness of refusing the kingdom. They are not a judgment on the Jewish people as a whole.
str: vv. 1–2: Jesus appoints and sends them in pairs; the harvest is plentiful, the laborers few; pray to the Lord of the harvest.
vv. 3–7: like lambs among wolves, with nothing in their hands; into every house they say “Peace”; they stay in one house.
vv. 8–12: if welcomed, eat, heal and proclaim that the kingdom has come near; if not, the warning.
kw: The same root as “apostle”. The seventy-two are sent as the Twelve are, with Christ's own authority.
Workers in the field. The Lord of the harvest owns the field; the laborers serve. The first thing Jesus asks is that his people pray for more laborers.
The kingdom of God is close at hand: in the person of Jesus and in his messengers. The disciples do not bring their own message but his.
vv: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
Jesus's own answer to the need is prayer. Those who pray for laborers will find themselves sent.
I am sending you out like lambs into the midst of wolves.
The mission is not safe and is not a show of strength. The messengers have no weapons but peace.
Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house!’
The first word of the mission is peace, shalom, the same word as in the greeting of the risen Lord (John 20:19). The house comes first because the gospel is carried from home to home.
the laborer deserves to be paid.
Those who serve the gospel may receive their support from the people they serve. Paul quotes this saying in 1 Timothy 5:18.
The kingdom of God has come near to you.
The message is that God is near. The healing of the sick is the sign that this is true.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the whole Church is apostolic: she is “sent out” into the whole world, and all her members share in this mission (CCC 863, in substance). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, wrote that the harvest is plentiful but the laborers few, and that we must pray for more, and sadly he said that there were many to hear and few to preach (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance). The Church prays today for vocations, not only to the priesthood but to every way of serving the gospel.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today the Seventy-two Heralds, the disciples sent ahead of the Lord in Luke 10:1. Two days ago the Church kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, who was sent to India. Today the whole Church is reminded that every disciple, and not only the apostles, shares in the Lord's mission. Pray for those who preach the gospel in our parishes and in distant lands.
study: Jesus first asks his disciples to pray for laborers. Do I pray for vocations, and might I be one of the ones he is sending?
Paul's authority is “for building up and not for tearing down”. In my family, work or parish, do my words and decisions build up?

lead: The Panchangam gives for today the readings for the memory of a bishop or priest, and both speak of those who lead. Hebrews says, “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you,” and, in the same breath, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” In Matthew, Jesus asks who is the faithful and wise slave whom the master finds at work when he arrives. The key words are remember and faithful.

set: These are the closing exhortations of Hebrews, a long sermon by an author the Church does not name; it was early received into the Pauline tradition, though most scholars see a different hand from Paul's. It was written for Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to fall back, and it has shown over twelve chapters that Christ fulfils everything in the worship of the old covenant. Now it turns to the practical life of the community.

The passage moves from the leaders who first preached to the community, to Christ who does not change, to the altar and the sacrifice outside the camp, and finally to the sacrifices of praise and sharing that the Christian offers.
str: vv. 7–9: remember the leaders and imitate their faith; Jesus Christ is the same; do not be carried away by strange teachings.
vv. 10–14: we have an altar; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate; let us go out to him; here we have no lasting city.
vv. 15–16: through him let us offer a sacrifice of praise, and do not neglect to do good and to share.
kw: Those who “lead”: the bishops and elders of the community. The writer speaks of leaders who have died (v. 7) and then, in v. 17, of living ones whom the community is to obey.
The place of sacrifice. Hebrews says that we have an altar, and the Church has long understood this of the Eucharist, where the one sacrifice of Christ is made present.
The Greek word for “praise” is of the same family as thanksgiving. It recalls Psalm 50:14 and 116:17, and the Church's own word for the Eucharist, which means thanksgiving.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
The community is to look back at those who first gave them the faith, and to follow the same faith. A Church that forgets its founders has lost its roots.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
The leaders pass away, but Christ remains. Faith rests not on the leaders but on the one whom they preached.
We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.

The Church has understood this altar as the table of the Eucharist, from which the faithful eat, and which fulfils the sacrifices of the old covenant. Some scholars see here the cross itself; the two are not opposed, since the Eucharist makes present the sacrifice of the cross.
For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.
The Christian is a pilgrim. This is not a rejection of the world; it is a reminder that our true home is with God.
Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
The praise of the Church goes to the Father through Christ, in his name. It is the sacrifice of the lips: the prayer and thanksgiving of the Church.
Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
Praise and love of neighbour belong together. The offering of the lips is joined to the offering of the hands.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is a “sacrifice of praise”, naming Hebrews 13:15 among the many names of the Eucharist (CCC 1330), and that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (CCC 1367). The sacrifices of praise and of sharing that Hebrews describes flow from the Eucharist and are joined to it; they do not replace it. The Church also takes verse 7 as the call to honour the memory of her bishops and priests, which is why today's reading is used for the memory of a bishop or priest.

set: This parable ends the first part of Jesus's last great teaching in Matthew, the discourse on the Mount of Olives (chapters 24–25). Jesus has spoken of the destruction of the temple and the end of the age, and has said that no one knows the day or the hour (24:36). The command to “keep awake” (24:42–44) leads into this parable.
Luke has a similar parable (12:41–48), where Peter asks whom it is for. In Matthew the picture is of a steward put in charge of his master's household, to feed his fellow servants at the right time.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise slave?
vv. 46–47: the faithful one is found at work, and he is put in charge of everything.
vv. 48–51: the one who says “My master is delayed” and abuses his fellow servants is surprised and cast out.
kw: Two qualities together: reliable and sensible. A faithful person keeps his trust, and a wise one knows what to do with it.
The steward's task is to feed others. Authority in the household of God is for nourishing others, not for ruling over them.
The master seems to be late. The test is what the servant does when it seems that nothing is happening.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
Jesus asks a question to which everyone must give an answer by his life. Those who have charge of others, in a family, a parish or the Church, are asked the same.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The blessing is for the one at work when the master comes: not waiting idly but doing what he was given to do.
My master is delayed,
The danger is the thought that there is time. The wicked servant uses the delay as an excuse to do wrong. Jesus asks his followers to be as faithful in the long wait as in the moment.
ch: The Church reads the parable as a call to watchfulness and to responsible service. The Catechism teaches that since the Ascension the coming of Christ in glory is imminent, even though it is not for us to know the times and seasons (CCC 673), and the Church has often applied the parable especially to bishops and priests, who are put in charge of the household of God to give the faithful their food at the proper time, the word and the sacraments.

rite: Today the Panchangam keeps the memory of Pulikkottil Joseph Ramban and gives the readings for the memory of a bishop or priest. We remember him in prayer, as the Epistle asks: “Remember your leaders.” The Panchangam also remembers St Maria Goretti, a young girl of Italy who died in 1902, aged eleven, after defending her purity against an attack, and who forgave her attacker before she died. The Church honours her as a martyr and as a model of forgiveness.
study: The Epistle says, “Remember your leaders”, and asks us to imitate their faith. Who first taught me the faith, and how can I thank them and pray for them?
The faithful slave is found at work. What has the Master put in my charge, and am I doing it as if he might arrive today?

lead: Both readings today are about faithfulness to Christ when danger and false voices are near. In the Epistle Paul, who feels a “divine jealousy” for the Corinthians, fears that they will be led away from a sincere devotion to Christ and will accept “another Jesus”. In the Gospel Jesus decides to go back to Judea, where he was nearly stoned, because his friend Lazarus has died, and Thomas answers, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” The key words are devotion and going with Jesus.

set: In chapters 10–13 Paul defends his ministry against newcomers in Corinth who despise him and boast of their own gifts. Many scholars think these chapters come from a sharper letter that Paul wrote separately; others read 2 Corinthians as one letter. Either way they are among the most personal pages he wrote.

Here Paul begins what is called his “fool's speech” (11:1 to 12:13). He dislikes boasting, but he agrees to speak as a “fool” for a while, because the Corinthians are being impressed by people who boast. He calls these people, with some irony, “super-apostles” (11:5). They preached something different from what Paul had preached, and Paul fears for the faith of a church he had founded.
str: v. 1: Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with a little foolishness.
vv. 2–3: his jealousy is divine; he has betrothed them to one husband, and fears the serpent's deceit.
v. 4: they accept readily another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel.
vv. 5–6: Paul is not inferior to the “super-apostles”: untrained in speech, but not in knowledge.
kw: a jealousy of God, a divine jealousy

In the Old Testament God himself is “jealous” for his people: he wants their whole love, as a husband wants the love of his wife (Exodus 20:5; Hosea 2). Paul shares that jealousy: it is not envy but a burning care for the faith of those he loves.

Paul speaks like the friend of the bridegroom, who brings the bride to her husband. He presents the community to Christ as a bride. The image runs through Scripture, from the prophets (Isaiah 54:5) to Ephesians 5:25–27 and Revelation 19:7.
Paul does not mean that there are two Jesuses. He means that a different message, with a Jesus who is not the Crucified and Risen Lord whom Paul preached, is no gospel at all.
vv: I feel a divine jealousy for you,
The apostle is like a father who has given his daughter in marriage and cannot bear that she be wooed away. His love for the Corinthians is the love of a pastor.
But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning,

The serpent in Genesis 3 did not begin by denying God outright; he twisted God's word a little. Paul fears the same subtle way for the Corinthians: not open denial, but a gradual drifting away from simple devotion to Christ.
I may be untrained in speech, but not in knowledge;

Corinth admired fine oratory. Paul admits that he is no orator (compare 1 Corinthians 2:1–5), but the knowledge of Christ that he gives is true and deep. The truth of the message does not depend on the polish of the messenger.
ch: The Church sees in these verses the image of herself as the bride of Christ, a bride whom the Lord “loved and handed himself over for” to make her holy (CCC 796). The same image shows why unity in the faith matters: the bride must remain faithful to the one Lord and the one Gospel handed down. This is why the Church guards the Apostles' teaching in her creeds and in her liturgy. Paul's warning about “another Jesus” is a reminder that the Jesus we worship is the Jesus of the Scriptures and the apostolic Tradition, and not a figure shaped to our own taste.

r.h: Let us also go, that we may die with him
set: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, is ill, and his sisters have sent word to Jesus (11:3). Jesus had left Judea for the other side of the Jordan after the authorities there tried to stone him (10:31, 39–40). He stays two more days where he is (11:6), and then says to his disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”

John's word “the Jews” here means the authorities and those in Judea who were hostile to Jesus (compare 10:24, 31), not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus, his disciples, Mary, Martha and Lazarus are all Jews. The disciples' fear is real: Bethany lies close to Jerusalem (11:18), and the danger there is the danger that leads at last to the Cross.
str: vv. 7–8: Jesus proposes to return to Judea; the disciples remind him of the stoning.
vv. 9–10: the parable of day and night: walking in the light.
vv. 11–13: Lazarus has fallen asleep; the disciples misunderstand.
vv. 14–15: Jesus speaks plainly: Lazarus is dead; he is glad, for their sake, that he was not there.
v. 16: Thomas: “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”
kw: The Jewish day was counted from sunrise to sunset in twelve hours. Jesus uses an everyday truth: there is a time set for work, and no one can stop the day. His “hour” is in the Father's hands, and he walks in the light of the Father's will.

Sleep was a common word for death in the Old Testament and the New (Daniel 12:2; Matthew 27:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:13). For believers death is a sleep from which the Lord wakes us. Jesus uses the word in this deeper way; the disciples take it only of ordinary sleep.
This is the Greek translation of the Aramaic Tomā, “twin”. John gives both names (11:16; 20:24; 21:2). We do not know who the twin was.
vv: Are there not twelve hours of daylight?

Jesus is not afraid of the danger, because the Father has fixed the time. Whoever walks in God's will walks in daylight and does not stumble. The one who walks without that light, “in the night”, has no light in himself.
Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to awaken him.

“Our friend”: Jesus speaks of Lazarus with love and calls him a friend of the disciples as well. His going to Bethany is the going of a friend, and his waking of Lazarus is the sign of what he will do for all.
Let us also go, that we may die with him.

The sentence is ambiguous: “with him” may mean Lazarus or Jesus. The context, and the disciples' fear of the stoning, make most readers take it to mean Jesus. Thomas is loyal and ready to die, though he does not yet understand. At the Supper he will ask, “How can we know the way?” (14:5), and after the Resurrection he will confess, “My Lord and my God!” (20:28).
ch: The Church reads the raising of Lazarus as a sign of the resurrection that Christ promises to all who believe in him (CCC 994). Jesus is the Lord of life: he goes into the place of danger to give life to his friend, and in this he foretells his own death and rising. The Church has long heard in Thomas's words a model of loyalty: to follow Christ may mean to go where the danger is. According to tradition, Thomas later carried the Gospel as far as India and gave his life there for Christ. Because of Christ, Christian death is not an end but a passage; as Paul says, “For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain” (Philippians 1:21; CCC 1010).

qa: Why does Jesus say he is glad that he was not at Bethany?

He does not rejoice in Lazarus's death, and in 11:35 he weeps. He is glad “for your sake”, because the disciples will now see something greater than a healing: the raising of a man already dead, and so a sign of his power over death itself. The delay is not neglect. It is the love of one who has a greater gift in hand (11:4).
study: Paul fears that the Corinthians may be led away from a “sincere and pure devotion to Christ”. What most easily draws my own devotion away: noise, fashion, or an easier gospel?
Thomas says, “Let us also go.” Where is the Lord asking me to go with him, even though it is difficult?

lead: Today's readings are about what we carry and what we forget. In the Epistle Paul, an old man in prison, pleads for Onesimus, a runaway slave who has become his son in the faith, and promises to repay whatever Onesimus owes. In the Gospel the disciples cross the lake having forgotten to bring bread, and Jesus uses their worry about bread to warn them of another kind of yeast, the wrong teaching that can spread through a whole community. The key words are welcome and remember.

r.h: Welcome him as you would welcome me
set: Philemon is the shortest of Paul's letters and the only one addressed chiefly to a single person on a private matter. Paul writes from prison (vv. 1, 9, 13) to Philemon, a Christian of Colossae in whose house the church met (v. 2; compare Colossians 4:9). Philemon's slave Onesimus had left him, perhaps with some debt or loss to his master, and had met Paul, who brought him to faith (v. 10). Where Paul was in prison is not certain: Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have each been proposed.

Paul now sends Onesimus back, with this letter in his hand. He does not give an order. He asks as a friend, an “old man” (v. 9) and the one who brought Philemon himself to Christ (v. 19). Our verses are the heart of the request.
str: v. 17: “welcome him as you would welcome me.”
vv. 18–19: if Onesimus owes anything, Paul will repay it.
v. 20: “Refresh my heart in Christ.”
vv. 21–22: Paul trusts Philemon to do even more, and hopes to visit.
kw: The word means one who shares in something with another; it is of the same family as koinōnia, “communion”. Paul reminds Philemon that they share a common life in Christ, and that this is stronger than the law about a runaway slave.
A word from the business of the time, used for putting a debt on someone's account. Paul takes Onesimus's debt on himself, as Christ took on himself the debt of us all.
The Greek word splanchna means the inward parts, the seat of strong feeling. Paul asks Philemon to bring peace to his deepest affection, by receiving Onesimus well.
vv: So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.
Paul does not say “forgive him” or “spare him”. He says: receive him as you would receive me. Onesimus takes Paul's place at Philemon's door.
If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.
Paul does not pretend there is no wrong. He admits that Onesimus may owe something, and then pays for it himself. This is love that deals honestly with the loss.
I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it.
Paul takes the pen from the secretary and writes these words himself, like a signature on a promissory note. Having said this, he gently remembers that Philemon owes him his very self.
ch: The Church reads this letter as a small page of the Gospel: in Christ a slave becomes “a beloved brother” (v. 16). Paul does not here condemn the institution of slavery in so many words, but by teaching that a slave is a brother he plants the seed that later grew. The Church today teaches that slavery and the trade in human beings are a grave offence against human dignity (CCC 2414; Gaudium et Spes 27). The Fathers also saw in Paul's offer a picture of Christ: as Paul stands between Onesimus and his master, so Christ stands between us and the Father and takes our debt upon himself. An old tradition identifies Onesimus with the bishop of Ephesus of that name, but this is not certain.

set: The scene follows two controversies. The Pharisees and Sadducees have asked Jesus for a sign from heaven, and he has refused them and left (16:1–4). He and his disciples cross the Sea of Galilee to the other side, and the disciples discover they have no bread. Jesus then speaks to them of yeast.

The Pharisees and Sadducees were different groups, often in disagreement with each other. Matthew names them together to show that the teaching Jesus warns against is not one party's alone: it is any teaching that closes the heart to the signs God gives. The Pharisees were pious and respected, and Jesus often agrees with them (Matthew 23:2–3). The warning is about a spirit of testing God and demanding signs, which can arise anywhere.
str: v. 5: the disciples have forgotten bread.
v. 6: Jesus warns: beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
v. 7: the disciples think he is speaking of bread.
vv. 8–11: Jesus reproaches their little faith; he recalls the two feedings.
v. 12: they understand: the yeast is teaching.
kw: Yeast is a little thing that works silently until all the dough is changed. In the Bible it can mean good influence (Matthew 13:33) or bad (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here it is the bad: a teaching that spreads quietly.
Matthew uses this word of the disciples several times (6:30; 8:26; 14:31). It is not unbelief but weak, anxious trust. Jesus does not drive them away; he teaches them.

Matthew uses a different word for the baskets of the first feeding (14:20, kophinoi) and for the second (15:37, spyrides). The Gospel keeps the memory of what the disciples gathered, as proof that Jesus always gives more than enough.
vv: You of little faith, why are you talking about having no bread?
The disciples have just seen Jesus feed thousands twice from a few loaves. To worry about a lack of bread in his company is to forget who is with them.
Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?
Jesus calls them to remember. Faith in the Gospel is partly memory: remembering what the Lord has done and trusting that he will do it again.
he had not told them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
Matthew gives the answer to the riddle himself. “Teaching” (didachē) is the way of thinking passed from teacher to disciple. Yeast of bread feeds the body; false teaching can spoil the soul.
ch: The Church has always read the two feedings as signs of the Eucharist (CCC 1335): Jesus gives bread that does not run out. The Fathers also took the warning about yeast as a call to guard the purity of faith and of teaching. For this the Church holds the Apostles' teaching in her creeds and teaches that the faithful must recognize true teaching from false (CCC 85–88). Yet yeast is not evil in itself; Jesus says the Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast hidden in flour (Matthew 13:33). The yeast of the Gospel, quiet and strong, is what the Church is called to be in the world.

qa: Did Paul accept slavery, since he sends Onesimus back?

Paul never calls slavery good. In the world of his day it was part of the whole order of society, and he does not here attack it directly. But he speaks of Onesimus as “my child” (v. 10) and “a beloved brother” (v. 16), and he asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul himself. When a slave is a brother, the old order is already undone from within. The Church teaches today that slavery is a grave evil that offends the dignity of the human person (CCC 2414).
study: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “as you would welcome me”. Whom is the Lord asking me to welcome in this way?
Jesus says, “Do you not remember?” What has the Lord done for me that I must remember when I am anxious about tomorrow?

lead: Both readings today are about God's patience and what he looks for. In the Epistle Paul ends his long reflection on Israel and the nations (Romans 9–11) with a hymn: God has shut up all in disobedience only to show mercy to all, and his ways are beyond our searching out. In the Gospel, on the Monday of his last week, Jesus is hungry and finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit. The key words are mercy and fruit.

r.h: The depth of the riches and wisdom of God
set: Chapters 9 to 11 of Romans form one argument. Paul is deeply grieved that so many of his own people, Israel, have not accepted the Gospel (9:1–5), and he asks whether God's word has failed. His answer is no: God has not rejected his people (11:1), and “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Gentiles who now believe are like wild olive branches grafted into Israel's own olive tree (11:17–24).
Our passage comes at the end. It sums up the whole history in two short sentences about mercy, and then Paul, who has been reasoning at length, can reason no more and breaks into praise.
str: vv. 30–31: Gentiles received mercy when Israel was disobedient; Israel too will receive mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles.
v. 32: God has shut up all in disobedience, to show mercy to all.
v. 33: wonder at the depth of God.
vv. 34–35: two questions drawn from Isaiah and Job: who has known his mind, who has given him a gift first?
v. 36: all things are from him, through him and to him; glory for ever.
kw: The word at the centre of the passage, used four times in verses 30–32. The mercy of God is not earned and not ended: it goes first to one, then to the other, so that no one may boast.

A word for shutting a catch of fish inside a net. Paul uses it in Galatians 3:22 as well. It does not mean that God causes sin. It means that God allows all, Jew and Gentile, to find that none can rescue himself, so that all must receive salvation as a gift.
A hunter's word: the footprints of God's ways cannot be followed to the end. Human reasoning must give way to adoration.
vv: For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.

This is the summary of the whole letter. Everyone, Jew and Gentile, has need of mercy (compare 3:9–24), and God's purpose in the whole of history is mercy. It is not a statement that all will be saved without conversion, but of God's will that mercy be offered to everyone.
O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!
Paul can say no more by argument. “Riches” of God's generosity, “wisdom” of his plan and “knowledge” of the heart: the thought opens into worship.
For from him and through him and to him are all things.

Creation comes from God, is held through him, and goes to him as its goal. The Fathers heard in the three little words a trace of the Trinity; this is a reading in the Church's tradition and not the main sense of Paul's sentence.
ch: The Church reads these verses as her guide in speaking of the Jewish people.
