The Second Vatican Council, quoting Paul, teaches that the Jews “remain most dear to God” because of their ancestors, “for he does not repent of the gifts he makes nor of the calls he issues” (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The Church awaits, with hope, the day when “all Israel” and the nations together will be gathered into God's people (CCC 674). She also confesses that God's ways are unsearchable. The Catechism says that no one can fully know why God permitted evil, and that only at the end shall we see the whole of his plan (CCC 309–314). Paul's hymn is the best prayer for that: not an explanation, but adoration. The doxology in verse 36 is the shape of every Eucharistic prayer, which gives thanks to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

r.h: A fig tree with leaves and no fruit
set: This short passage is the first part of one of Mark's “sandwiches” (a story with another set inside it). Mark opens one story, inserts another, and closes the first, so that each explains the other. Here the cursing of the fig tree (11:12–14) is followed by Jesus' cleansing of the Temple (11:15–19), and then by the finding of the withered tree the next morning (11:20–25).
It is the Monday of Jesus' last week. On Sunday he rode into Jerusalem, looked about the Temple, and went out to Bethany (11:11). Now, on the way back into the city, he is hungry.
str: v. 12: Jesus is hungry on the road from Bethany.
v. 13: a tree in leaf in the distance; nothing but leaves; it was not the season for figs.
v. 14: “May no one ever eat fruit from you again”; the disciples hear it.
kw: Mark names Jesus' hunger in plain words. The Son of God is truly man, and he knows hunger as we do. Elsewhere he is asleep in the boat (4:38).

In the Old Testament the fig tree often stands for the people of God and for peace (Micah 4:4). Its failure to bear fruit is a figure used by the prophets to warn: “no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree” (Jeremiah 8:13; compare Hosea 9:10).
for it was not the season for figs

A hard clause. Mark says that figs were not in season; yet Jesus looks for fruit. Readers explain it in different ways, but all agree that Mark wants us to see that the story is an acted parable and not an event of nature.
vv: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry.
Bethany is the home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, where Jesus has found a resting place during these days. He leaves it to go to Jerusalem, where the Passion awaits.
he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

A tree in leaf seems to promise fruit; the leaves make a show. The tree makes a promise that it does not keep. Many readers have seen here the warning against religion that has the outward look of life but no fruit of love.
May no one ever eat fruit from you again.

Jesus does not show anger at a tree. His words are a prophet's sign, like those of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, who also acted out God's message. The next verses explain what the sign is about: the Temple, which should be “a house of prayer for all the nations” (11:17), but has become a place of trade.
ch: The Fathers did not see in this scene a cruelty to a tree, but a warning to every soul. St Augustine, preaching on the barren fig tree, took the leaves without fruit to be words without deeds (Sermon 89, in substance). The Church has also understood the sign as a call to the leaders and people of Jesus' own time, and to all who hold a sacred charge, to bear the fruit that God asks. It must never be read as a rejection of the Jewish people: the Temple, the prophets and the Scriptures are the Church's inheritance as well, and Jesus acts here as a prophet within Israel. The Church prays that every Christian may bear “much fruit” (John 15:8) and teaches that faith without love and good works is dead (James 2:17).

qa: Why did Jesus curse a tree that could not have had fruit yet?

The question is old, and Mark does not answer it directly. The key is that Mark tells the story as part of a pair, with the Temple cleansing between its two halves. Jesus is not angry at a tree; he is acting out a prophet's sign about a people and a Temple that were full of religious show but were not bearing the fruit God looked for. Some readers also note that in spring a fig tree in leaf may have early green fruit, so that a leafy tree promised something. Whichever explanation is taken, the teaching is the same: God looks for fruit.
study: Paul ends by praising God and not by explaining him. What in my own life can I only entrust to God's “unsearchable ways”?
A tree with leaves and no fruit. Where in my own life is there a show of religion without the fruit of love?

lead: Both readings today turn on a single question: has everything been lost? In the Epistle Paul asks whether Israel's stumbling means that Israel has fallen for good, and answers, “By no means!” The root is holy, and so are the branches. In the Gospel, coming down from the mountain of the Transfiguration, Jesus meets a father whose only son is held by an evil spirit that the disciples could not drive out, and he gives the boy back whole. The key words are holy root and given back.

set: These verses belong to the same argument of Romans 9–11 as yesterday's, but they come earlier in it. Paul has just said that God has not rejected his people (11:1–10): a remnant of Israel believes, as Paul himself does. Now he asks a second question: those who have not accepted Christ, have they fallen beyond recovery?

Paul writes to a church in Rome that includes many Gentile Christians, and he speaks to them directly (v. 13). He is afraid they may look down on the Jews who have not believed. He wants them to see that they have been brought into a story that began with Israel, and that they must not boast.
str: v. 11: Israel's stumbling is not a fall; through it salvation has come to the Gentiles.
v. 12: if their stumbling brings riches to the world, how much more their full inclusion.
vv. 13–14: Paul, apostle to the Gentiles, honours his ministry in the hope of saving some of his own people.
v. 15: their rejection has meant reconciliation for the world; their acceptance will be life from the dead.
v. 16: two images: the first fruits and the dough; the root and the branches.
kw: Paul distinguishes between the two. A man who stumbles may rise again; one who falls is down. Israel has stumbled, but the Lord who calls them has not let them go.

Paul takes a word from Deuteronomy 32:21, where God says he will make Israel jealous with “a foolish nation”. Here he hopes that the Gentiles' joy in Christ may awaken a holy longing in his own people to share it.
The word means filling up to the full measure. Paul looks to the day when Israel is included in its fulness, a day whose time is in God's hands.
The first of the dough or the harvest offered to God makes all the rest holy (Numbers 15:17–21). Paul sees in the patriarchs and in the first believers a first fruit that sanctifies the whole people.
vv: So I ask, have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means!
“By no means” is Paul's strong refusal of a thought that the Roman Christians may have held. God's call to Israel has not failed.
For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead!

“Their rejection” does not mean that God has cast them out, for in 11:1 Paul has said the opposite. It means the setting aside of those who have not yet accepted the Gospel, through which the Gospel has gone to the world. “Life from the dead” may refer to the general resurrection at the end, or to a great spiritual renewal; Catholic commentators have read it in both ways.
if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.

The holiness of the patriarchs passes to the whole people. The next verses (11:17–24) will take up the image of the olive tree and tell the Gentiles that they do not carry the root, but the root carries them.
ch: The Church gathers from these verses a teaching that she has repeated since the Second Vatican Council: God has not rejected his people, the Jews remain beloved because of the patriarchs, and the Church “cannot forget that she received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people with whom God, in his inexpressible mercy, concluded the Ancient Covenant” (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839–840). The Church does not replace Israel; she is grafted into the root that supports her. The Catechism teaches that the Church's own pilgrimage looks to the day when Israel will recognise the Messiah, and that this day is in the hands of God (CCC 674). Meanwhile the Church works and prays with respect for the Jewish people, and rejects every hatred and every persecution of them (Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: He gave him back to his father
set: The scene follows the Transfiguration. Peter, James and John had been with Jesus on the mountain, where they saw his glory and heard the Father's voice, “This is my Son, my Chosen; listen to him!” (9:35). “On the next day” they come down, and a crowd is waiting. The same incident is told in Matthew 17:14–21 and Mark 9:14–29; Luke tells it more briefly and puts the weight on the father and his only son.

Luke notes three times in his Gospel that someone's only child is in danger: Jairus's daughter (8:42), the widow's son at Nain (7:12) and here. In each case Jesus gives the child back to the parent. Luke is also fond of showing Jesus' compassion for the parent's sorrow.
str: v. 37: after the mountain, a great crowd meets Jesus.
vv. 38–40: the father begs for his only son; the disciples could not cast out the spirit.
v. 41: Jesus' lament and his command, “Bring your son here.”
v. 42: the spirit throws the boy down; Jesus rebukes it and gives the boy back to his father.
v. 43: all are astounded at the greatness of God.
kw: Luke uses the word for the daughter of Jairus, the widow's son and this boy. It is the word John later uses of Jesus himself, the Father's “only Son”. The father's grief points to the Father who will give his only Son.

Jesus' words recall Deuteronomy 32:5, where Moses speaks of a “crooked and perverse generation”. Moses had also come down from a mountain to find the people in failure (Exodus 32). Luke has placed Moses on the mountain of the Transfiguration (9:30), and the likeness is deliberate.

A rare word in the New Testament. Peter uses it of the glory of Christ seen on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:16). The people see in the healing the same majesty that the three disciples saw on the mountain.
vv: I beg you to look at my son; he is my only child.
The father does not give orders; he asks Jesus to “look upon” his son, with the word used elsewhere of God's gracious regard for a person in need. It is the prayer of every parent.
You faithless and perverse generation, how much longer must I be with you and bear with you?

This is a sigh and not an outburst. Jesus speaks to everyone present, the crowd and the disciples who could not heal, not as one outside Israel, but from within the long history of God's patience with his people; the words come from Moses' own song. The words are not a judgment on the Jewish people.
healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.

The same phrase is said of the widow's son at Nain, who was given back to his mother (7:15). Jesus does not only cure; he restores the child to his family. Salvation in Luke is always a gift that gives people back to one another.
And all were astounded at the greatness of God.
The people see more than a cure: they see God at work. Luke moves at once to the Passion prediction (9:44): the glory of God and the cross belong together.
ch: The Church sees here a sign of Jesus' victory over the evil one. The Catechism teaches that Jesus' exorcisms show that his kingdom is stronger than Satan's (CCC 550), and the Church carries on this ministry in Christ's name, with prudence, in the rite of exorcism (CCC 1673). The same paragraph says that the Church takes care, before an exorcism, to be sure that it is the presence of the Evil One and not an illness. The Church prays for the sick and for their families with equal care. The scene is also a lesson on discipleship: the disciples could not heal because they trusted their own strength; Mark records Jesus' answer, “This kind can come out only through prayer” (Mark 9:29). The Church returns to the Lord in prayer, above all in the Holy Qurbono, for those whom she cannot help herself.

qa: Was the boy suffering from epilepsy, or from an evil spirit?

The Gospels describe the sufferings of the boy carefully; Matthew uses a word that is often translated “epileptic” (17:15). The Gospel writers do not separate medicine from the spiritual struggle as we sometimes do. The Church today asks that sickness always be treated with care and with every medical help, and that exorcism be used only after the possibility of illness has been properly excluded (CCC 1673). What the passage teaches is that Jesus has authority over every power that harms people, whatever name we give it.
study: Paul says, “the root is holy”. How does my gratitude to the people through whom God first spoke show itself in the way I speak about them?
A father brings his only son to Jesus and begs. Whom do I bring to Jesus in prayer today, and do I trust that he “gives back” what he heals?

lead: On this Eighth Sunday after Pentecost the readings are about the God who speaks and the people who hear. In the evening Gospel (Mark 4:1–12) Jesus sits in a boat on the lake and teaches the crowd in parables, beginning with the word “Listen!” and ending, “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!” Job 23:1–7 gives the voice of a man in great suffering who longs to find God and put his case before him. Jeremiah 7:21–25 repeats the Lord's first command to his people, “Obey my voice, and I will be your God.” Isaiah 65:13–16 promises that God's servants will sing for gladness of heart and will bless themselves by “the God of faithfulness”. In 1 Peter 2:4–10 the believers, coming to Christ the living stone, are built up as a spiritual house, a chosen race, a royal priesthood.

We study three readings more closely. In Exodus 3 the Lord speaks to Moses from the bush, hears the cry of his people and gives his name. Hebrews 4:12–16 says that the word of God is living and active, and that we have a high priest who sympathizes with our weakness. In the Gospel (Mark 4:1–20) the sower scatters the word on four kinds of ground, and Jesus himself explains the parable. The key words today are word, hearing and fruit.

set: Moses, brought up in Pharaoh's house, had fled Egypt after killing an Egyptian, and for many years he had been a shepherd in Midian, tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro. One day he leads the sheep to Horeb, “the mountain of God”, and sees a bush that burns without being consumed (3:1–3). Our verses are the middle of the conversation that follows.

The Lord has already said that he has seen the misery of his people, heard their cry and “come down to deliver them” (3:7–8). Now he turns to Moses with the word “So come” (v. 10): the God who comes down sends a man. The scene is the call of Moses, and it shows the pattern of every call in Scripture: God sees, God sends, the human being objects, and God answers with his presence.
str: v. 9: God has heard the cry of Israel and seen the oppression.
v. 10: “I will send you to Pharaoh.”
v. 11: Moses' first objection: “Who am I?”
v. 12: God's answer, “I will be with you”, and a sign still in the future.
vv. 13–14: Moses asks for the name; God answers “I am who I am”.
v. 15: the name given in its covenant form: the Lord, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; “my name forever”.
kw: The cry of those who are wronged and have no helper. In the Bible God always hears it: it is first heard in Genesis 4:10, the blood of Abel, and again here, and later in the Psalms. The God of Israel is the God who listens to the cry of the oppressed.

The Hebrew can also be rendered “I will be who I will be”. It does not give a definition, but a promise and a presence: I am the God who is truly there, and who will be there for you. The Greek of the Septuagint (egō eimi ho ōn, “I am the one who is”) opened the way for later reflection on God as Being itself.

The word means that by which something is remembered and called upon. God gives a name that the people can use in prayer and worship for all generations. The Jewish people, out of reverence, do not pronounce the divine name but say Adonai, “Lord”; the Church follows this in her liturgy.
vv: I have also seen how the Egyptians oppress them.
God does not speak of oppression as a general idea. He has “seen”. For the Bible the Lord is a God who looks at human suffering and does not turn away.
Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh, and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?

The first of Moses' objections. The great prophets feel their smallness; so did Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:6). God does not tell Moses that he is great enough. He says, “I will be with you.” The call does not rest on the strength of the one called.
I will be with you;
The answer is a promise, and the sign follows: “you shall worship God on this mountain”. The sign will come only after the task is done. Faith goes first, and the sign comes afterwards.
I am who I am
The name is both open and hidden. God is not an object that we can grasp, and he is not a distant power. He makes himself known by being with his people.
This is my name forever, and this my title for all generations.

The God who is beyond all things is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whose faithfulness goes through the generations. Jesus draws on this very passage when he teaches that God “is God not of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12:26–27).
ch: The Catechism sees in the name given at the bush the heart of God's revelation to Israel: “I am who I am” says both that God is faithful, always with his people, and that he is the mystery beyond our grasp (CCC 205–213). The Church reads the passage as pointing towards Jesus Christ. In John's Gospel Jesus says, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58) and speaks of himself with the “I am” sayings (6:35; 8:12; 10:11; 11:25; 14:6). The Church also keeps the reverence of Israel for the divine name: in 2008 the Holy See asked that the name written in the Hebrew text as four letters not be pronounced in Catholic liturgy, but that the traditional “Lord” be used. The Fathers saw in Moses' reluctance a lesson in humility: God chooses those who know that they are not enough.

r.h: The word living and active, the high priest who sympathizes
set: The Letter to the Hebrews is a long sermon written for Jewish Christians who were growing weary and tempted to give up. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture, and the Syriac tradition reads it among the letters of Paul. The author does not give his name, and many scholars, ancient and modern, have thought that it was written by a disciple in Paul's circle; the Church has not defined the question.

Our verses end a long passage (3:7 to 4:13) built on Psalm 95: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” The wilderness generation heard God's voice and failed to enter his rest; the readers are urged not to do likewise. Verses 12–13 close that warning, and verses 14–16 open the next theme, Christ as high priest, which will fill the middle of the letter.
str: v. 12: the word of God is living and active, sharper than a two-edged sword.
v. 13: nothing in creation is hidden from God; we must give account to him.
v. 14: we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens; let us hold fast to our confession.
v. 15: he sympathizes with our weaknesses, tested as we are, yet without sin.
v. 16: let us approach the throne of grace with boldness.
kw: In the letter it first means what God has said in Scripture, which the writer has just been quoting. The Church has also heard in it the Word who is the Son, through whom God has spoken (Hebrews 1:2). Both senses live together.
The word of God is not a dead record. It does what it says: it works in those who hear it. The same word is used for the “power” by which God works (Philippians 2:13).

The title contains the central teaching of the letter: Jesus is the priest who offers himself and who stands in the presence of God for us. “Passed through the heavens” recalls the high priest of Israel passing through the veil on the Day of Atonement.
A word for plain, open speech before one's superiors. We may come to God's throne not trembling like slaves but with the confidence of children, because our priest has gone before us.
vv: Indeed, the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword,
The word of God cuts, but to heal, as a surgeon's knife does. It reaches the thoughts and intentions of the heart, where we cannot deceive even ourselves.
And before him no creature is hidden, but all are naked and laid bare to the eyes of the one to whom we must render an account.
The first effect of the word is the truth about ourselves. Before God we are seen as we are. The comfort comes in the next verses: the one before whom we stand is the high priest who understands.
For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses,
The Greek says that Jesus can “suffer with” us. He does not look at human weakness from a distance. He has entered into it.
Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness,
The POC reads “with hope” where the NRSV has “with boldness”, which is the sense of the Greek word. The throne of God is for those who come as the weak: there they receive mercy and grace to help.
ch: The Church teaches that God speaks to us in Scripture and that “the Christian faith is not a ‘religion of the book’” but of the Word of God, living and incarnate (CCC 108; Dei Verbum 21 says the Church venerates Scripture as she venerates the Body of the Lord). The Catechism cites verse 15 to show that Jesus was truly tempted yet without sin (CCC 540), and the Council of Chalcedon says he is “like us in all things except sin” (CCC 467). Because he is both God and man, he is the one mediator who can bring us near. In the Holy Qurbono the whole of the first part is a listening to the word, and the second part an approach to the throne of grace: the Church acts out the movement of these verses every Sunday.

r.h: A sower went out to sow
set: In Mark 3 Jesus' family and the scribes from Jerusalem have both misjudged him (3:20–35), and the question of who truly belongs to him has been raised: “Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.” Chapter 4 now gives Jesus' first long teaching in parables. The teaching takes place by the lake, with Jesus seated in a boat as a pulpit and the crowd on the shore.

The sower was a familiar sight in Galilee. The seed was scattered by hand over the field before it was ploughed in, so some fell on the footpath that crossed the field, some on rock just below the thin soil, some among thorn roots, and some on good earth. In verses 10–20 Jesus is alone with the Twelve and others and explains the parable. Many scholars think the explanation reflects the early Church's preaching; others hold that it comes from Jesus. In either case the Church receives it as the word of Christ.
str: vv. 1–2: the lake, the boat, the crowd; teaching in parables.
vv. 3–9: the parable of the sower: three failures and then the great harvest; “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
vv. 10–12: the disciples ask about the parables; “the secret of the kingdom of God”.
vv. 13–20: Jesus explains the parable: the four kinds of ground.
kw: The Greek word translates the Hebrew māšāl, which means a riddle, a proverb or a comparison. A parable is a picture from ordinary life that holds the hearer by its surprise and asks for an answer.

The “secret of the kingdom” is not a puzzle to be solved by the clever. It is the plan of God that is being revealed in Jesus and that can only be received. The disciples are given it, not because they are better but because they have come close to Jesus.
The word begins and ends the parable (4:3, 9). In the Bible to hear means to hear and obey. The whole chapter is a call to listen the right way (see also 4:23–24).
vv: Listen! A sower went out to sow.

The chapter opens with a command to listen. The Jews prayed each day, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4); Jesus opens his teaching with the same call to the same people, but now the word is the Kingdom.
Other seed fell into good soil and brought forth grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.

A harvest of thirty- or sixty-fold would be good. A hundredfold is an amazing harvest, the kind that Scripture describes as a sign of God's blessing (Genesis 26:12). The sower is not discouraged by the waste, because the end is a harvest beyond measure.
To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God,

The secret is a gift, “given”. Those who stay close to Jesus and ask him, as the disciples do, receive the meaning. “Those outside” are not a particular people, but anyone who stays at a distance and does not ask. The saying must never be read as speaking of the Jews as a people; the crowd, the disciples and the Twelve are all Jews.
Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand all the parables?
Jesus does not praise his disciples' understanding. In Mark they are often slow, and that is a comfort: those who follow Jesus do not have to be quick, but to keep coming back to ask.
The sower sows the word.
In the early Church “the word” means the Gospel (compare Acts 6:7). The sower is Christ, and after him all who preach in his name.
they hear the word and accept it and bear fruit,
The good soil is described by three actions: they hear, they accept, they bear fruit. The fruit is not for display; it is a life changed and a love that serves.
ch: The Church sees in this parable the pattern of all preaching and of every response to the word of God. The Catechism teaches that Jesus invites everyone to enter the Kingdom, and that to those who accept the word the secrets of the Kingdom are opened (CCC 546). The “fruit” of the word is the sanctity of the faithful and the growth of the Church (Lumen Gentium 5). The four kinds of ground have been understood by many preachers as four ways of hearing the word within one person, rather than four kinds of people; each of us has a path, a rock, a bush of thorns and some good earth. The Fathers and the liturgies pray that God will make the heart good soil. In the Syriac tradition the Gospel is carried and honoured in procession because it is the sowing of the Word.

qa: Why does Jesus say he speaks in parables “so that” people may not understand (Mark 4:12)?

The saying is hard, and Matthew softens it by writing “because” (Matthew 13:13). Jesus here quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, a passage that speaks of a people whose hearts have grown dull. Most Catholic commentators understand the verse not as God's wish to keep anyone away from the truth, but as a description of what happens when a word is heard without openness: the same parable that opens the mind of one who asks leaves another with nothing but a story. The parable is a call and an invitation. Mark himself shows that the disciples did not understand at first (4:13), and that the way is open to all who come to Jesus and ask.
Does “thirty, sixty and a hundredfold” mean that some Christians are more important than others?

No. The three numbers describe the fruitfulness of the word, not ranks among the faithful. All are called to the fullness of the Christian life and to holiness (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013), each according to his or her own path. The point of the parable is the wonder of the harvest: whatever God sows, in whatever measure it comes, is a gift beyond what the sower could have expected.
If Jesus was tempted “as we are”, could he have sinned?

The Church teaches that Jesus was truly tempted, and that the temptation was a real trial (CCC 540), and that he is “like us in all things except sin” (CCC 467). His sinlessness does not come from his being spared the struggle. It comes from the fact that he is the Son of God made man, whose human will was perfectly joined to the will of the Father. So when the Letter to the Hebrews says that he sympathizes with our weakness, it means that he has known the pressure of temptation from the inside, and has not yielded to it.
rite: In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost invite the Church to listen to the Lord who sends the Spirit and speaks to his people. The Holy Qurbono has two parts: first the table of the Word, with the readings and the Gospel, and then the table of the Body and Blood. Before the readings the deacon calls the people to stand and listen with care, and the Gospel is received standing, as Christ himself speaking. Today's three readings give a good picture of the Qurbono. In Exodus the Lord says, “I will be with you”; in Hebrews he is the high priest who stands for us at the throne of grace; in the Gospel he is the sower of the word. The faithful are asked to hear the word with the same reverence with which they receive the Sacrament.
study: God says to Moses, “I will be with you.” Where in my life do I need to hear this promise, and what task has God asked of me that I have thought too great for me?
Hebrews says the word of God lays bare “the thoughts and intentions of the heart”. When I hear the Scriptures at the Holy Qurbono, do I let the word look at me, or do I only look at it?
Which kind of ground is my heart this week: the footpath, the rock, the thorns or the good earth? What do I need to clear away?
The sower scatters his seed generously, with no fear of waste. How can I speak of Christ in my family or parish with the same generosity and hope?

lead: Both readings today are about the kind of ministry that is true. In the Epistle Paul defends himself by pointing to his unpaid, costly service to Corinth, and warns against those who disguise themselves as apostles of Christ. In the Gospel Jesus walks by the Sea of Galilee and calls two pairs of fishermen, who leave their nets and boat and follow him at once. The key words are serving and following.

set: This passage belongs to Paul's “fool's speech” (11:1 to 12:13), which began at 11:1 with the question of who may boast. Now Paul takes up a charge that seems to have been made against him in Corinth: that he did not accept support from the church there, and so showed that he did not really love them or that he was not a true apostle.

Paul had come to Corinth working at his trade as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:1–3). Other travelling preachers, who came later, took money from the community. Paul chose a different way, in order not to be a burden, and now has to defend that choice.
str: vv. 7–9: Paul preached without payment, supported by gifts from Macedonia.
vv. 10–11: he will keep to this; it is not for lack of love.
v. 12: he will go on in order to deny an opening to those who boast.
vv. 13–15: such people are false apostles, disguised as apostles of Christ, as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
kw: A strong word for what soldiers do in taking spoil. Paul uses it with bitter irony: other churches, above all Philippi (Philippians 4:15–16), supported him so that he could serve Corinth, and he speaks as if he had plundered them.

The word appears only here in the New Testament. Scholars discuss who these people were and what exactly they taught, and the Church does not decide the question. Paul's concern is clear: they preached themselves, not the crucified Christ.
to disguise, to change one's outward form
The same verb is used three times in verses 13–15. The danger is of something that looks like the truth and is not. A false teacher seldom looks false.
vv: I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.
Paul speaks sharply. The Corinthians, who were well off, had given him nothing, and poorer churches had supported him. He is not asking for repayment but showing the Corinthians what they are doing.
I did not burden anyone,

Paul chose not to claim a right that he held (1 Corinthians 9:12–15). This does not mean that preachers may not be supported: Paul himself says that “those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).
Because I do not love you? God knows I do!
Love is behind the whole defence. Paul does not wish to win an argument, but to win back the Corinthians.
Even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

The Old Testament does not say this in so many words; it reflects Jewish thought of Paul's time, in which Satan is a deceiver. The point for Paul is that great spiritual brilliance is not proof of truth. The test is Christ crucified and the teaching handed down.
ch: The Church holds two truths together here. First, she teaches that the faithful have a duty to provide for the needs of the Church, so that her ministers may give themselves to serving (CCC 2043), and that Paul himself defended the worker's right to a living. Second, she values the example of Paul, who for the sake of the Gospel asked nothing. The warning about disguise is a call for discernment: the Church asks the faithful to test what they hear against the faith handed down from the apostles, as John also says, “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits” (1 John 4:1). The Church also teaches that her ministers are servants and not masters of the faithful (Lumen Gentium 27).

r.h: Follow me, and I will make you fish for people
set: After his baptism and the temptation in the wilderness, Jesus leaves Nazareth and settles in Capernaum on the shore of the Sea of Galilee (4:12–13). Matthew sees in this the fulfilment of Isaiah: “the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light” (4:15–16). Jesus begins to proclaim, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near” (4:17). Our passage then tells of the first disciples.

The fishermen of Galilee were working people who owned boats and nets, and sometimes employed hired hands (compare Mark 1:20). Jesus does not call scholars or priests but those who work with their hands. The scene is brief and bare. Four men are called, and they follow.
str: v. 18: Jesus sees Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew, casting a net.
v. 19: the call: “Follow me”, and the promise: “I will make you fish for people”.
v. 20: they leave their nets at once and follow.
vv. 21–22: James and John, with their father Zebedee in the boat, are called, and follow.
kw: The words mean literally “come behind me”. In the world of the rabbis, students chose their teacher. Here the teacher chooses. To follow Jesus means to walk behind him, to go where he goes.

Jesus takes the work that they already know and gives it a new purpose. They will draw people out of the waters of death into the life of the kingdom. In the Bible the sea is often a symbol of chaos and danger, so to draw people out of it is to save them.
Matthew uses this word of the response to the call. It is not a calculation of gains and losses. The call is met with the whole life.
vv: Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.
The call has two parts: “follow me” and “I will make you”. Jesus does not ask them to be ready first. He promises that he himself will form them.
Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
They left what they were holding. For fishermen the nets were their livelihood. The text does not hide that this is a real cost; it simply shows the call as stronger than the cost.
Immediately they left the boat and their father, and followed him.

James and John leave the family business and their father. Jesus' call comes before even the family's claim, though not against it; in the same Gospel he teaches the commandment to honour father and mother (15:4). Zebedee is left, not rejected.
ch: The Catechism says that from the beginning Jesus associated his disciples with his own life, shared the mystery of the Kingdom with them and gave them a share in his mission, his joy and his sufferings (CCC 787). The Church sees in this call the beginning of every vocation, to priesthood, to religious life, to marriage and to every Christian service; each begins with the Lord's “Follow me” and is answered willingly. The Catechism adds that parents must respect and encourage the vocation of their children (CCC 2232). The calling of Peter and Andrew, James and John is also read as the beginning of the apostolic ministry, which continues in the bishops, the successors of the apostles. The Syro-Malankara Church, which holds that the apostle Thomas, according to tradition, brought the Gospel to India, remembers that the apostles' mission began with a call by the lake and went out to the ends of the earth.

qa: Did the fishermen abandon their families by following Jesus?

The Gospel does not say that they stopped loving their families. It says that the call of Christ came first. Peter's mother-in-law is later healed in Peter's own house in Capernaum (Matthew 8:14–15), so Peter still had a home. Zebedee is left in the boat with the hired men (Mark 1:20), who could carry on the business. The call asks for a change in what comes first, not for a rejection of those one loves. Such a call is also lived in marriage and family, with the Lord first.
study: Paul chose to give up what was his by right so that the Gospel would not be hindered. What have I the right to that I might give up for the sake of someone else's faith?
“Follow me, and I will make you.” What holds me back from answering Jesus' call, and what do I hold in my hands that he is asking me to put down?

lead: Today our calendar remembers Mar Sheelas, the Silas of the Acts of the Apostles, a trusted companion of Paul. The two readings fit his memory well. In the Epistle Paul says that no Christian lives or dies for himself or herself alone: “whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.” In the Gospel Jesus looks at the crowds with compassion, “like sheep without a shepherd”, and asks his disciples to pray for labourers. Silas was one of those labourers, and he was answered in his own life. The key words are belonging and harvest.

set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome from Corinth, around AD 57. In chapters 14 and 15 he speaks to a quarrel in the Roman community. Some believers (Paul calls them “the strong”) felt at liberty to eat anything and did not keep special days; others (“the weak”) ate only vegetables and kept certain days as holy (14:1–6). Each side was tempted to look down on the other. Paul does not say who is right on every point. He asks both sides to remember who they belong to.
Our verses give the reason. Whatever we do, we do for the Lord, because he is Lord of the living and the dead.
str: vv. 7–8: no one lives or dies for himself or herself; living or dying, we are the Lord’s.
v. 9: this is why Christ died and lived again: to be Lord of the dead and the living.
v. 10: so why judge or despise a brother or sister? All will stand before God.
vv. 11–12: a word of Scripture: every knee will bow and every tongue give praise to God; each of us will be accountable to God.
¶ Paul moves from belonging, to the Lord’s death and resurrection, to the call for gentleness among believers.
kw: Paul uses this word again and again in these verses. In verse 11 he quotes Isaiah 45:23, where the speaker is the Lord, the God of Israel, and he applies the promise to Christ, as he does in Philippians 2:10–11.

The main verb of chapter 14 (see vv. 3, 4, 5, 10, 13). Paul does not forbid every kind of judging; he forbids despising a brother or sister over matters on which believers may differ in good conscience.
A raised platform from which a magistrate gave his verdict. Paul himself was brought before the bēma of the governor Gallio at Corinth (Acts 18:12–17), the city from which he writes.
vv: We do not live to ourselves, and we do not die to ourselves.
The Christian is not a private owner of his or her life. The sentence is not a burden but a comfort: our life and our death both have a meaning outside ourselves.
whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.
This is one of the shortest summaries of Christian life in the New Testament. Nothing, not even death, takes us out of his hands.
For to this end Christ died and lived again, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
The cross and the resurrection are the ground of the Lordship of Christ. Because he has passed through death, no one who has died is beyond his care.
For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God.

Some later manuscripts read “of Christ” here, borrowing the words of 2 Corinthians 5:10. The NRSV and the POC follow the oldest reading, “of God”. The meaning is the same in the end, since the Father judges through the Son (John 5:22).
every knee shall bow to me

Paul takes the words from Isaiah 45:23, which the Greek Old Testament renders with “every tongue shall confess”. The prophet pictures the nations turning to the one God; Paul reminds us that this same God is the judge of all, so no believer is the judge of another.
ch: The Catechism uses verse 9 when it speaks of the Lordship of Christ: Christ died and rose “that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living” (Romans 14:9), and so his Lordship reaches the whole of history and the world of the dead (CCC 668). The Church also teaches that full right to pass final judgment on the works and hearts of men belongs to Christ as Redeemer of the world (CCC 679). That is why Paul’s lesson is humble: the judge is already chosen, and it is not we. In the Roman funeral lectionary these verses are among the readings offered, because they tell the mourning that the dead are still “the Lord’s”. We pray in the Holy Qurbono for the living and the dead for the same reason: they belong to him, and we belong to one another in him.

set: These verses close the first great section of Matthew’s Gospel. In chapters 5–7 Jesus teaches (the Sermon on the Mount); in chapters 8–9 he heals and forgives. Matthew now sums up both in a single sentence, almost word for word like the summary in 4:23, so that the two chapters are enclosed between matching verses: “teaching … proclaiming … curing”.

Then he lets us see Jesus’ heart. The crowds are not a problem to be managed; they are scattered people to be gathered. The next verse, 10:1, begins the sending of the Twelve, so the prayer of 9:38 is answered at once by the people who are asked to pray.
str: v. 35: Jesus in all the towns and villages: teaching, proclaiming, healing.
v. 36: his compassion for the crowds, harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd.
vv. 37–38: the harvest is great, the labourers few: pray to the Lord of the harvest.
kw: From splanchna, the inner organs, the “gut” where deep feeling is felt. The word is used in the Gospels almost only of Jesus, or of figures in his parables who show God’s mercy. It is a love that moves a person to act.

In the Old Testament the Lord is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34), and the leaders who fail the people are blamed as bad shepherds. Jesus sees the people as the flock that God himself promised to gather.
The verb literally means “to cast out, to thrust out”, and it is the same one used for driving out demons. The strong verb stresses how urgent the harvest is.
vv: Then Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and curing every disease and every sickness.
Jesus goes to the people where they are. His teaching and his healing belong together: word and deed show the same kingdom.
When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.

The picture comes from Numbers 27:17, where Moses asks that the community not be “like sheep without a shepherd”, and God gives him Joshua, whose name in Hebrew is the same as Jesus. Jesus is the shepherd for whom Moses prayed.
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few;
Jesus does not say that the field is poor. The need is large, and God’s work is ready; what is lacking is the hands.
therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
The harvest belongs to God, and so does the sending. Prayer is the first work of everyone who cares for the Church’s mission. And those who pray find that they are sometimes the answer.
ch: The Church has always taken verse 38 as the command to pray for vocations: priests, deacons, monks and nuns, catechists and missionaries, and the faithful who serve in the world. The Catechism teaches that all the baptized share in Christ’s mission as priest, prophet and king (CCC 783–786), so “laborers” include every disciple, each in his or her own way. Mar Sheelas, whom we remember today, shows what this means. He was one of the leaders chosen by the apostles and elders at Jerusalem to carry their letter to Antioch (Acts 15:22), and he went with Paul on his second journey. At Philippi, in prison with Paul at midnight, he was heard “praying and singing hymns to God” (Acts 16:25). He prayed for the harvest, and then he went into it.

qa: Paul says “do not judge”. Does that mean Christians may never say that something is wrong?

No. In the same letter Paul speaks plainly of sin, and in 1 Corinthians 5–6 he asks the community to correct grave wrongdoing. What he rules out here is contempt: looking down on a brother or sister over matters on which believers may differ in good conscience, such as foods or customs. The final judgment of a person’s heart belongs to God alone (CCC 679). To tell the truth about good and evil, with love, is not the same as despising a person.
study: Paul says that we are the Lord’s in life and in death. How would this change one worry that I carry today?

Jesus sees the crowd and feels compassion before he gives any instruction. How can I look at the people around me, at home and in the parish, in the same way? Whom shall I pray for by name today, as a labourer for the harvest?

lead: Both readings today ask where the power in a Christian life comes from. In Corinth the believers were boasting about their teachers, “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos”; Paul answers that teachers only plant and water, and that “God gave the growth.” In the Gospel two blind men follow Jesus and cry for mercy, and he answers “According to your faith let it be done to you.” In both, the work belongs to God, and our part is to serve him and trust him. The key words are growth and faith.

set: Paul founded the Church in Corinth about AD 50–51 and stayed there for a year and a half (Acts 18:1–11). Afterwards Apollos came, a learned Jew from Alexandria, powerful in the Scriptures and in speech (Acts 18:24–28). When Paul writes from Ephesus a few years later, the community has split into parties: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos”, “I belong to Cephas”, “I belong to Christ” (1:12). Some people compared the teachers like favourite athletes.
In 3:1–4 Paul has told them that this rivalry shows how immature they still are. In our verses he gives a picture from the farm to put the teachers in their place, and to put God in his.
str: v. 5: who are Apollos and Paul? Servants, each with the task the Lord gave.
v. 6: Paul planted, Apollos watered, God gave the growth.
v. 7: so the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing beside God.
v. 8: planter and waterer share one purpose, and each will receive a reward for his own labour.
v. 9: we are God’s servants working together; you are God’s field and God’s building.
kw: The word means one who serves at table or carries out a task for another. Paul and Apollos are not rival masters but servants. Our word “deacon” comes from it.
Paul uses it twice, in verses 6 and 7. In verse 6 the Greek tense (“God was giving the growth”) suggests that God keeps on giving it, long after the planting and the watering are done.
The Greek says literally “God’s fellow workers”. Paul does not make us equals of God; he says that God has chosen to carry out his work through human helpers, and that they labour together under him.
vv: What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each.
Paul asks “what”, not “who”. The question reduces the teachers to their role. Each has a task the Lord has assigned, and none of them has a task of his own choosing.
I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.

Paul’s own work was the first preaching and the founding of the community; the work of Apollos was to teach and strengthen it. Both were necessary, and both were small beside the living power that makes a seed grow.
So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
This is not an insult to Paul or Apollos. It releases them, and us, from the weight of thinking that the Church lives by the talent of its leaders.
The one who plants and the one who waters have a common purpose, and each will receive wages according to the labor of each.

The Greek says that planter and waterer “are one”. There is no ranking among them. The reward is real, and it is given to each “according to the labor”. The Church teaches that even this merit is itself a gift of God’s grace (CCC 2008).
you are God’s field, God’s building.
Two images follow. The field is the Church seen as a living, growing thing; the building, which Paul develops in 3:10–17, shows her as a house with one foundation, Jesus Christ.
ch: The Church has always taken these verses as a lesson on how she grows. The Catechism says that the Church is God’s “tilled field”, and that the building of God is built on Christ the cornerstone (CCC 755–756). The Second Vatican Council gathers images such as the field and the building to describe the Church (Lumen Gentium 6). Priests, parents and catechists take comfort from verse 6: they sow and water, but the growth is God’s work, and the harvest will be seen in his time. And because the planter and the waterer have “a common purpose”, rivalry among those who serve in a parish is a sign that something has been forgotten.

set: This is the second of a series of healings that Matthew gathers in chapters 8–9. It comes straight after the raising of the daughter of the synagogue leader and the healing of the woman with the flow of blood (9:18–26). Matthew likes pairs: he mentions two blind men here, and two again at Jericho (20:29–34), where Mark tells of one, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). The next story, a mute man who speaks, closes the series (9:32–34).

The cry of the blind men, “Son of David”, is the first time in Matthew that anyone other than the narrator gives Jesus this title in a healing story. It is the title of the promised king from David’s line, and the prophets said that in his time “the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isaiah 35:5).
str: v. 27: two blind men follow Jesus, crying for mercy to the Son of David.
v. 28: in the house Jesus asks, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” and they answer, “Yes, Lord.”
v. 29: he touches their eyes: “According to your faith let it be done to you.”
v. 30a: their eyes are opened.
vv. 30b–31: he orders silence, and they spread his fame throughout the district.
kw: The Greek of the cry is eleēson hēmas, “have mercy on us”, the same word as in the “Kyrie eleison” of the liturgy. It asks for help from someone who has the power and the kindness to give it.
Jesus puts faith before healing. He asks first whether they trust that he is able, and their “Yes, Lord” shows that they call him more than a healer: they call him “Lord”.
A strong verb, used of a stern warning (see also Mark 1:43). Jesus does not want his healing to be known as the work of a wonder-worker before people understand who he is and what road he will take.
vv: two blind men followed him, crying loudly, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”
The men cannot see, but they know who he is. The prayer is short and complete: a title that confesses his identity, and a request that trusts his kindness.
“Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.”
Jesus’ question is not a test of their cleverness. It invites them to say, out loud, what they hope for. Their answer is simple, and nothing more is demanded.
“According to your faith let it be done to you.”
These words do not make faith a kind of magic power that forces God’s hand. Jesus is the one who heals; their faith opens their hands to receive what only he can give.
Then Jesus sternly ordered them, “See that no one knows of this.”

In Matthew Jesus often asks for silence about his miracles (8:4; 12:16). He does not wish to be seen only as a wonder-worker, or as an earthly king, before the cross and the resurrection have been revealed.
But they went away and spread the news about him throughout that district.
They do not obey. It is hard to blame people who have just received their sight for speaking, and Matthew records it without a word of reproach. Good news cannot be locked in.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ miracles are signs that invite faith in him; to those who come to him in faith, he grants what they ask (CCC 548). The Fathers of the Church often read the healing of the blind as a picture of the enlightenment of Baptism, when the eyes of the heart are opened to see Christ (in substance). In the Syriac liturgy the cry of the two men continues in every Holy Qurbono, when the people sing again and again “Kurielaison”, “Lord, have mercy”. The cry is not only for physical sight. We ask that he open our eyes to see his will, and the neighbour in need.

qa: If healing comes “according to your faith”, does a person who is not healed lack faith?

No. Jesus’ words are a promise to these two men, not a rule that every sick person will be cured if his or her faith is strong enough. The Church teaches that God hears every prayer, but his answer is his own: sometimes healing, sometimes strength to carry the cross, and always his closeness. Saint Paul prayed three times that a “thorn” be taken from him, and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). To say that an illness shows a lack of faith would add suffering to the sick.
study: Paul says that he planted and Apollos watered, and that God gave the growth. Who has planted or watered in my faith, and for whom do I do so?
The two blind men were asked, “Do you believe?” What would I answer if Jesus asked me today, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?”, about the greatest need in my life?

lead: Today our Church remembers Archbishop Geevarghese Mar Ivanios, who died on 15 July 1953. He is the founder and first Metropolitan Archbishop of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, and the Holy Qurbono is offered today for the people. His cause for canonisation is in progress. The Lectionary gives a rich set of readings for a shepherd of the Church: the evening Gospel of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30), the sending of Moses with the promise “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:9–12), the death of Moses on Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:1–8), the joy of the Lord’s servants (Isaiah 65:13–16), and Paul’s farewell to the elders of Ephesus, “Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock” (Acts 20:25–35). The Panchangam also remembers Mar Kuriakose and Morth Yulithi (Sts Cyriacus and Julitta), the child and his mother who, according to tradition, were martyred at Tarsus.

We study three readings more closely. Ben Sira tells us to honour the Lord’s ministers and then to stretch out our hand to the poor, the mourning and the sick. The Letter to the Hebrews asks us to remember our leaders, to imitate their faith, and to follow Jesus “outside the camp”. In the Gospel the master puts one servant in charge of the household “to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time”, and blesses the servant who is found at work when he arrives. The key words are shepherd, faithfulness and the Lord who is the same.

r.h: Honour his ministers, and remember the poor
set: The Book of Sirach (also called Ecclesiasticus) was written in Hebrew by Jesus ben Sira, a teacher in Jerusalem, around 180 BC. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt, about 132 BC, as he tells us in his own preface. The Catholic and the Orthodox Churches receive it among the inspired books of the Old Testament; the Council of Trent listed it in the canon. It is a book of practical wisdom, as the Book of Proverbs is, and it shows what life in Israel looked like in the time before the Maccabees.

Chapter 7 gathers short sayings on how to treat other people: friends, family, servants, the priest and the poor. Our verses place two duties side by side: reverence for the Lord and his priests, and tenderness for the poor, the grieving and the sick. For Ben Sira, worship and mercy belong together.
str: vv. 29–31: fear the Lord and honour his priests; give them the portion that the Law commands.
v. 32: stretch out your hand to the poor.
vv. 33–35: be generous to the living, faithful to the dead, a companion to those who weep, a visitor to the sick.
v. 36: in all you do, remember the end of your life.
¶ The passage moves from the temple to the street, from the altar to the sickbed, and ends by reminding us that all of life is lived in view of its end.
kw: In the wisdom books “fear” is not terror but reverent awe before God: the beginning of wisdom. It is a love that knows who God is and who we are.

Verse 31 lists the portions that the Law gave to the priests of the Temple (see Leviticus 7:31–34; Numbers 18:8–20), who had no land of their own. The principle that God’s ministers should be supported by the community remains in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 9:13–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).
The Greek of verse 36 says literally “remember your last things”. From this word the Church’s teaching on death, judgment and the world to come is called eschatology.
vv: With all your soul fear the Lord, and revere his priests.
Reverence for God is placed first, and reverence for his ministers follows from it. The priest is honoured because of the Lord whom he serves, not for his own sake.
Fear the Lord and honor the priest, and give him his portion, as you have been commanded
Ben Sira says that the support of the ministers is not a favour but an obligation, “as you have been commanded”. Worship is not carried on without a community that provides for it.
Stretch out your hand to the poor, so that your blessing may be complete.
Blessing is “complete” only when it reaches the poor. Another verse of the book says that almsgiving atones for sin (3:30). The same Church that honours the priest is bound to the poor.
Do not avoid those who weep, but mourn with those who mourn.
Paul gives the same advice in other words: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Ben Sira asks for presence, not only advice.
In all you do, remember the end of your life, and then you will never sin.
Remembering death is not meant to frighten but to give things their weight. A person who knows how short life is, and who will receive it back from God, is slower to waste it on sin.
ch: The Church receives Sirach as a book that teaches how faith and daily conduct fit together. Its list of mercies (visiting the sick, comforting the grieving, burying the dead) stands behind the Church’s tradition of the works of mercy (CCC 2447). The call to remember the end of life agrees with the Catechism’s counsel to prepare ourselves for the hour of death by prayer and by the sacraments (CCC 1014). St Athanasius, in his Festal Letter of AD 367, recommended Sirach, with a few other books, for those newly joining the Church who wished to be instructed in the word of godliness (in substance). Today, with Mar Ivanios in mind, we see a bishop’s double duty in these verses: to honour the altar, and to stand beside the poor.

set: Hebrews is a long homily, which ends with a short letter-like conclusion. The writer does not name himself. The Eastern Churches, including the Syriac tradition, long attached the letter to Paul, while many scholars today think that it came from someone in Paul’s circle. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case. It was written to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to give up their faith under pressure, and the writer shows that Christ has fulfilled the worship that God gave to Israel.

Chapter 13 gives practical counsels: love one another, show hospitality, honour marriage, be content (13:1–6). Our passage then turns to the leaders of the community, and to the “altar” which Christians have.
str: v. 7: remember your leaders, who spoke God’s word to you; imitate their faith.
v. 8: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever.
v. 9: do not be carried away by strange teachings; let the heart be strengthened by grace.
vv. 10–12: we have an altar; the bodies of the sin-offerings were burned outside the camp, and Jesus suffered outside the city gate to sanctify the people with his own blood.
vv. 13–14: let us go to him outside the camp; here we have no lasting city.
vv. 15–16: through him let us offer a sacrifice of praise, and not neglect to do good and to share.
kw: Literally “those who lead”. Verse 7 speaks of leaders who have died or gone from the community (they “spoke the word of God to you”), and verse 17 of those who now lead and keep watch over souls. The Church is held together by a chain of witnesses who pass on one faith.

The word used in the Greek Old Testament for the altar of sacrifice. For many Fathers and for the liturgical tradition, “we have an altar” points to the altar of the Eucharist, where the sacrifice of Christ is made present.

An expression from the Greek Old Testament (Leviticus 7:12; Psalm 50:14, 23), which translates the Hebrew tôdâ, “thanksgiving”. The thank-offering was a meal of joy shared in the Temple. The Greek word for thanksgiving, eucharistia, gives the Eucharist its name.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
The writer asks the community to look at the “outcome” of their leaders’ lives, a lifetime of service ending in faithfulness. We are asked to imitate their faith, not their personalities.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

Leaders come and go, but Christ does not. The Church can change her language and her customs, but she cannot change her Lord. This sentence stands between the memory of the leaders and the warning against strange teaching.
We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.

The writer is speaking of the Old Covenant’s sin-offerings, which were burned outside the camp, so that the priests could not eat of them. He does not despise the Temple, which he elsewhere calls a shadow of heavenly things (8:5); he says that Christ’s sacrifice is the one to which those shadows pointed. The tradition of the Church reads “altar” as the Eucharistic altar.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.

In the sacrifice of the Day of Atonement the bodies of the sin-offerings were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). Jesus was crucified outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:20). The letter sees that as an act of love for all who stand outside.
For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.
This is the pilgrim’s verse. Christians love their homeland and serve it, but their final home is the city of God (Hebrews 11:10; Revelation 21).
let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
Praise flows from the one sacrifice of Christ, which we offer and receive at the altar. It does not replace that sacrifice; it is our response to it, and it goes out into the day.
Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
The writer adds to praise the work of mercy. A life of praise and a life of sharing are one sacrifice. They are the fruit of the grace of verse 9, which strengthens the heart.
ch: The Church sees in verse 15 a name for the Eucharist itself: the Catechism lists “sacrifice of praise” (Hebrews 13:15) among the names of the Holy Qurbono (CCC 1330), and teaches that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (CCC 1367). The “spiritual sacrifices” of praise and of mercy flow from the Eucharist and lead back to it; they do not replace it. Verse 7 shows the Church’s respect for her pastors, and verse 8 her conviction that the faith handed down is the faith of the living Christ.

set: These verses come from Jesus’ last great discourse in Matthew (chapters 24–25), given on the Mount of Olives in the last days before his Passion. After describing the signs of the end, Jesus says that no one knows the day or the hour (24:36), and then gives a series of short stories on being ready: Noah’s days, the householder and the thief, and our parable. In chapter 25 the discourse continues with the ten bridesmaids, the talents (the evening Gospel today) and the last judgment.

The story is about a servant whom the master leaves in charge of the household while he is away. The servant’s task is a very simple one: to see that those under his care have food “at the proper time”. The master’s delay is the test. Matthew’s readers, waiting for the Lord’s return, understood that this was their own situation.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise servant put in charge of the household?
vv. 46–47: blessed is the servant found at work; he will be given charge of all the master’s possessions.
vv. 48–49: the wicked servant: “My master is delayed”; he beats his fellow servants and eats and drinks with drunkards.
vv. 50–51: the master comes unexpectedly, and the servant is severely punished.
¶ A question opens the parable, and the two answers (the faithful and the unfaithful servant) show what is at stake.
kw: The same word is used of the man who builds his house on rock (7:24) and of the five bridesmaids who bring oil (25:2). Biblical wisdom is practical: to do the right thing in the right way because one expects the Lord.
The servant’s task is to feed the household. The picture suits shepherds of the Church: to give the people the word and the sacraments when they need them, not when it suits the shepherd.

The verb is the same one used in the parable of the bridesmaids, where the bridegroom “was delayed” (25:5). The temptation is to say, “My master is delayed” (24:48), and to behave as if there were no master.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
Jesus asks a question rather than makes a statement, and so each hearer must ask, “Am I that servant?” The trust given to the servant is a gift; the servant is a “slave” (doulos), not the owner.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The servant is not found anxious or idle. He is “at work”, doing quietly what he was asked to do. Faithfulness is not noisy; it is ordinary tasks done in the master’s name until he comes.
Truly I tell you, he will put that one in charge of all his possessions.
The reward is greater responsibility, a share in the master’s own concerns. In the Kingdom, faithfulness in a small trust opens into a greater one (see 25:21).
But if that wicked slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’
The sin begins in the heart, “says to himself”, before it appears in action. Whoever has stopped expecting the Lord soon begins to treat others badly.
the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour that he does not know.
The warning echoes 24:36 and 24:42–44. The point is not to calculate dates but to live every day as one who is accountable.
where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

These are Matthew’s words for the loss of the Kingdom (see 8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 25:30). The harsh image (“cut him in pieces”) is the language of warning. It shows how seriously Jesus takes the abuse of trust, above all by those who have charge of others.
ch: The Church has always read this parable especially of those who are put in charge in her household: bishops, priests, parents and teachers, and, in a wider way, every Christian, who must give an account of what he or she has been given (CCC 1036). The Catechism also reminds us that God wishes all to be saved, and that no one is predestined to damnation; a person must by his or her own choice turn away from God for that to happen (CCC 1037). The parable is therefore a call to vigilance, not a threat made to frighten us. In the Holy Qurbono we pray for our shepherds by name, because the faithfulness described here is hard and needs grace.

qa: Why do we read Sirach, which is not in every Bible?

The Catholic and Orthodox Churches have received Sirach as inspired Scripture since early times; the Greek Old Testament, which the apostolic Church used, contained it, and the Council of Trent confirmed it in the canon. Some Christian communities place it among books they read for edification but not for doctrine, and the Jewish canon does not include it, although Jewish teachers quoted from it for centuries. We read it with respect for all, and because the Church has found in it much wisdom for daily life.
Does “We have an altar” mean that Christians offer only a sacrifice of praise?

No. Hebrews says that Christ gave himself once for all (9:26–28; 10:10), and the Church believes that this one sacrifice is made present in the Holy Qurbono, so that we share in it (CCC 1367). The “sacrifice of praise” is the thanksgiving of the Eucharist (eucharistia means thanksgiving), and it spreads into the praise and mercy of our daily life. Our praise and our good works are offered through Christ; they depend on his sacrifice and do not replace it.
How can a loving master punish a servant so severely?

Jesus is describing the seriousness of unfaithfulness in strong, traditional language. The parable aims to wake the hearer, not to make God look cruel. The Church teaches that God does not will anyone’s ruin, and that the judgment follows a person’s own choice to refuse him (CCC 1037). The servant of the parable is not condemned for a small mistake but for beating his fellow servants and living in selfish indulgence, after he forgot that he had a master.
rite: Mar Ivanios was born in 1882 in Mavelikara, and was named Geevarghese. Before 1930 he was a teacher and a man of prayer, and he founded the Bethany Ashram and the Bethany Sisters, communities of prayer and service. On 20 September 1930 he and a few companions were received into full communion with the Catholic Church, asking to keep their own Syriac liturgy and the traditions of the Malankara Church. In 1932 the hierarchy of the new Church was established, and he became its first Metropolitan Archbishop, at Thiruvananthapuram. He died on 15 July 1953, and his tomb is at St Mary’s Cathedral, Pattom.

The day’s readings help us to read his life. The leaders of Hebrews leave a faith to be imitated; Jesus Christ is “the same yesterday and today and forever”. The servant of the Gospel gives food at the proper time: he cared for the poor and the sick, and he opened schools and homes. And Paul’s words in Acts 20:28, “Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock”, are the words of an apostle to the elders of Ephesus. We honour all who love and serve the Church in every part of the Body of Christ; and in the Qurbono we pray, as Christ prayed, “that they may all be one” (John 17:21).
study: Ben Sira asks us to honour the Lord’s ministers and also to stretch out a hand to the poor. Which of the two is easier for me, and what would the other ask of me this week?
The letter asks me to remember those who first spoke the word of God to me. Who were they? What have I never thanked them for?
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” What in my life, or in the life of the parish, changes constantly? Where do I need this fixed point?
The faithful servant is found “at work”. What is the ordinary task that the Lord has entrusted to me, and what does faithfulness in it look like today?

lead: Today our calendar remembers Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and the two readings look at the Mother of the Lord from two sides. Paul says that “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman”: God’s plan has a place in it for a mother. In Luke a woman in the crowd cries, “Blessed is the womb that bore you!” and Jesus answers, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” Read together, the two readings show that Mary is blessed twice, as the mother of the Son of God and as the first and best hearer of his word. The key words are fullness of time and blessed.

r.h: God sent his Son, born of a woman
set: Paul wrote to the Churches of Galatia, in the centre of what is now Turkey, to answer teachers who said that Gentile Christians must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people. His answer, from chapter 3 onwards, is that all who are baptized into Christ are children of Abraham and heirs of the promise (3:26–29).

In 4:1–3 Paul compares the time before Christ to the time of a child who is heir to a great estate but is no better than a slave until the day his father has set. Our verses describe that day. The key event is that “God sent his Son”, and the result is that we are no longer slaves but children.
str: v. 4: when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law.
v. 5: purpose: to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption.
v. 6: because we are children, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying “Abba! Father!”
v. 7: so no longer a slave but a child, and an heir through God.
kw: The time was “full” as a cup is full, ready to receive. God had prepared his people through the Law and the Prophets, and in his time he sent his Son.

Paul uses the same verb for the sending of the Son (v. 4) and for the sending of the Spirit of the Son (v. 6). The Father sends both, and the two sendings belong together: the Son in our flesh, the Spirit in our hearts.

A word from Greek and Roman law, for the full acceptance of a child as heir. Paul uses it for the new relationship that God gives us in Christ. We are not children by nature, as the Son is; we are made children by grace.

An Aramaic word from the language of Jesus, the word he used in his own prayer in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Paul keeps it in his Greek letters because it was treasured in the early community as the voice of the Spirit.
vv: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,

Paul’s phrase “born of a woman” says that the Son of God really became human, with a human mother. Paul does not name Mary here, but the Church has long seen her in these words. “Born under the law” means that Jesus was a Jew, who lived under the covenant given at Sinai.
in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.

The Son comes into our condition so that we may come into his. The Fathers of the Church said this in a brief saying, that the Son of God became man so that men might become sons of God (CCC 460, in substance).
And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit is the guarantee of sonship. Prayer is the sign: whoever says “Abba” in the Spirit is speaking as a child of the Father.
So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.
Paul says “you” in the singular. Each of us is addressed. We are not heirs because we earned it but “through God”, by his gift.
ch: The Catechism uses verse 4 to speak of the Incarnation (CCC 422) and of Mary’s place in it: God sent forth his Son, “born of a woman”, and for that wished the willing co-operation of a creature (CCC 488). The Second Vatican Council begins its teaching on Mary with these words of Paul (Lumen Gentium 52). The Church also teaches that Mary is truly the Mother of God, because the child she bore is the Son of God in person. In the Syriac tradition this is the faith expressed in the title Yoldath Aloho, “Mother of God”. For Paul and for the Church, what is said about Mary is said for the sake of the Son.

r.h: Blessed rather are those who hear
set: Jesus has just driven out a demon that made a man mute, and some say that he does it by the power of Beelzebul (11:14–26). In the midst of this argument a woman in the crowd cries out in praise. Only Luke tells the story.

The woman’s cry is a blessing for the mother of Jesus. It is the kind of blessing that belongs to Luke’s Gospel: Elizabeth had said to Mary, “Blessed is she who believed” (1:45), and Mary herself had said in the Magnificat that “all generations will call me blessed” (1:48).
str: v. 27: a woman in the crowd blesses the womb that bore Jesus and the breasts that nursed him.
v. 28: Jesus answers: blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it.
kw: The word the Bible uses for the person whom God has favoured (Psalm 1:1; Matthew 5:3–11). It is joy that comes from God, and not simply good fortune.

This small word can mean “no, rather” or “yes, and more”. Many interpreters hear the second meaning here: Jesus does not take back the woman’s blessing, but he completes it and says what makes it greatest.
To “keep” is to guard, as one guards a treasure. Luke uses closely related words of Mary, who “treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (2:19; see also 2:51).
vv: a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!”
The woman speaks from ordinary human admiration for a mother. Her words are warm and true, and Jesus does not rebuke her for them.
But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”

Jesus points to what makes his mother greatest. She was blessed because she heard the word of God, said “let it be with me according to your word” (1:38), and kept it to the cross. The beatitude is open to every disciple who does the same.
ch: The Church reads this Gospel as praise of Mary, not as a lesson against her. The Second Vatican Council quotes it: Jesus “declared blessed those who heard and kept the word of God, as she was faithfully doing” (Lumen Gentium 58). The Catechism calls Mary the most perfect example of the obedience of faith (CCC 148). St Augustine says in the same spirit that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (On Holy Virginity 3, in substance). Her motherhood and her faith are not two things: she became the mother because she believed, and she believed with all her being. In this we are invited to follow her.

qa: Does Jesus play down his mother here?

No. Luke has already shown Mary’s greatness (1:28–45), and the same Luke tells how she stood by her Son to the end (Acts 1:14). Jesus is not correcting the woman’s respect for his mother but saying what that respect should rest on. The Church honours Mary as Mother of God, and honours her most when it follows her example of hearing and keeping the word.
rite: The feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel comes from the Carmelite hermits who settled on Mount Carmel in the Holy Land in the twelfth century and built a chapel in honour of Mary. The same mountain is where the prophet Elijah called on the Lord (1 Kings 18), and we remember him on 20 July.
