In the Syriac tradition we call Mary Yoldath Aloho, the Mother of God, and the Fast of the Assumption (Shunoyo Nombu), which prepares us for her feast, begins on 1 August. Today’s readings ask us to love her as the first listener to the word.
study: God sent his Son “born of a woman”. What does it mean to me that the Son of God had a human mother?
Mary was blessed for hearing and keeping the word of God. Which word of God have I heard recently that I have not yet “kept”?

lead: Today the Panchangam remembers St Alexius of Rome; according to an old story, which first circulated in Syriac, he gave up wealth and a promising marriage to live as a poor pilgrim. The readings it gives are those of the weekday. In the Epistle Paul says that those who preach Christ are “the aroma of Christ to God”, a fragrance that reaches everyone and is received in different ways. In the Gospel Jesus stands up in the synagogue at Nazareth and reads the prophecy that tells what his mission is: good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind. Tomorrow is the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The key words are fragrance and anointing.

set: Paul’s relations with the Corinthians had gone through a painful time. After a hard visit he wrote them a severe letter (2:1–4) and sent it by Titus. He then left Ephesus for Troas, hoping to meet Titus there with news of how the letter was received. Titus was not at Troas, and Paul, though the Lord had opened “a door” for preaching, could not rest. He went on to Macedonia, where Titus met him with good news (7:5–7).

At that point Paul breaks off the story (2:13) and turns in thanksgiving to God: his anxiety has not stopped his mission. The verses that follow are some of the most vivid in the letter: a triumphal procession, the smell of incense, and a question that every minister of the word must ask.
str: vv. 12–13: Paul at Troas: a door opened for the gospel, but no peace of mind without Titus.
v. 14: thanks to God, who leads us in triumph in Christ and spreads the fragrance of knowing him everywhere.
vv. 15–16a: we are the aroma of Christ, for those being saved and those perishing: life to life, death to death.
v. 16b: “Who is sufficient for these things?”
v. 17: not peddlers of God’s word, but persons of sincerity sent from God.
kw: The word comes from the Roman triumph, in which the victorious general rode through the city with his army and captives, while incense burned along the road. Scholars are divided whether Paul sees himself as a captive led in God’s train or as a soldier sharing in the victory. In either case the victory is God’s.

The smell of the incense of the triumph meant honour to the victors and death to the captives. Paul uses the image of the Gospel: the same fragrance is received as life by some, and refused by others. In the Old Testament the smell of a sacrifice rising to God is a sign that it is accepted (Genesis 8:21; Exodus 29:18).

The word was used of retail traders, especially wine-sellers, who, as many explain, watered down their wine to make a bigger profit. Paul’s opponents, he implies, thin out the word of God for gain. He prefers to give it undiluted.
vv: When I came to Troas to proclaim the good news of Christ, a door was opened for me in the Lord;
A “door” is an opportunity. Paul recognises that the opening comes from the Lord, and in the next verse, that even an open door does not give him rest while the Corinthians are on his heart.
But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads in every place the fragrance that comes from knowing him.

Paul’s thanksgiving appears suddenly, after his anxiety. He says that the mission does not depend on his state of mind. “Through us” God spreads a fragrance: the apostle is the carrier and not the source.
For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing;

Paul says that the aroma is offered “to God”: whatever the response, the preaching is a pleasing offering. The one aroma has two effects, depending on how it is received. He says “being saved” and “perishing”, in the present: the outcome is still open.
Who is sufficient for these things?
This is the honest question of every priest, catechist and parent. Paul answers in 3:5: “our competence is from God”. The minister does not have to be enough; God is.
For we are not peddlers of God’s word like so many; but in Christ we speak as persons of sincerity, as persons sent from God and standing in his presence.
Sincerity means speaking and living “in his presence”. The gospel is God’s word, and no one may water it down to please a crowd or to gain from it.
ch: The Church has found in this passage a picture of her own ministry. Those who preach the gospel are sent by God and speak “in Christ”, and the fruit does not depend on them. The use of incense in worship, so dear to the West Syriac tradition, has long been understood as a sign of the prayer of the Church rising to God and of the fragrance of Christ spreading from the altar into the world. In this way the Holy Qurbono teaches what Paul teaches: those who receive Christ become, in their turn, a fragrance for others. The Church also remembers what Paul says in verse 16, “death to death” or “life to life”: the word of God is serious, and the response to it matters.

r.h: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me
set: This is the first public teaching of Jesus that Luke describes in detail, after his baptism, his temptation and his return to Galilee “filled with the power of the Spirit” (4:14). Luke places it at Nazareth, where Jesus grew up, and presents it as the programme of his whole ministry. He goes into the synagogue “as was his custom”, which tells us that Jesus prayed with his own people, and he stands up to read.

The passage he reads is from Isaiah 61:1–2, with a line from Isaiah 58:6 about the oppression that must end. It is a prophecy of the one who is anointed by the Spirit to announce God’s liberating favour. Jesus stops reading before the words “and the day of vengeance of our God”; and after he sits down he says, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21).
str: v. 16: Jesus at Nazareth on the sabbath, as was his custom, stands to read.
v. 17: the scroll of Isaiah is given to him, and he finds the place.
v. 18: the Spirit is upon him; he is anointed to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, and to set the oppressed at liberty.
v. 19: to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour.
kw: The verb behind “Christ”, “the Anointed One”. In Israel kings, priests and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil to show that God had set them apart. Jesus is anointed by the Spirit at his baptism, and at Nazareth he says that this anointing is for the poor.
The verb of the Gospel itself (euangelion). The first to hear the good news are the poor, as in Mary’s hymn, “he has filled the hungry with good things” (1:53).
The same word is used twice in verse 18, and elsewhere for the forgiveness of sins (Luke 24:47). The release that Jesus proclaims includes freedom from every chain: of debt, of illness, of sin.
the year of the Lord’s favour
An echo of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25), when slaves were released, debts cancelled and land returned. Jesus announces that the great Jubilee has begun in his own person.
vv: When he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, he went to the synagogue on the sabbath day, as was his custom.

Jesus prays in the synagogue every sabbath, as his own people do. The Church, which learned from Israel to gather for prayer and the reading of Scripture, keeps the same pattern in the Liturgy of the Word.
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.

The whole Trinity is in this sentence: the Spirit, the Lord, and the one who is sent. The “poor” are those who have nothing to rely on but God, and not only those without money. The Church has always read this as the programme of the mission of Christ and therefore of his Church.
He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to let the oppressed go free,
Luke’s Gospel will show these things in action: the healing of a man with a withered hand, a woman bent over for eighteen years, a blind beggar near Jericho. The release is real, in body and in soul.
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”

The “year of favour” is the time of God’s mercy, not a calendar year. Jesus says that this time has come, and that it is “today”. Every time the Gospel is read in the Holy Qurbono, the same “today” is heard again.
ch: The Catechism explains that “Christ” means “anointed”, and that Jesus is the Christ because he was anointed by the Spirit for the mission that this word signifies (CCC 436). The Church sees in today’s Gospel the programme of her own mission, which she carries out in Christ’s name and with a love for the poor that belongs to her constant tradition (CCC 2443–2446). The Church’s reading does not turn against Israel. The Prophet Isaiah is Israel’s prophet, and Jesus is reading Israel’s Scripture in Israel’s synagogue. The Catechism teaches that the Spirit who anointed the Lord at the Jordan is the same Spirit who anoints every Christian in Baptism and Chrismation (CCC 695).

qa: Why did Jesus stop reading in the middle of the sentence in Isaiah?

Isaiah 61:2 goes on, “and the day of vengeance of our God”. Jesus reads only “the year of the Lord’s favor” and then closes the scroll. Many interpreters see this as a sign of the character of his mission, which at this first coming is the proclamation of mercy. The day of judgment is not denied; it belongs to the end, when he comes again. The Church reads the passage as one of the clearest places where we see that the kingdom Jesus announces is first of all grace.
study: Paul asks, “Who is sufficient for these things?” and answers that competence comes from God. Where in my service do I feel inadequate, and how can I place it in God’s hands?
Jesus says that the scripture is fulfilled “today”. What word from the Gospel do I need to hear as spoken to me today, and for whose sake?

lead: On this Ninth Sunday after Pentecost the readings ask what a holy community looks like and how it lives among others. In the evening Gospel (Matthew 13:24–35) Jesus tells three parables of the kingdom: wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest, a mustard seed that becomes a tree, and yeast hidden in three measures of flour. Sirach 13:1–7 warns against the company of the proud and of the powerful who use others. Psalm 22:1–11 begins with the cry that Jesus took on the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”, and turns to trust: “In you our ancestors trusted”. Isaiah 24:1–5 describes the earth polluted by those who have “broken the everlasting covenant”. In Acts 28:11–22 Paul reaches Rome; when the brothers come out to meet him on the road, he “thanked God and took courage”, and he tells the leaders of the Jews that he is in chains “for the sake of the hope of Israel”.

We study three readings more closely. In Deuteronomy 4:1–6 Moses tells Israel that the statutes God has given them will show their wisdom to the nations. In 1 Corinthians 6:1–11 Paul tells a community of quarrelling believers that they have been “washed … sanctified … justified”, and so should live as people who are no longer what they were. In the Gospel (Luke 14:7–11) Jesus watches the guests choosing the best places, and tells them that “all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.” The key words are wisdom, holiness and humility.

r.h: This great nation is a wise and discerning people
set: Deuteronomy is Moses’ farewell, spoken on the plains of Moab, with the Jordan before the people and the promised land on the other side. In chapters 1–3 he recalls the forty years in the desert. In chapter 4 he turns from the past to the future with the words “So now, Israel”: what the people have seen of God’s works must now become obedience.

The word translated “statutes and ordinances” is the Law that God gave at Horeb (Sinai). To Moses these are not a burden but the people’s life: “so that you may live”. The chapter goes on to say that no other nation has a God so near, or laws so just (4:7–8).
str: v. 1: listen to the statutes and ordinances, so that you may live and take the land.
v. 2: add nothing, take nothing away; keep the commandments.
vv. 3–4: the lesson of Baal of Peor: those who followed him were destroyed; those who held fast to the Lord are alive today.
vv. 5–6: Moses teaches them to keep the commandments, which will show their wisdom to the peoples, who will say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and discerning people!”
¶ The passage moves from obedience, to the memory of a failure and a rescue, to witness before the nations.
kw: The command is the first word of the great prayer of Israel, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4). In the Bible to “hear” means to listen and to obey. Faith begins with listening.

A pair of words for God’s whole instruction: the decrees and the judgments that shape life in the covenant. The Hebrew word tôrâ, “Law”, means more precisely “teaching”, a father’s instruction to his children.
The verb used in Genesis 2:24 of a man who “clings” to his wife. Israel is called to cling to the Lord with a love that does not let go. Verse 4 contrasts them with those who left him for Baal.
Wisdom is the skill of living well, and understanding is the discernment to see what God is doing. Moses says that Israel’s observance of the Law will make these visible to other nations.
vv: So now, Israel, give heed to the statutes and ordinances that I am teaching you to observe, so that you may live
Obedience is the road to life. The Law is not given to make the people anxious but so that “you may live”, in the land and in the friendship of God.
You must neither add anything to what I command you nor take away anything from it

The command protects God’s word from human changes. Jesus, quoting Isaiah, warns against replacing God’s commandments with human traditions (Mark 7:8–9). The Church teaches that the deposit of faith is handed on whole: its understanding can grow, but its content cannot be altered (CCC 66, 94).
while those of you who held fast to the Lord your God are all alive today.
The reference is to Numbers 25, when many Israelites joined in the worship of the Baal of Peor and a plague broke out. Moses reminds the survivors that their life was a gift linked to their loyalty.
You must observe them diligently, for this will show your wisdom and discernment to the peoples
Israel’s mission is public. Its way of life is meant to be seen, and to draw the respect of other peoples. The nations do not see a conqueror but a community that has been taught by God.
Surely this great nation is a wise and discerning people!
This is the answer Moses hopes to hear from the nations. The prophets later foresee them coming to learn the Lord’s ways in Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3).
ch: The Church receives the Law of Moses as God’s gift to Israel and as a preparation for the Gospel: the Catechism calls the Old Law “the first stage of revealed Law”, which Christ did not abolish but fulfilled (CCC 1961–1964; Matthew 5:17). The wisdom that Moses speaks of finds its fullness in Christ, in whom “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). Paul’s teaching about the Church as a holy people among the nations, which we hear today in the Epistle, continues the same call: to live so that others may see God’s wisdom in the way we live.

r.h: You were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus about AD 54–55. After dealing with divisions (chapters 1–4) and a case of grave immorality (chapter 5), he turns to another scandal: believers were taking each other to court before the city’s magistrates. Corinth was a busy Roman colony where legal disputes were common, and the courts favoured the rich and well connected.

Paul does not ask whether the law of the land is wrong. He asks what it says about the community of the baptized if it cannot settle its own quarrels. His answer is short: the Church is a holy people, and the life of holiness has begun in Baptism.
str: vv. 1–3: the shame of seeking justice from unbelievers, when the saints will judge the world, and even angels.
vv. 4–6: surely a wise person in the community can decide between believers.
vv. 7–8: lawsuits among believers are already a defeat; better to be wronged than to wrong.
vv. 9–10: a warning: wrongdoers will not inherit the kingdom of God.
v. 11: “And this is what some of you used to be. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified.”
¶ The passage moves from a practical matter to the baptismal grace that makes the community holy.
kw: Paul’s name for all the baptized, not for a few heroes. It means those set apart for God. To be called “saints” is the community’s starting point, not its prize.

A word for washing the body, used here for Baptism (see also Acts 22:16; Titus 3:5). The Greek verb can be read as “you had yourselves washed”: they came to Baptism of their own will, and received the grace.
you were sanctified … you were justified
Paul puts holiness and justification together, in the order of Baptism. They are God’s gift, “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God”: the whole Trinity is at work.
vv: Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?
The Scriptures speak of the faithful sharing in God’s judgment (Daniel 7:22; Wisdom 3:7–8; Matthew 19:28). If they are destined for that, Paul asks, how can they be unable to settle a small quarrel?
I say this to your shame.
Paul speaks sharply because the matter is serious. He wants the Corinthians to see how far their conduct is from what they are.
In fact, to have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?

These words echo the teaching of Jesus about turning the other cheek (Matthew 5:39–40). Paul does not ask believers to be silent about justice; he asks them to put the bond of the community above the winning of every dispute.
Do you not know that wrongdoers will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived!

The list that follows names serious sins: idolatry, adultery, theft, greed, drunkenness, abuse, robbery, and sexual sins. Paul’s purpose is not to condemn certain people but to warn that these acts close the door of the kingdom unless the person turns from them. The Church teaches respect, compassion and sensitivity towards every person, and that every sign of unjust discrimination is to be avoided (CCC 2358).
And this is what some of you used to be. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.

This is the centre of the passage. “Used to be” says that no one is bound for ever by what he or she has been. Baptism washes, sanctifies and justifies, by the grace of the Trinity, and not by anything the Corinthians had done.
ch: The Catechism takes the three verbs of verse 11 as a description of Baptism: the sacrament is called “the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1215), and justification is the work of grace, which cleanses us from sin and gives us God’s own righteousness (CCC 1987). The Church has also always taught that those who fall into grave sin after Baptism may be reconciled by the sacrament of Penance, which the Fathers called “a laborious kind of baptism” (CCC 980, 1446). Paul’s warning in verses 9–10 and his comfort in verse 11 belong together: the warning is serious because the grace is real. The call to settle quarrels within the community has its source in Jesus’ own advice (Matthew 18:15–17), and the Church carries on this work of reconciliation and justice through her own tribunals and pastors.

r.h: Those who humble themselves will be exalted
set: Jesus has been invited to eat on the sabbath in the house of a leader of the Pharisees (14:1). The invitation shows that he continued to eat with Pharisees, as Luke tells in other places (7:36; 11:37). Before the meal he heals a man suffering from dropsy and asks whether it is lawful to heal on the sabbath (14:2–6). Then, as the guests find their places, Jesus notices how they choose the seats of honour, and tells them a parable.

The advice has a long root in Israel’s wisdom: “Do not put yourself forward in the king’s presence … for it is better to be told, ‘Come up here,’ than to be put lower in the presence of a noble” (Proverbs 25:6–7). Jesus takes the old counsel and deepens it. In the next verses (14:12–14) he turns from the guests to the host, and says to invite the poor and the sick.
str: v. 7: the occasion: Jesus sees how guests choose the places of honour.
vv. 8–9: do not take the best seat at a wedding feast; the host may ask you to give it up, and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest.
v. 10: take the lowest place, so that the host will say, “Friend, move up higher”, and you will be honoured.
v. 11: the saying: those who exalt themselves will be humbled, those who humble themselves will be exalted.
kw: At a formal Greek or Roman dinner, guests reclined on couches, and the places nearest the host were the most honoured. The word names the competition for status that is as old as the table.

The word comes from tapeinos, “low”. In the Bible humility is not self-contempt but the true place of a creature before God, and of a person before others. Mary says that God “has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant” (1:48).
The verb is used of God’s reversals in Scripture. In the passive form, “will be exalted”, Jesus speaks of God’s act without naming God: it is God who raises up and God who lowers (see 1:52).
vv: When he noticed how the guests chose the places of honor, he told them a parable.
Jesus watches. The parable begins from ordinary life, and its first lesson is to see ourselves as we are when we come to a gathering.
When you are invited by someone to a wedding banquet, do not sit down at the place of honor
The wedding banquet is a frequent image in the Gospels for the kingdom of God (Matthew 22:1–14). The lesson on the guests’ seats is also a lesson on how to take our place before God.
But when you are invited, go and sit down at the lowest place, so that when your host comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher’
Jesus does not tell us to pretend to be small in order to win a better place. The point is that the host decides, and that those who come humbly receive more than they expected.
For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.
This saying appears in several places (Luke 18:14; Matthew 23:12). The Lord’s own life fulfils it: he “humbled himself”, and God “highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:8–9).
ch: The Church teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer: “Man is a beggar before God” (CCC 2559). St Teresa of Avila said that humility is truth (in substance): to see ourselves as God sees us, and no greater or smaller. Many preachers have heard in this Gospel an invitation to the banquet of the Eucharist, where no one holds a reserved place by merit, and where the Lord himself serves (Luke 22:27). The Church also looks to Mary as the model of this humility, whom God lifted up (Luke 1:48, 52), and whose Assumption we shall soon celebrate.

qa: Does Paul say that Christians should never go to court?

No. Paul is speaking of lawsuits between believers before unbelieving judges, and of the scandal of a community that cannot reconcile itself. He asks that quarrels be settled within the Church, in the spirit of Jesus’ own advice (Matthew 18:15–17). The Church has its own law and tribunals, and it respects the just laws and courts of civil society. When justice requires it, to seek it is not a sin. The aim is that Christians should first look for reconciliation, as brothers and sisters, before looking for victory.
What does it mean that “the saints will judge the world”?

The Scriptures say that God’s people will share in his judgment at the end (Daniel 7:22; Wisdom 3:7–8; Matthew 19:28; Revelation 20:4). Paul’s argument is simple: if we are called to take part in the great judgment, we should be able to settle small disputes. The Church teaches that the final judgment belongs to Christ alone (CCC 679), and that we share in it by his grace, not by our own power.
Is it wrong to want to do well, or to accept honour?

No. Jesus does not condemn work well done or honour rightly given; he condemns the struggle for the first place, and the habit of measuring ourselves by it. True humility is truth: to know that every gift comes from God and to use it for others. The proud person is always afraid of being found out, and the humble person is at ease being himself or herself.
rite: In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost show the Church that the Holy Spirit has gathered, and teach her how to live. Today’s lesson is humility. We are the “saints” of Corinth, washed in Baptism, and we come to the table of the Lord as guests, not as owners. The Fast of the Assumption (Shunoyo Nombu) begins on 1 August, in preparation for the feast of the Assumption of Mary, Mother of God, on 15 August. The humble servant of the Lord, whom God has lifted up, is the model we are given. As we prepare for the fast, we may ask for the grace of her humility, so that we too may be found among those whom God exalts.
study: Moses says that Israel’s way of life should show wisdom to the nations. What does my family’s or parish’s way of life show to our neighbours?
Paul says, “And this is what some of you used to be.” What would it mean for me to live as one who has been washed, sanctified and justified, and not as the person I used to be?
Is there a quarrel in my family or parish in which I could choose to be wronged, for the sake of peace?
Where do I look for the best seat, in the home, in the parish, at work? What would the lowest place look like there?

lead: Both readings are about the difference between faith and a demand for proof. In 2 Thessalonians, Paul says that evil is already at work, and that those who are lost are lost because they “refused to love the truth”. In Mark, the Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign from heaven, and he sighs and refuses. Today the Panchangam also remembers Morth Makrina (St Macrina the Younger, who died in 379), sister of St Basil the Great and St Gregory of Nyssa. The key words are truth, sign and deception.

set: Some in Thessalonica had been shaken by a report, perhaps a letter claimed to come from Paul, that “the day of the Lord is already here” (2:2). The letter answers that certain things must happen first: the rebellion, and the revealing of “the lawless one” (2:3). Many scholars think 2 Thessalonians was written by a disciple in Paul's name, because it is so close to 1 Thessalonians and yet differs in its picture of the end; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case.

Our verses are among the hardest in the New Testament. Paul had told the Thessalonians more in person (2:5), so we are hearing half of a conversation. “The one who now restrains” the lawless one is not named. Early Christian writers made different guesses, often the Roman order of law and government; modern commentators have proposed others. The Church has never defined it, and we should not pretend to know.
str: v. 7: the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, held back for now.
v. 8: the lawless one will be revealed, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth.
vv. 9–10: his coming is by Satan's working, with lying signs and every wicked deception, for those who are perishing.
vv. 11–12: the reason: they refused to love the truth, and so a powerful delusion leads them on to condemnation.
kw: Literally “being without law”. In the Bible it is not only breaking a rule; it is a rebellion against God's order. Jesus uses the same word in Matthew 24:12, where lawlessness makes love grow cold.
A trick, an enticing lie. The evil Paul describes does not usually look like evil. It comes with signs and wonders, and it is believed by people who have stopped wanting the truth.
Not only agreeing with the truth but loving it, being drawn to it. The danger Paul names is not that people lack information. It is that they refuse to love what is true.
vv: For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work,

“Mystery” here means something hidden that is being worked out in history, as the mystery of God's plan is. Evil is not only a future event. It is already present, and Christians must not be surprised by it.
whom the Lord Jesus will destroy with the breath of his mouth, annihilating him by the manifestation of his coming.
The words recall Isaiah 11:4: “with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked”. The Lord does not need an army. His coming is enough, as light is enough to end darkness.
because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.
Salvation here is tied to loving the truth. The Church teaches that faith is the willing response of the whole person, and that no one can be forced to believe (CCC 160).
For this reason God sends them a powerful delusion, leading them to believe what is false,

Hebrew thought often says that God does what he allows to happen. The Church teaches that God is in no way the cause of moral evil, but permits it out of respect for freedom, and brings good out of it (CCC 311). The delusion follows a choice already made: first they refused the truth, and only then were they handed over to what they had chosen.
ch: The Catechism uses this passage when it speaks of the final trial that will shake the faith of many believers. It teaches that the Church will enter the glory of the kingdom only through this last Passover, and that the supreme religious deception is that of the Antichrist, a pseudo-messianism in which man glorifies himself in place of God (CCC 675–677). The Church has never named a person, a date or a nation as the lawless one, and she warns against every attempt to do so. The Christian answer is not fear but watchfulness: to love the truth, to hold to what we have been taught (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and to trust that the final word belongs to the Lord Jesus.

set: Mark has just told the feeding of the four thousand (8:1–9), and Jesus has landed at Dalmanutha (8:10). At once the Pharisees come to argue and ask for a sign from heaven. They had seen healings and the multiplication of bread; they wanted something beyond all that, a proof from the sky that would settle the question. Not every Pharisee was hostile to Jesus (compare Luke 13:31); Mark speaks here of those who came to argue with him.

After our verses, Jesus gets into the boat and speaks to his own disciples about “the yeast of the Pharisees” (8:14–21). Right after this scene Mark places the healing of the blind man at Bethsaida (8:22–26), then Peter's confession (8:27–30): sight and blindness run through the whole section.
str: v. 11: the Pharisees ask him for a sign from heaven, to test him.
v. 12: Jesus sighs deeply and refuses: no sign will be given to this generation.
v. 13: he leaves them and crosses to the other side.
kw: The same word is used of Satan's temptations in the wilderness (1:13). A demand for a sign meant to test God is a way of putting God on trial.
A strong word for a groan that rises from the depth of the heart. Mark often shows the feelings of Jesus: here sorrow, not anger.

In the Old Testament a faithless “generation” is the people who tested God in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:5; Psalm 95:10). Jesus is not condemning a nation but pointing to a way of resisting him that any generation can share.
vv: The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, asking him for a sign from heaven, to test him.
They already had signs in plenty. What they asked for was a sign made to their own measure. Faith that sets its own conditions is not yet faith.
And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, “Why does this generation ask for a sign?
The question is a real one, asked with sadness. Jesus grieves over hearts that will not open, as he wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41).
Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.

This is the form of an oath, a flat refusal. Matthew adds “except the sign of Jonah” (Matthew 16:4), pointing to the Resurrection. Mark leaves the refusal bare, so that the reader will think of the whole Gospel as the sign.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the miracles of Jesus are signs of the kingdom that invite belief. To those who come to him in faith he grants what they ask; but he refuses signs that satisfy curiosity or feed unbelief (CCC 547–548). The greatest sign is the Cross and Resurrection, and the Church keeps that sign in front of the world in every Holy Qurbono, where the Lord's death and rising are proclaimed until he comes. Faith asks no further proof than the one already given.

qa: Does this mean it is wrong to ask God for a sign or a proof?

Asking God for light is not wrong. Gideon, Hezekiah and others asked for signs, and God sometimes gave them. What Jesus refuses is a demand made to test him, by people who have already seen enough and decided not to believe. The Church invites us to ask humbly, to read the signs that God has already given in Scripture and in the life of the Church, and to say, with the father of the sick boy, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24).
rite: The Panchangam remembers today Morth Makrina, the elder sister of Basil and Gregory. Morth is the Syriac title for a holy woman, as Mor is for a holy man. Macrina taught her younger brothers, and turned the family estate in Pontus into a community of women and servants who lived in prayer and work. Her brother Gregory of Nyssa wrote her life soon after her death, and also a dialogue in which she is the teacher: On the Soul and the Resurrection. She loved the truth and helped others to love it, which is the opposite of what Paul describes in the epistle. We ask her prayers when we are tempted to demand proofs instead of trusting.
study: Paul says some people “refused to love the truth”. Is there a truth about my own life, or about my faith, that I have been avoiding?
The Pharisees asked for one more sign. Where do I ask God for one more proof before I will do what I already know he asks?

lead: Today the Panchangam remembers Elijah the Prophet, and the Gospel brings him to the mountain road: the disciples come down from the Transfiguration and ask why the scribes say Elijah must come first. Jesus answers that Elijah has come, and that the Son of Man must suffer. The epistle warns the Colossians not to let anyone judge them over food, festivals and sabbaths, because these were a shadow and the substance is Christ. The key words are shadow, substance and restore.

set: Paul writes to a church he has not visited (2:1), warning against teachers who offered a “philosophy” (2:8) of rules, visions and special practices. We do not know exactly what these teachers taught, only what Paul answers. Many scholars think Colossians was written by Paul himself while in prison; some think it was written by a disciple in his name. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case.

Paul does not say that the feasts and sabbaths of Israel were bad. God gave them, and they pointed ahead. His point is that nothing in them may be set up as a rival to Christ, and that the Colossians should not allow anyone to condemn them for not following a particular set of rules.
str: v. 16: let no one condemn you over food, drink, festivals, new moons or sabbaths.
v. 17: these are a shadow; the substance belongs to Christ.
v. 18: let no one disqualify you by false humility, worship of angels and visions.
v. 19: such people are not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body grows.
kw: A shadow is real and shows the shape of a body, but it is not the body. The same image is used in Hebrews 10:1 for the Law, which has “only a shadow of the good things to come”.
The word means a body. In verse 17 the real body that casts the shadow is Christ; in verse 19 the same word names the body that grows from the Head, the Church.
Christ is the head of the body, the Church (1:18). A body that is cut off from the head may keep every outward rule and still not live.
vv: Therefore do not let anyone condemn you in matters of food and drink or of observing festivals, new moons, or sabbaths.
These were the signs of Israel's covenant. Paul does not mock them. He tells Gentile believers that they are not to be judged by someone else's standard of observance.
These are only a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
The Old Testament is not cancelled. It was a true shadow, cast by the Christ who was coming. A shadow gives shape and direction, and we recognise the body because we have first seen the shadow.
and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, nourished and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows with a growth that is from God.
Life does not come from the joints and sinews by themselves. It flows from the Head through them. The Church lives by being joined to Christ, not by its own machinery.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Old Testament is an indispensable part of Scripture; its books are divinely inspired and keep their permanent value, because the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121). The Old Law is a preparation for the Gospel (CCC 1964). Reading Colossians in that light, the Church does not set Israel's worship against Christ's but sees it as pointing to him, and she asks that no one use these verses against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4). The words about angels are balanced by what the Church teaches elsewhere: angels watch over us and pray for us (CCC 336), but adoration belongs to God alone (CCC 2096).

set: Jesus and three disciples are coming down from the mountain of the Transfiguration (9:2–8), where Moses and Elijah appeared with him. He tells them to say nothing “until after the Son of Man had risen from the dead”, a phrase they cannot understand. Their question shows what was in their minds: the scribes taught that Elijah must come before the Messiah, as the prophet Malachi had promised (Malachi 4:5–6; 3:23–24 in the Hebrew).

Elijah had been taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11), and it was believed that he would return. The Gospels identify the one who came in his spirit and power as John the Baptist (Matthew 17:13; Luke 1:17). Mark has already dressed John like Elijah, in a garment of camel's hair with a leather belt (Mark 1:6; compare 2 Kings 1:8).
str: vv. 9–10: the command to silence, and the disciples' puzzlement about rising from the dead.
v. 11: the question: why do the scribes say Elijah must come first?
v. 12: the answer: Elijah comes first to restore all things; and the Son of Man must suffer.
v. 13: Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased.
kw: To set right again, to bring back to the original order. Malachi's promise was that Elijah would turn the hearts of fathers to their children and children to their fathers, and so heal what was broken.

Literally “counted as nothing”. A related word is used in the Greek of Psalm 22:6 for the righteous sufferer “despised by the people”. Jesus joins the glory of the Son of Man to the suffering of the righteous one.
Mark's way of saying that what happens is part of God's plan in Scripture, even the suffering. Nothing is out of control.
vv: So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead could mean.
The disciples knew that the righteous would rise at the end of time. What they could not grasp was that this Son of Man would rise before the end, after dying. They will not understand until Easter.
He said to them, “Elijah is indeed coming first to restore all things.
Jesus accepts the scribes' teaching and shows how it is fulfilled. The restoration of all things is not a restoration by force. It begins with a call to repentance.
But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written about him.”

“They did to him” points to the fate of John, whom Herod seized and put to death (Mark 6:17–29). Some think “as it is written” points back to the story of Elijah himself, hunted by Jezebel (1 Kings 19:2, 10). Both Elijah and John were persecuted by rulers who did not want to hear God's word.
ch: The Catechism teaches that John the Baptist is “Elijah who must come”, the forerunner of the Lord, in whom the fire of the Holy Spirit dwells (CCC 718). It also recalls Elijah as the prophet of fire who by his prayer brought fire from heaven on Mount Carmel (CCC 696) and as the father of the prophets, who teaches us to seek God's face (CCC 2581–2584). At the Transfiguration, Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, speak with Jesus about his departure, which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The cross and the glory are one story.

qa: Is John the Baptist Elijah returned?

No. John himself said he was not Elijah in person (John 1:21). Jesus says he is the Elijah who was promised, because John came, as the angel said, “with the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). He had the same mission and the same zeal, but he was a new prophet. The Church does not teach reincarnation.
study: The Colossians were told not to let anyone condemn them over rules. Do I ever judge others by the outward rules I keep, and forget the Head from whom all life comes?
The disciples did not understand what rising from the dead meant. What part of the Gospel do I hear again and again without really understanding it?

lead: Today the Panchangam remembers Daniel the Prophet, whose book speaks of a kingdom that begins as a small stone and fills the whole earth. In the Gospel Jesus tells two short parables of the kingdom: a mustard seed and a pinch of yeast, both small, hidden and growing. In the epistle Paul asks the strong in faith to bear with the weak, as Christ did. The key words are seed, yeast and steadfastness.

set: From 14:1 Paul has been speaking to a church divided over food and holy days. Some Christians in Rome, probably many of them Jewish believers, felt bound to avoid certain foods and keep certain days; others, probably many of them Gentiles, felt at liberty to eat anything. Paul names the first group “the weak” in faith and the second “the strong”, and he places himself with the strong (15:1; compare 14:14). Our verses are the conclusion of that long section.

He does not tell the strong to prove they are right. He asks them to carry the weaker, as Christ carried them. The whole passage ends with a prayer for harmony and for one voice of praise (15:5–6), so that the Roman Church, made up of different people, would worship together.
str: v. 1: the strong must bear with the weak and not please themselves.
v. 2: each should please the neighbour for the neighbour's good, to build up.
v. 3: the example of Christ, who bore insults.
v. 4: Scripture was written for our instruction, to give hope.
vv. 5–6: a prayer that, in harmony, they may glorify God with one voice.
kw: to bear, to put up with
The word can mean to carry a load. Paul asks the strong to take up the weight of the weak, as one carries another's burden (Galatians 6:2).
A building image that Paul loves. The test of an action in the Church is whether it builds up the neighbour (14:19; 1 Corinthians 14:26).
Patient endurance under pressure. It is a gift of “the God of steadfastness and encouragement” (15:5), and Scripture itself feeds it.
vv: We who are strong ought to put up with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Strength in faith is for service. It is not a reason to look down on others. A strong conscience that has no patience for a weaker one has forgotten what it was given for.
For Christ did not please himself; but, as it is written, “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”

Paul quotes Psalm 69:9; the New Testament often applies Psalm 69 to the Passion (John 2:17; 15:25; 19:28–29). Christ took on himself the insults that were meant for God. Our patience with the weak is a small share in that.
For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, so that by steadfastness and by the encouragement of the scriptures we might have hope.

“Former days” means the Old Testament, which Paul reads as written for Christians too. Hope is not a feeling that things will turn out well. It is built from steadfastness and from the comfort that Scripture gives.
so that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The goal of the whole argument is worship. Differences over food and days must not break the one voice that rises in the Holy Qurbono.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that Sacred Scripture is the food of the soul, “the pure and perennial source of spiritual life”, and that the Church should give her children easy access to it (Dei Verbum 21–22; CCC 131–133). Paul's words in verse 4 are one of the Church's oldest statements that the whole Bible is meant for our instruction. Today's verses also speak to every parish. The Church teaches that the variety of gifts and peoples within her does not oppose her unity (CCC 814), and that charity is what holds it together. The strong are asked to give way for the sake of the weak, and the weak are not asked to be silent, but to be loved.

r.h: The kingdom small, hidden and growing
set: Chapter 13 gathers the parables of the kingdom. Jesus has told the Sower, the Weeds and the Wheat, and now tells the Mustard Seed and the Yeast, two short parables that go together as a pair, one with a man in a field, the other with a woman in a kitchen. Matthew explains why Jesus teaches in parables (13:10–17, 34–35): the parables reveal the kingdom to those who are open to hear and hide it from those who are not.

The mustard plant of Palestine is a garden herb that can grow to the height of a small tree. Jesus speaks as people spoke: it was the smallest seed that a farmer would sow in his field, and he is not giving a lesson in botany. The picture of a tree where “the birds of the air” nest recalls Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4:12, where a great tree stands for a mighty kingdom sheltering the nations. There the tree is an empire; here it starts from the smallest seed.
str: vv. 31–32: the mustard seed: the smallest seed becomes the largest plant, and birds nest in it.
v. 33: the yeast: a woman hides it in three measures of flour until it is all leavened.
vv. 34–35: Jesus speaks to the crowds only in parables, as the psalmist said: things hidden since the foundation of the world.
kw: A tiny seed, used in Jewish speech for anything very small. Jesus also uses it for faith that can move mountains (Matthew 17:20).
Usually in the Bible a sign of corruption that spreads (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Mark 8:15). Jesus surprises his hearers by using it for the kingdom, which also works from within and cannot be stopped.
Literally “hid in”. The woman does not stir the yeast in sight; she hides it in the flour. The kingdom works quietly, from the inside.
vv: The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in his field;
The kingdom does not begin with power. It begins with a Child in Bethlehem, a small group of disciples, a Cross. Jesus invites us to trust that what is small in God's hand will grow.
it is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree,
The contrast is the point: from the smallest to the greatest. The later growth of the Church out of a handful of apostles, as Matthew's first readers could see, is a living illustration.
The kingdom of heaven is like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.

Three measures is a very large batch, more than twenty litres of flour. The little yeast works until the whole is changed. The kingdom is not only something to be reached at the end of time; it is already at work in the world.
I will open my mouth to speak in parables; I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world.
Matthew quotes Psalm 78:2, the psalm that tells Israel's story from Egypt to David. Jesus is the teacher who now tells what has been hidden since the beginning.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church “receives the mission to proclaim and to establish among all peoples the kingdom of Christ and of God, and she is, on earth, the seed and the beginning of that kingdom” (Lumen Gentium 5; CCC 764). Many of the Fathers read the mustard seed as Christ himself, buried in the earth and rising to become a tree (in substance), and the yeast as the Gospel quietly at work in the world. The kingdom is not a worldly power that wins by force. It spreads by the Word, by prayer, by love hidden in daily life, and by holy lives of people nobody noticed.

qa: Is the mustard seed really the smallest of all seeds?

In botany it is not; orchid seeds are smaller. Jesus uses the way ordinary people spoke. For the farmers of Galilee, the mustard seed was the smallest seed they sowed, and the proverb “as small as a mustard seed” was familiar. The point of the parable is the contrast between a tiny beginning and a surprising end, not a lesson in botany.
study: Paul asks the strong to carry the weak. Whom has God given me strength to carry, in my family or parish, and do I carry them gladly?
Both parables are about small, hidden things that grow. What small thing, a prayer or a kind act, is God asking me to plant today without seeing the result?

lead: Today the Panchangam remembers St Mary Magdalene, and both readings fit her well. Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation and that God has given us the ministry of reconciliation, to be ambassadors for Christ. In the Gospel, Mary stands weeping at the empty tomb, is called by name by the risen Lord, and is sent to tell the disciples: “I have seen the Lord.” The key words are new creation, reconciliation and sent.

r.h: A new creation and a ministry of reconciliation
set: Second Corinthians is Paul's most personal letter. He has been defending his ministry against those in Corinth who doubted him, and in chapter 5 he explains what drives him: “the love of Christ urges us on” (5:14). Christ died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves but for him who died and was raised (5:15). From that moment, Paul says, he no longer looks at people “from a human point of view” (5:16).
Our verses are the heart of that explanation. Paul speaks of what God has done, which he calls reconciliation, and then of what God asks of those who have received it.
str: v. 17: anyone in Christ is a new creation.
v. 18: all this is from God, who reconciled us through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.
v. 19: in Christ God was reconciling the world, not counting trespasses, and entrusted the message to us.
v. 20: we are ambassadors for Christ; God appeals through us: be reconciled.
v. 21: God made the sinless one to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God.
kw: The words echo Isaiah 43:18–19 and 65:17, where God promises to do a new thing and to create new heavens and a new earth. In Christ that creation has already begun in each baptized person (Galatians 6:15).
Restoring a relationship that was broken. Paul uses it only of what God does: God reconciles us. We do not first reconcile God; God's love comes first.
The word used for an envoy who speaks in the name of a king. An ambassador does not speak for himself. When the apostles speak, God himself is making his appeal.
vv: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
Being in Christ, which Baptism makes real, is not a small improvement. The old life with its slavery to sin has ended, and a new life begins that will be complete only at the resurrection.
in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting the message of reconciliation to us.

God does not wait until we repent before he begins to love us. In Christ he comes to us first, and then he asks us to carry the message. The message is a gift entrusted to people, not an idea they own.
So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us;
An ambassador lives in a foreign land for the sake of a home country. Christians are sent into the world with the authority of the one who sends them.
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Christ was without sin and was treated as sin for us. Many interpreters hear a reference to the sin-offering of the Law, in which the Greek word for “sin” can also mean the offering for sin. The exchange is the Gospel in a sentence: he takes our place, and we are made righteous in him.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 21 when it teaches that God made Christ “to be sin” for us, to reconcile us to himself, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (CCC 602). It also teaches that Christ entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to the apostles, and that in the Church this ministry is exercised in the sacrament of forgiveness (CCC 1442). Paul's word “ambassadors” is a reminder that priests who forgive sins in the name of Christ are not acting by their own right, and that all the baptized share in this task when they forgive and seek peace with their neighbours.

set: John tells the discovery of the empty tomb in 20:1–10: Mary comes early on the first day of the week, finds the stone rolled away and runs to Peter and the Beloved Disciple. They run to the tomb, see the grave clothes and believe, but leave. Our reading joins 20:1–2 to 20:11–18, which tells what happened to Mary after they had gone. The Gospel puts her alone with the Risen Lord, and the scene is set in a garden (19:41), recalling the first garden of Genesis.

Mary Magdalene, that is, Mary from Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, is named in all four Gospels. Luke says that seven demons had gone out of her (Luke 8:2) and that she followed Jesus and helped to provide for him and his disciples out of her own resources. She stood by the Cross (John 19:25) and watched the burial (Mark 15:47). She is not the sinful woman of Luke 7:36–50, and she is not Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. The Gospels never say so. Both identifications were made in the West by later preachers, and the Church does not teach them.
str: vv. 1–2: Mary comes while it is dark, finds the stone removed and tells Peter and the other disciple.
vv. 11–13: Mary weeps at the tomb; two angels ask why she weeps.
vv. 14–15: Jesus stands there; she thinks he is the gardener.
v. 16: he calls her name: “Mary!” and she answers “Rabbouni!”
vv. 17–18: he sends her to his brothers; she announces: “I have seen the Lord.”
kw: Jesus says just one word and she knows him. He had said, “the sheep hear his voice. He calls his own sheep by name” (10:3). The Risen Lord calls his own by name.
An Aramaic word, a little more personal than rabbi. John translates it as “Teacher”. Mary answers with the old relationship, and Jesus must teach her that things are now different.
do not hold on to me
Literally “stop clinging to me”. Mary is told not to hold the old way of being with him, because he is going to the Father; a new and deeper presence will be given through the Spirit.
vv: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.
“The first day of the week” is the day of the new creation; “still dark” is Mary's grief and also the darkness that the Light is about to end. Her love brought her before anyone else.
Jesus said to her, “Mary!” She turned and said to him in Hebrew, “Rabbouni!” (which means Teacher).
The whole Gospel turns on this moment. She had looked at him and not known him; she knows him when he speaks her name. Faith is a personal meeting.
Do not hold on to me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father.
Jesus is not refusing love. He is saying that the time of holding him in the old way is over, and the next stage begins: his return to the Father and the gift of the Spirit.
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”;

The first witness of the Resurrection is a woman, and her message is the whole Easter faith in five words: “I have seen the Lord.” The Lord's “brothers” are the disciples, now called brothers because the Father of Jesus is their Father too (20:17).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Mary Magdalene and the holy women were the first to meet the Risen Lord, and thus the first messengers of the Resurrection to the apostles themselves (CCC 641). Hippolytus of Rome called the women at the tomb apostles to the apostles (in substance), and St Thomas Aquinas, commenting on this passage, calls Mary Magdalene “apostle of the apostles” (in substance). In 2016 the Roman Church raised her memorial to the rank of a feast, in recognition of that title. The Panchangam keeps her memory today with this Gospel of her meeting with the Risen Lord.

qa: Was Mary Magdalene the sinful woman who washed Jesus' feet?

The Gospels do not say so. Luke 7:36–50 tells of an unnamed sinful woman; Mary Magdalene is introduced only in Luke 8:2, and no Gospel connects the two. A homily by Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century joined them, with Mary of Bethany, and the Western tradition followed him for centuries. Most scholars today keep them apart, and so does the Church's present liturgy. What the Gospels tell us about Mary Magdalene is enough: she was healed by Jesus, followed him, stood at the Cross and was the first to see the Risen Lord.
rite: Every Sunday the Church of the Syriac tradition proclaims the Resurrection of the Lord, and the first person who did so was a woman, Mary Magdalene. She reminds the preacher and the faithful that what the Church has to say is not an idea but an encounter: “I have seen the Lord.” In the Holy Qurbono the faithful receive the peace of the Risen One, who said to his disciples, “Peace be with you” (John 20:19), and who calls each of us by name.
study: The Lord called Mary by her name, and she knew him. When have I heard the Lord speaking to me personally, in Scripture, in prayer or in someone's words?
Paul says we are ambassadors for Christ. Whom am I sent to, in my family or at work, with a message of reconciliation?

lead: Today the Panchangam remembers Ezekiel the Prophet, the watchman among the exiles, who warned his people and also promised them a new heart and a new spirit. Both readings speak to a people in a hard time. Paul thanks the Father who has rescued us from the power of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his Son. In the Gospel Jesus warns the disciples of wars, false teachers, hatred and cold love, and promises: “the one who endures to the end will be saved.” The key words are rescued, watch and endure.

r.h: Rescued from darkness into the kingdom
set: After the greeting, Paul tells the Colossians that he thanks God for their faith and love (1:3–8) and prays that they may be filled with the knowledge of God's will (1:9–11). Our verses continue that prayer in the form of thanksgiving, and they lead straight into the great hymn to Christ, the image of the invisible God (1:15–20).

Paul's words are rich with the memory of Israel. The “inheritance” recalls the land given to Israel as its share, and the “rescue” is the vocabulary of the Exodus. What God did for Israel in bringing it out of Egypt, he has now done in Christ for those who believe, whether Jew or Gentile.
str: v. 12: thanksgiving to the Father, who has made us fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light.
v. 13: he rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son.
v. 14: in the Son we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
kw: The word for a portion assigned by lot, the share of the land that each tribe received. Here the share is “in the light”, a place in God's own life, which is given and not earned.
The word was used for moving a whole people from one land to another. We have been moved out of one kingdom into another, as the people of Israel passed from Egypt to the land of promise.
Literally a release by the payment of a ransom. In the Old Testament it recalls the release of slaves and Israel's rescue from Egypt. Paul identifies it with the forgiveness of sins.
vv: giving thanks to the Father, who has enabled you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light.
Paul begins with thanks. Our place in the light is something we have been enabled to receive. It is the Father's gift, and the right response to a gift is gratitude.
He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son,
Paul uses the past tense: it has happened. “His beloved Son” is literally “the Son of his love”, so the kingdom is the kingdom of the one whom the Father loves, and we are brought into that love.
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
Some later manuscripts add “through his blood” here, from Ephesians 1:7; it is not in the oldest ones. The truth of the added words is clear from other texts, such as Colossians 1:20.
ch: The Church sees in these verses the meaning of Baptism, in which we are delivered from sin and from the power of the evil one and brought into the family of God. The rite of Baptism includes exorcisms that express this liberation (CCC 1237), and the Catechism teaches that by Baptism all sins are forgiven (CCC 1263). The Syriac Fathers loved to speak of the font as a womb from which the baptized are born again, clothed in a robe of glory (Mar Aphrem, in substance). Giving thanks, as Paul does, is also the meaning of the Eucharist, which in Greek means “thanksgiving”, the Church's prayer of gratitude for being rescued.

r.h: The one who endures to the end
set: Jesus has just left the Temple and told his disciples that not one stone will be left on another (24:1–2). On the Mount of Olives, facing the Temple, they ask him privately: when will this be, and what will be the sign of his coming and of the end of the age? This is the beginning of the long discourse of Matthew 24–25, often called the Olivet Discourse. Many interpreters see in it both the coming destruction of the Temple and the end of the age, spoken of together, as the prophets often did.

Our verses are the first part. Jesus does not give dates or maps. He gives the disciples a way to live in the time between his departure and his return: do not be led astray, do not be alarmed, stay faithful, and preach the Gospel to all nations.
str: vv. 3–4: the disciples' question and the first warning: do not be led astray.
vv. 5–8: false messiahs, wars and rumours, famines and earthquakes: only the beginning of the birth pangs.
vv. 9–12: persecution, falling away, betrayal, false prophets, and the cooling of love.
vv. 13–14: endurance leads to salvation; the Gospel is preached to all the nations, and then the end.
kw: The pains of a woman in labour. In the Old Testament the pains of childbirth are an image for the trials that come before God acts (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–9). Pains that lead to a birth are not meaningless.

Not passive waiting but staying under a load and holding on. It is the great virtue of the disciple in a hard time, and the same word family appears in Paul's prayer just before our verses, that the Colossians may be prepared to endure everything with patience (Colossians 1:11).

The Gospel will be proclaimed “as a testimony to all the nations”. The word is the root of martyr: the witness of disciples, sometimes at the price of their lives, is how the good news reaches the world.
vv: Jesus answered them, “Beware that no one leads you astray.
The first danger Jesus names is not persecution but deception. The disciples need clear eyes more than fearful hearts.
all this is but the beginning of the birth pangs.
Wars and disasters are not the end. They show a world still in labour. Jesus tells his disciples not to read every shock as the final sign, and not to panic.
And because of the increase of lawlessness, the love of many will grow cold.
The saddest line of the passage. The danger within the community is not only the enemy outside but the loss of love inside. The remedy is to keep love warm.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
Salvation is promised to those who hold on in faith, and it is God's grace that makes holding on possible. The disciple does not endure by his own strength alone.
And this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the world, as a testimony to all the nations; and then the end will come.

The Church's mission is not a side matter. The Gospel goes out to all peoples, and this is part of how history moves to its end. The same promise stands at the end of the Gospel: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (28:19).
ch: The Catechism teaches that since the Ascension, Christ's coming in glory is imminent, yet no one knows the day or the hour, and the times belong to the Father (CCC 673). Before his coming the Church will pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers (CCC 675). The Church reads Jesus' words not as a timetable, but as a call to watchfulness, mission and faithfulness. Hope, the Catechism says, means that each of us should hope, with the grace of God, to persevere to the end (CCC 1821). Today many Christians in many lands suffer for their faith, and others suffer for other reasons; we pray for all who suffer, and for those who wrong them, that their hearts may be changed.

qa: Does this passage tell us when the world will end?

No. Jesus warns against exactly that kind of calculation. A few verses later he says that about “that day and hour” no one knows, “neither the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (24:36). The Church has always rejected attempts to fix dates. What the passage gives is a way of life: watch, do not be afraid, keep love warm, hold on, and proclaim the Gospel.
study: Paul says the Father has “rescued us from the power of darkness”. What has God rescued me from, and have I given thanks for it?
Jesus says the love of many will grow cold. What helps me to keep my love warm: in my family, in my parish, towards people I find difficult?

lead: Both readings are about turning towards the Lord and not looking back. In 2 Corinthians Paul says that when anyone turns to the Lord the veil is taken away, and that with unveiled faces we are being transformed into the Lord's image. In Luke, Jesus meets three would-be disciples on the road and tells them what following him will cost. Today the Panchangam remembers St Sharbel, the monk and hermit of Lebanon (1828–1898), who left everything to follow Christ. The key words are veil, image and follow.

set: In 2 Corinthians 3 Paul defends his ministry by comparing it with the ministry of Moses. He writes to Corinthians who have been troubled by rival teachers, and he calls the Corinthians themselves his “letter of recommendation”, written by the Spirit on human hearts (3:1–3). Then he reads the story of Exodus 34:29–35, where Moses came down from Sinai with his face shining, and put a veil over it. Paul gives that old story a new meaning.

Paul himself was a Jew and a loyal one, and he did not say that the old covenant was bad. He calls Moses' ministry glorious (3:7). His point is that what came with Christ is more glorious still, and that to read the Law of Moses without Christ is to read with a veil over the mind. The Church has always said that the gifts and call of God to Israel are irrevocable (Romans 11:29).
str: v. 12: because of such a hope we act with great boldness.
v. 13: unlike Moses, who veiled his face.
vv. 14–15: the veil remains on minds when the old covenant is read, since only in Christ is it set aside.
v. 16: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
vv. 17–18: the Lord is present as the Spirit, where there is freedom; with unveiled faces we are transformed into his image.
kw: Plain, open speech without fear. The apostles have nothing to hide, because the glory they proclaim is not fading. Boldness is the mark of a Christian witness (Acts 4:13, 31).
The word can mean “beholding as in a mirror” or “reflecting like a mirror”. Both ideas are true: we see the Lord's glory, and, like polished metal, we begin to shine with it.
The verb used for the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:2). The change is slow and continuous: “from one degree of glory to another”.
vv: Since, then, we have such a hope, we act with great boldness,
Hope is the source of boldness. The apostle is not bold because he is clever or strong, but because what he has seen in Christ is lasting.
but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
The sentence echoes Exodus 34:34, where Moses removes the veil whenever he enters the presence of the Lord. Paul now says this is true of every person who turns to the Lord.
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
Paul does not mean that the Son and the Spirit are the same person. He means that the Lord who met Moses is now present among us through the Spirit, who gives the freedom of the children of God.
And all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another;
We are transformed by looking at the Lord. The more we look at him in the Gospel, in prayer and in the Holy Qurbono, the more we come to resemble him.
ch: The Church has always seen in this passage the goal of Christian life. The Catechism says that the Son of God became man so that we might share in the divine nature (CCC 460; 2 Peter 1:4). The Syriac Fathers, and Mar Aphrem above all, speak of the glory that Adam lost as a “robe of glory”, which Christ restores to the baptized (in substance). On the Jewish people, the Church teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121), and that the Jews remain most dear to God (Nostra Aetate 4). Paul's “veil” is a mystery of reading Scripture, not a verdict on any people.

r.h: Follow me, and do not look back
set: In Luke 9:51 Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem”. From there Luke tells the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51 to about 19:28), in which Jesus teaches what it means to follow him on the road to the Cross. Just before our verses a Samaritan village has refused to receive him (9:52–56). Now, on the road, three people come forward or are called, and each receives a hard answer.

The first is eager but has not counted the cost; the second is called by Jesus himself but asks for a delay; the third offers to follow after a farewell. The answers sound severe, but they show how serious the call is. The last scene recalls Elijah's call of Elisha, who was ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen. Elisha asked to kiss his father and mother, and Elijah allowed it (1 Kings 19:19–21). Jesus asks for even more.
str: vv. 57–58: the first man: “I will follow you wherever you go”; Jesus: the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
vv. 59–60: the second: “first let me go and bury my father”; Jesus: proclaim the kingdom of God.
vv. 61–62: the third: “let me first say farewell”; Jesus: whoever looks back from the plough is not fit for the kingdom.
kw: In the Gospels to follow Jesus means to be a disciple: to walk behind him, to learn from him, to share his road. It is not a feeling but a way of life.
Literally “well placed” or “useful”. A ploughman who keeps looking back cannot plough a straight furrow. The kingdom needs the whole attention of the one who serves it.
The word means to announce far and wide. To the man whose first thought was a funeral, Jesus gives another urgent task: the kingdom must be announced.
vv: Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
Jesus has no house of his own on the road. He asks his disciples to share a life that is poor and on the move, which is also how he lived.
But Jesus said to him, “Let the dead bury their own dead; but as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.”

The saying is hard. Burying the dead is a duty of mercy (Tobit 1:17–19), and Jesus does not despise it. Many commentators think the man's father was perhaps not yet dead, and that the request meant waiting for the father's death. In either case, “the dead” are those who do not yet know the life of the kingdom, and the call of God comes first.
No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.
Lot's wife looked back (Genesis 19:26). To plough a straight furrow, one must look ahead. Following Christ means to move forward with full attention.
ch: The Church reads these three answers as teaching on vocation. The Catechism says that family ties are important but not absolute, and that as a child grows to maturity, the vocation that comes from God asserts itself more clearly (CCC 2232). It also teaches that Christ proposes the evangelical counsels to every disciple in various ways (CCC 915), and that burying the dead is one of the corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447). Neither call cancels the other: the Gospel asks for first place in the heart, and everything else is then loved rightly.

qa: Does Jesus say we should not bury our dead or say goodbye to our families?

No. The Church honours the dead and teaches respect for the body (CCC 2300), and Jesus himself was buried with care. These sayings are strong, even shocking, on purpose, to show that the call of the kingdom cannot be delayed and must have first place. The same Lord commands the love of father and mother (Mark 7:10–13). The Gospel asks for the right order of love, not for the loss of the other loves.
rite: St Sharbel, born Youssef Makhlouf in 1828 at Bekaa Kafra in northern Lebanon, left his village at twenty-three to become a monk of the Lebanese Maronite Order, taking the name of an early martyr of Edessa. He lived many years in the monastery of St Maron at Annaya, was ordained priest in 1859, and from 1875 lived as a hermit in prayer, silence and manual work. He died on Christmas Eve 1898 after a stroke suffered while celebrating the Holy Qurbono. Pope Paul VI beatified him in 1965 and canonized him in 1977. Pilgrims of many faiths still come to his tomb at Annaya. The Maronite Church, like our own Church, belongs to the West Syriac tradition, and in Sharbel the Church sees the monk who followed the Lord without looking back.
study: Paul says that with unveiled faces we are transformed by looking at the Lord. How much of my day is spent looking at him: in Scripture, in prayer, in the Holy Qurbono?
Jesus gave three people three hard answers. Which of the three, the eager one, the one who asked for a delay, or the one who wanted to look back, is closest to me today?

lead: On the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost the readings speak of a God who heals and who draws near. In the evening Gospel (Luke 9:12–17) Jesus tells the apostles, “You give them something to eat”, and five loaves and two fish feed the crowd: “all ate and were filled”. In Exodus 15:23–27 the bitter water of Marah is made sweet, and the Lord says, “I am the Lord who heals you.” In Job 42:7–17 the Lord restores Job after he has prayed for his friends. Psalm 112 praises the one who fears the Lord and gives to the poor. In Isaiah 57:14–21 the Holy One who dwells on high also dwells “with those who are contrite and humble in spirit”, and promises, “I will heal them.” In Acts 28:23–30 Paul, a prisoner in Rome, spends a whole day explaining the kingdom of God to the Jewish leaders of the city, some of whom are convinced, and he goes on welcoming everyone who comes to him.

We study three readings more closely. At Marah the people find water that cannot be drunk, and God answers a complaint with a piece of wood and a promise of healing. Paul tells the Romans that the word of salvation is not far away, high in heaven or deep in the abyss, but “on your lips and in your heart”, and that the same Lord is generous to Jew and Greek alike. In Matthew, Jesus puts a child in the midst of the disciples who are arguing about greatness, warns against causing the little ones to stumble, and tells of the shepherd who goes after the one sheep that has gone astray. The key words are bitter and sweet, near and little ones.

r.h: Marah: the bitter water made sweet
set: The Israelites have just crossed the sea and sung the Song of Moses (15:1–21). Three days later they are in the wilderness of Shur and have found no water (15:22). The song of victory is hardly finished when the first complaint is heard. The story is the first of several “wilderness” stories in Exodus and Numbers in which God tests his people and teaches them to trust (see 16:4; 17:1–7).

Marah is a Hebrew word meaning “bitter”. The place is not certainly identified today. In verse 25 the Lord shows Moses a piece of wood; it is cast into the water and the water becomes sweet. There “the Lord made for them a statute and an ordinance”, which means that the first lesson of the journey is also the first lesson of the law: listen to the voice of the Lord. The reading ends at Elim, a place of twelve springs and seventy palm trees, where God gives more than the bare minimum.
str: v. 23: Marah: water that cannot be drunk, and a place named for its bitterness.
v. 24: the people complain against Moses.
v. 25: Moses cries to the Lord; the wood makes the water sweet; statute and test.
v. 26: if they listen and obey, they will not suffer the diseases of Egypt; “I am the Lord who heals you”.
v. 27: Elim, with its springs and palm trees.
¶ The complaint (v. 24) and the cry (v. 25) are placed side by side: the people complain to Moses, and Moses cries out to the Lord.
kw: The name of the place tells the whole story: the first stop after the sea is a place of bitterness. Israel will learn that God turns bitterness to sweetness, but only by teaching hearts to trust.
he put them to the test
The same word is used of Abraham in Genesis 22:1. A test in the Bible is not a trap but a school: it brings to light what is in the heart and makes it grow.
Literally “the one who heals you”. God takes this title for himself. The healing here is of body, community and heart, and it is tied to listening to his voice.
vv: they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter.
Right after the great deliverance comes ordinary thirst. The life of faith does not remove difficulty, but it teaches us where to take it.
the Lord showed him a piece of wood; he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet.
The cure comes from God, not from the wood. Moses must be shown the wood; he does not find it himself. The healing is a gift, received in obedience.
there he put them to the test.
The same moment is both a gift and a test. God gives water and also asks for trust.
I am the Lord who heals you.
The promise is conditional on listening, but it is mainly a revelation of who God is. He does not only punish; he heals.
ch: Several of the Fathers, among them Tertullian and Origen (in substance), saw in the wood that sweetened the water a figure of the cross, which turns the bitterness of the old letter and of death into sweetness. The Church has also heard in “I am the Lord who heals you” the voice of Christ the physician.
