The Catechism recalls that Christ’s compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a resplendent sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503). The Church’s care for the sick, and her sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, continue that healing. The passage also teaches how to meet complaint: not by silencing it, but by bringing it to God as Moses did, and then waiting to be shown the wood.

set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably in the winter of AD 56–57, to a church he had not founded and hoped to visit on his way to Spain. Chapters 9–11 are about Israel, his own people, whom he loves so much that he would wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake (9:3). Just before our passage he says, “my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved” (10:1). He is not speaking against the Jewish people but as one of them, in grief and in hope.

Verses 5–8 set two ways of speaking side by side. Verse 5 quotes Leviticus 18:5, where Moses promises life to those who keep God’s commandments. Verses 6–8 take words from Deuteronomy 30:12–14, where Moses tells Israel that the commandment is not “in heaven” or “beyond the sea”, but “very near to you”. Paul hears in that nearness the nearness of Christ himself. Interpreters differ on exactly how Paul sets verse 5 against verses 6–8, but they agree that for him the word of God has come close in Christ and calls for faith.
str: v. 5: Moses and the righteousness that comes from the law.
vv. 6–8: the righteousness that comes from faith: the word is near, on your lips and in your heart.
vv. 9–10: confessing with the lips and believing in the heart.
vv. 11–13: for everyone: Jew and Greek, the same Lord; whoever calls on his name will be saved.
kw: Paul uses the word rhēma, the spoken word that is proclaimed. Faith “comes from what is heard” (10:17). The Gospel is announced, and the Church’s preaching is the way that the word comes near.
To say the same as another, to speak in agreement. To confess that Jesus is Lord is to agree with God’s own word about him. The earliest Christian creed is this short cry.

In the Greek Old Testament kyrios is the word used for the name of the God of Israel. To call Jesus “Lord” is to give him the honour due to God, and it is a work of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).
vv: The word is near you, on your lips and in your heart

Paul reads Deuteronomy 30:14 in the light of Christ. We do not have to climb to heaven or go down to the abyss to find him; he has come to us. The Church’s Gospel, sacraments and prayer are how the nearness is lived.
if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

Heart and lips go together. Faith is a gift of God received with the whole person, and it is expressed in public confession. For Catholics this faith is lived in the Church and sealed in Baptism; it is also the root of the works of love (compare CCC 1815).
No one who believes in him will be put to shame.
Paul quotes Isaiah 28:16. Faith is never put to shame, because the one in whom we trust does not fail.
there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all and is generous to all who call on him.

The one Lord is the Lord of Jews and Gentiles. Paul does not set Jews aside: he teaches that Gentiles are welcomed into the same promise (see 11:1, 29, where he says that God has not rejected his people and that his gifts and call are irrevocable).
ch: The cry “Jesus is Lord” is the earliest confession of the Church. The Catechism teaches that the title Lord expresses the divinity of Jesus and that to call Jesus “Lord” is to confess his divine sovereignty (CCC 446–449). The same Catechism says that believing in Jesus Christ and in the One who sent him is necessary for obtaining salvation (CCC 161). In the Syriac tradition the Creed is said aloud by the whole people at the Holy Qurbono, so that heart and lips speak together, as Paul says. The passage is also read with Romans 11 in mind: the Church has never taught that God has rejected the Jewish people, and Nostra Aetate 4 recalls that God does not repent of the gifts he has made nor of the calls he issues.

r.h: Become like children; the sheep that went astray
set: Matthew 18 is the fourth of the five great discourses of the Gospel, often called the discourse on the community or the Church. It begins with a question about rank (v. 1) and goes on to teach humility (vv. 1–5), care for the little ones (vv. 6–10), the search for the lost sheep (vv. 12–14), and then fraternal correction, forgiveness and the prayer of two or three gathered in his name (vv. 15–35). In Mark 9:33–37 the dispute about greatness arises on the road to Capernaum, and Luke 9:46–48 tells of it too.

In the ancient world a child had little status and no rights, and “the little ones” can mean children, but also all those who are small, humble or easily overlooked in the community, as the phrase “who believe in me” in verse 6 shows. The sayings about the hand, foot and eye (vv. 8–9) are typical Semitic exaggeration: they teach how seriously sin must be fought, not that the body is to be harmed. One note on the text: verse 11 (“For the Son of Man came to save the lost”) appears in many manuscripts but is not in the earliest ones, and the NRSV omits it; the sense is the same as Luke 19:10.
str: vv. 1–5: who is the greatest? A child is placed in the midst; whoever welcomes one such child welcomes Christ.
vv. 6–9: woe to those who cause the little ones to stumble; renounce whatever causes sin.
v. 10: do not despise the little ones; their angels see the Father’s face.
vv. 12–14: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that has strayed; the Father does not want one of them lost.
kw: The Greek verb is “to turn around”, the same idea as the Hebrew word for repentance. To become like a child is not to become childish but to turn: from the question “who is greatest?” to trust and dependence on the Father.
Originally the trigger of a trap. Here it is whatever makes a believer fall. The warning is very severe because the little ones belong to Christ.
The same verb is used of the sheep that wanders. The shepherd’s search is not a punishment for the wanderer but a sign that the sheep is precious.
vv: unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
The condition is humility. A child receives everything as a gift and does not keep a score of merits. Greatness in the kingdom is the opposite of climbing.
Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.
Christ makes himself one with the little ones. Welcome given to a child, to a poor person or to a new member of the parish is welcome given to him.
Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks!
Jesus says that stumbling blocks are bound to come, but this does not excuse anyone. Anyone who leads a young believer into sin, by scandal or neglect, answers for it.
in heaven their angels continually see the face of my Father in heaven.
The little ones have heavenly guardians who stand in the Father’s presence. The text is the main biblical root of the teaching on guardian angels.
it is not the will of your Father in heaven that one of these little ones should be lost.
The passage ends with the will of the Father: not one lost. The shepherd acts out the Father’s will.
ch: The Catechism takes “become like children” as the way to enter the kingdom: the Gospel shows that to become a child in relation to God is the condition for entering it (CCC 526). It also teaches that from infancy to death human life is surrounded by the watchful care and intercession of the angels, and that beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd (CCC 336, citing St Basil). Scandal is defined as an attitude or behaviour that leads another to do evil (CCC 2284), and the Church takes with great seriousness the duty to protect children and the vulnerable. St Gregory the Great, preaching on the lost sheep in another Gospel, hears in it Christ taking our nature on his shoulders (Homilies on the Gospels 34, in substance). The Church’s pastoral work is a continuation of that search.

qa: Marah’s bitter water was made sweet by a piece of wood. Was that a miracle or a natural event?

The text says that the Lord showed Moses the wood and that the water became sweet. Some scholars note that plants with such properties exist in the Sinai, and they may be right, but this does not take anything from the story. The point is that the people were saved by what God showed and what Moses did in obedience. The Church sees in it a sign of God’s power to turn bitter things sweet, and in the wood a figure of the cross.
Does Paul say that we are saved by words, by simply saying “Jesus is Lord”?

No. Paul joins the lips and the heart: the confession is the expression of a faith that comes from God and is lived. Elsewhere he writes that no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3), and that faith works through love (Galatians 5:6). Jesus himself warns that not everyone who says “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom (Matthew 7:21). Faith, Baptism and a life of love belong together.
Why does Jesus use such strong words about cutting off a hand or an eye?

He is using a vivid Semitic way of speaking to say that nothing is worth more than life with God. No Christian teaching asks us to hurt the body. The “hand”, “foot” and “eye” stand for whatever we hold dear and which leads us to sin, such as a habit, a friendship, or a source of income. The Church asks us to break with it, by repentance and by the grace of the sacraments.
rite: In the Syro-Malankara tradition, as in the other Eastern Churches, children receive Baptism, Chrismation with the Holy Mooron and the Holy Qurbono together, so the child whom Jesus places in the midst is truly at the table of the Lord. This Sunday also falls in the long season after Pentecost, in which the Church reads the Scriptures steadily and hears them as the unfolding of the Spirit’s work in the life of the community. The evening Gospel of the loaves and fish prepares us for the Holy Qurbono, where Christ still says, “You give them something to eat”, and gives the apostles and their successors bread to set before the crowd. The cry “Kurielaison” (Lord, have mercy) in the Qurbono and the hours is the cry of the one who has found the water too bitter and calls on the name of the Lord, in the words of Romans 10:13.
study: At Marah the people complained and Moses cried out to the Lord. When bitterness comes into my life, do I complain, cry out, or do both, and who helps me to see “the wood”?
Paul says that the word is near, on my lips and in my heart. What word of the Gospel has been closest to me this week, and have I confessed it aloud to anyone?
Jesus puts a child in the midst and says that whoever welcomes such a child welcomes him. Whom in my family or parish do I overlook as “too small”, and how can I welcome them?
The Father does not want one of the little ones lost. Is there someone who has strayed from the Church whom I can search for with patience, as the shepherd does?

lead: Both readings are about a change of heart that God asks for and longs to receive. In Corinth, Paul rejoices that the grief his letter caused led the Corinthians to repentance and not to despair. On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus laments over a city that he wanted to gather like a hen with her chicks, and he does not turn back from the road that leads to his own death. The key words are grief that leads to repentance and gathering.

set: Second Corinthians is the most personal of Paul’s letters. After a painful visit and a severe letter written “out of much distress and anguish of heart and with many tears” (2:4), Paul waited anxiously for news. Titus met him in Macedonia with good news: the Corinthians had been grieved by the letter, had taken it to heart and had set matters right (7:5–9). Scholars discuss whether the “severe letter” is lost or is part of what we have in the canon; either way, our verses are the heart of Paul’s relief.
Paul does not rejoice that they were hurt, but that the hurt led somewhere (7:9). He draws a lesson from what happened: not every sorrow is good, and the difference is in the direction it takes.
str: v. 10: two kinds of grief: godly grief leads to repentance and salvation; worldly grief leads to death.
v. 11: the fruits of godly grief in Corinth: earnestness, eagerness, longing, zeal.
vv. 12–13: Paul’s purpose in writing: that their zeal for him be made known before God; the comfort of Titus.
vv. 14–16: his boasting about them proved true; Titus’s affection; Paul’s full confidence in them.
kw: Repentance is a change of mind and heart. The second word means “not to be regretted”, and Paul uses it for a sorrow that one never has to take back.

Sorrow in line with God’s own will. It looks at the wrong done and also at the God who forgives, and so it turns toward him. Worldly grief looks only at the damage to oneself and may end in bitterness.
Eagerness, haste to do what is right. Real repentance shows itself in action, in the list of fruits that Paul gives in verse 11.
vv: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret
The sorrow that God gives is a grace. It is not the end of the road but a door: it opens to the mercy that heals.
see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you
Paul’s long list shows that repentance is a change in whole life, with action, zeal and a longing to put things right.
we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus
Paul’s joy is shared joy. The comfort of one pastor, Titus, adds to the comfort of another, Paul, and the whole community is knit together by it.
ch: The Church uses this chapter to teach about contrition. The Catechism describes interior penance as a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return to God, with sorrow for sin and the intention to sin no more (CCC 1431), and it teaches that contrition is a sorrow of the soul and a detestation of the sin committed, together with the resolution not to sin again (CCC 1451). The line between godly and worldly sorrow is the line between Peter, who wept and was restored, and a despair that closes the heart. In the Syro-Malankara and other Eastern traditions, the prayers of repentance are often full of hope, because the sinner is always speaking to a merciful Lord.

set: Jesus is on the journey to Jerusalem that fills the middle of Luke’s Gospel (9:51–19:27). Just before our passage he has taught about the narrow door (13:22–30). Some Pharisees now come with a warning: Herod wants to kill him. We should note that Luke shows Pharisees helping Jesus here, and not only opposing him; they care about his life.

“That fox” is Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, who had John the Baptist beheaded (9:9; 3:19–20). In Jesus’ day the fox was a symbol of cunning, but also of someone with small power. Jesus speaks of his work as a timetable set by God: “today and tomorrow, and on the third day”. He must reach Jerusalem, where the prophets are sent, and where he will give his life.
str: v. 31: Pharisees warn Jesus about Herod.
vv. 32–33: Jesus’ answer: his work continues, and his road leads to Jerusalem.
v. 34: the lament: the hen who wants to gather her chicks.
v. 35: the house is left to them until the day they say, “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord”.
kw: The verb is used for gathering a scattered people (the prayer in 2 Maccabees 1:27 asks God to gather those who are dispersed). Jesus is the one who gathers the children of Jerusalem.
Jesus’ own will, spoken with tenderness. The final words, “you were not willing”, show that God’s love invites and never forces.
blessed is the one who comes
A line from Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims at the temple. Luke’s crowds will sing it on Palm Sunday (19:38).
vv: I am casting out demons and performing cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I finish my work.
Jesus is not frightened. His work is directed by the Father, and it will be completed, in the Gospel’s own pattern, on “the third day”.
it is impossible for a prophet to be killed outside of Jerusalem.
A sad irony: the holy city, God’s city, is the place where prophets have often met their end. Jesus knows that his own road will end there too.
How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
One of the most tender images in the Gospels. The “wings” recall the psalms that speak of shelter under God’s wings (Psalms 17:8; 36:7; 91:4). Jesus loves Jerusalem as one of its own children.
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.
The lament ends with a promise: the day will come when this blessing is said, and it is Christ who comes.
ch: Christian tradition has long read the lament as the love of Christ, who weeps over the city, as in Luke 19:41. The words do not condemn the Jewish people. Jesus himself is a Son of Israel, speaking out of love for his own city and people, and the Church teaches that what happened in his Passion cannot be blamed on all the Jews then living, nor on the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The Church also reads in the hen’s wings the motherly tenderness of God, and in verse 35 the hope of a final welcome of the Lord who comes.

study: Paul distinguishes godly grief from worldly grief. When I am sorry for something I have done, does my sorrow turn me toward God’s mercy or in on myself?
Jesus says, “How often have I desired to gather your children together.” Where in my parish or family is God trying to gather people, and what in me says, “I am not willing”?

lead: Today’s readings ask what we do with the time God gives us. Paul, in the middle of the weakness of the body, is confident because he walks by faith and wants only to please the Lord. In Luke, a gardener begs for one more year for a barren fig tree. The time we have is a mercy, and the mercy is meant to bear fruit. The key words are aim to please and one more year.

r.h: We walk by faith, not by sight
set: Paul has just spoken about the earthly “tent” of the body and the “building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (5:1). He writes after a time in which he was close to death (1:8–10), and he is thinking honestly about death and about what lies beyond it.

These verses are neither a wish for death nor a fear of it. Paul says that he is confident, even though he is away from the Lord while he lives in the body, and he would rather be at home with him. But his chief aim, whether he is alive or dead, is to please the Lord, for the Lord is also the judge.
str: vv. 6–7: confidence now: away from the Lord in the body, but walking by faith.
v. 8: the preference: to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
v. 9: the aim in both states: to please him.
v. 10: all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
kw: The Greek word for “sight” can also mean “appearance”. We live by what God has said and promised, not by what we can see or feel.
Literally, “we are ambitious” (from the love of honour). Paul turns the word of worldly ambition toward a single goal: to please the Lord.
A raised platform on which a judge sat. It stood in the public square at Corinth (Acts 18:12), so the readers knew exactly what Paul meant.
vv: we walk by faith, not by sight.
Faith is a way of walking: a step at a time, trusting God, even when the road ahead is not visible.
we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
Paul looks to death without fear, because of the Lord who waits there. He does not despise the body, which will be raised (see 4:14), but longs for closer union with Christ.
we make it our aim to please him.
This is the centre of Christian life. We do not act in order to earn God’s love but to answer it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that death ends the time in which we can accept or reject the grace God offers us in Christ (CCC 1021), and that each person receives, at the moment of death, an eternal retribution in an individual judgment (CCC 1022). Judgment is not meant to terrify: the Church sees in the judgment seat of Christ the face of the one who died for us. At the Holy Qurbono we meet the Lord under signs, by faith and not by sight, and this is a foretaste of the day when we shall be at home with him.

set: The parable follows Jesus’ teaching on repentance after two tragic events: Pilate’s killing of Galileans in the temple and the fall of the tower of Siloam (13:1–5). Jesus warns, “unless you repent, you will all perish” (13:3, 5), and then tells this story to show what repentance is for: fruit.

In the Old Testament the fig tree and the vine often stand for Israel (Hosea 9:10; Joel 1:7; Micah 7:1). But Luke gives the parable to every hearer, not only to a nation: “unless you repent, you will all perish” is said to the whole crowd. The vineyard is the place of God’s care, and the three years and the extra year suggest patience that is real but not endless.
str: v. 6: a man plants a fig tree in his vineyard and finds no fruit.
v. 7: his verdict: three years without fruit; cut it down.
v. 8: the gardener’s plea: leave it one more year; he will dig and manure.
v. 9: the open ending: if it bears fruit, well and good; if not, cut it down.
kw: The fruit of repentance, as John the Baptist taught (3:8). Fruit is not a show but what grows from a living root.
The same word is the usual Greek word for “forgive” (as in the Our Father, 11:4). The gardener’s request is a request for forgiveness and mercy.
The one who cares for the vineyard. The parable gives him a voice for the patient intercession that Christians have always heard in the prayer of Christ for us.
vv: he came looking for fruit on it and found none.
The owner’s search is reasonable. God looks for fruit because he has planted us and cared for us.
let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it.
The gardener does not defend the barren tree. He asks for time and promises extra work. Mercy gives time, and it also takes trouble.
If it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.
Jesus does not tell us how the story ends, for it is our story. The ending is left to the hearer.
ch: The Church hears in the gardener the intercession of Christ, who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). The Catechism teaches that Jesus calls us to conversion, which is at once a gift of grace and a task of daily life (CCC 1427–1428). The time we are given is therefore not neutral: it is time for fruit, shown in prayer, penance, the care of the poor and the peace we make. The parable should not be read as a threat. It is a gentle warning, spoken by someone who has dug around the roots of the tree and given it manure, and is willing to do so again.

study: Paul’s chief aim is to please the Lord, whether in life or in death. What is the chief aim that drives my days, and what would change if it were his?
The gardener asks for one more year and promises to dig and to fertilise. Whose “one more year” has someone given me, and who needs my patience and my help to bear fruit?

lead: Both readings speak of life that comes through dying with Christ. Paul says that he has been crucified with Christ and that Christ now lives in him. Jesus says that a grain of wheat bears much fruit only when it falls into the earth and dies. The day also remembers Morth Alphonsa, whose hidden life of suffering offered to God bore fruit far beyond her convent. The key words are crucified with Christ and the grain that dies.

set: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being told that Gentile Christians must also keep the whole Jewish law, including circumcision, to be saved. Just before our verses he tells how he rebuked Peter at Antioch for withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentile believers (2:11–14), and he states the heart of the Gospel: a person is justified through faith in Jesus Christ (2:16).

Paul is himself a Jew, proud of his people, and he does not despise the law. The law was holy and good (Romans 7:12). But for him a new reality has come in Christ, and it is this that our verses describe in the first person: his old life has been put to death with Christ, and a new life has begun.
str: v. 19: through the law I died to the law, to live to God; I have been crucified with Christ.
v. 20: no longer I, but Christ lives in me; a life of faith in the Son of God who loved me.
v. 21: I do not nullify the grace of God; otherwise Christ died for nothing.
kw: A single Greek verb in the perfect tense: it happened once and remains true. Baptism joins the believer to the death of Christ (Romans 6:3–6), and Paul’s life continues from that point.
faith in the Son of God
The phrase can be read “faith in” or “the faithfulness of” the Son of God. Both meanings are true: we believe in him, and we are held by his own faithful love.
If righteousness came through the law alone, Christ’s death would be without purpose. Paul’s whole argument rests on the cross as the work of God’s grace.
vv: I have been crucified with Christ
Paul joins his life to the cross. This is not only a hard saying; it is a description of Baptism, in which we die to sin and rise to new life.
it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.
Christ does not erase Paul. Paul is still Paul. But Christ is now the centre of his life, and his love and his actions come from Christ.
who loved me and gave himself for me
The faith of Paul is personal: the Son of God loved “me”. Each of us may say this.
I do not nullify the grace of God
Grace is not set aside by anyone who trusts in Christ. Obedience, works and love are all the fruit of grace and never a way around it.
ch: The Catechism uses the words “who loved me and gave himself for me” to teach that Jesus knew and loved each one of us personally during his life, agony and passion, and gave himself for each (CCC 478). Union with Christ in Baptism is the Church’s reading of “crucified with Christ”; the baptized are called to live as those who are dead to sin and alive to God. The reading fits the Catholic teaching on grace: our life and merit are possible only because God first loves us and gives himself, so that all that is good in us is his gift.

set: Jesus says this when some Greeks have come to Philip and ask to see him (12:20–22). Jesus answers that “the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (12:23). The hour of his glory is the hour of his death, and the coming of the Gentiles to him is a sign that the fruit is about to be gathered.

The image is simple and well known to a farming people. A seed buried in the soil appears to be lost, but it is the way to the harvest. Jesus then applies the image to his disciples: whoever clings to life as to a possession will lose it, and whoever gives it away in love will keep it for eternal life.
str: v. 24: the grain of wheat that dies and bears much fruit.
v. 25: loving and losing life; hating life in this world and keeping it for eternal life.
v. 26: serving Christ means following him; where he is, his servant will be; the Father honours the servant.
kw: A single seed. The Gospel speaks of the one Christ, who becomes the first of many, as Paul says of the first fruits of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20).
A Semitic way of speaking: to love something less than another. It does not mean despising life, which is God’s gift, but putting Christ before it. Compare Luke 14:26.
The usual word for discipleship: to walk behind. The servant goes where the master goes.
vv: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Jesus speaks first of himself. His death is not a defeat but the sowing of the new life of the Church.
Those who love their life lose it
A life closed on itself is lost. A life poured out for others is kept. This is the logic of the cross.
Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.
Where Jesus is going is the cross and then the glory. The disciple’s road is the same road, and the promise is that he will not be alone on it.
ch: The Fathers read the grain of wheat as Christ and, after him, the martyrs. Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed (Apology 50, in substance). The Catechism teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473), and that Christian death is a sharing in the death of Christ (CCC 1010). The same words also speak to the quieter martyrdom of daily life, when love gives up what it wanted for the good of another.

rite: Today the Church also remembers Morth Alphonsa, who was born Annakutty in 1910 at Kudamaloor in Kerala. She entered the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam, where she received the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception. She was often ill and endured long suffering with patience and prayer, and she died on 28 July 1946, aged 35. She was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1986 and canonized by Pope Benedict XVI on 12 October 2008, the first woman of India raised to the altars. Her life is a grain of wheat that fell into the earth: a short, hidden life that has borne fruit in the prayers of millions. Her tomb at Bharananganam is visited by pilgrims of every Church and many faiths. Paul’s words, “it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me”, help us to see what she lived.
study: Paul says that Christ loved him and gave himself for him. Can I say the same sentence about myself, and what changes in my day when I do?
Jesus says that the grain must fall into the earth and die. What “hidden” work of mine (a patience, a prayer, a service) may be the seed of someone else’s good?

lead: Hebrews closes with practical love: stay faithful to one another, welcome strangers, remember those in prison, honour marriage and trust God instead of money. In Luke, Martha welcomes Jesus into her home while Mary sits at his feet and listens. The day also remembers the three friends of Jesus at Bethany, Martha, Mary and Lazarus. Their home shows how love of the Lord is made of service and of listening, and neither can be left out. The key words are hospitality and the one thing needed.

set: Chapter 13 is the closing section of Hebrews. After long teaching about Christ our high priest, the author gives short, practical instructions for the community. Who wrote Hebrews is not known: Christian tradition has linked it with Paul, while many scholars think it was written by another follower of the apostle, but the Church has always received it as inspired Scripture.

Verses 1–6 are a list of concrete duties. Love for the brothers and sisters, hospitality to strangers, care for prisoners and for the tortured, respect for marriage, and a trusting detachment from money. The readers are a community that has suffered (10:32–34), so these are not abstract words.
str: v. 1: let mutual love continue.
v. 2: hospitality to strangers: some have entertained angels.
v. 3: remember those in prison and those being tortured.
v. 4: marriage honoured by all.
vv. 5–6: freedom from the love of money; trust in the promise “I will never leave you”.
kw: The word for family love, used here for the bond of the Church. It is already a duty, “let it continue”, because the community has loved before (10:32–34).
Literally “love of strangers”. In the early Church travelling missionaries and believers depended on it. Abraham’s welcome of three visitors (Genesis 18) is the model.
The author asks for a way of life, a “manner” (tropos), that is not governed by the love of money. Contentment comes from the promise that God is with us.
vv: Let mutual love continue.
Short and plain. Love in the Church is not something to start but something to keep alive.
Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.
The allusion is to Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 18) and perhaps Lot (Genesis 19). Whoever welcomes a stranger may be welcoming more than he knows.
Remember those who are in prison, as though you were in prison with them
Compassion means to share. We are asked to feel the situation of a prisoner as our own, and to act.
I will never leave you or forsake you.
The promise of God to Joshua (Joshua 1:5) is applied to every believer. Freedom from money does not come from willpower but from trust in this promise.
ch: The Church’s corporal works of mercy include visiting the imprisoned and welcoming the stranger (CCC 2447), and she teaches that Christ himself is present in those who suffer (Matthew 25:35–36). The Catechism also teaches that marriage is a sacred bond to be honoured by all (CCC 1601–1602). The line “I will never leave you” is why the Church can speak to those who suffer in many lands, and pray for them and for those who wrong them, with a hope that does not depend on circumstance.

set: The story follows the parable of the Good Samaritan and shows the other side of discipleship. The Samaritan teaches how to love the neighbour in need; Martha and Mary show how to love the Lord himself who comes to the door. Luke does not name the village. John tells us that Martha, Mary and Lazarus lived at Bethany near Jerusalem (John 11:1; 12:1–3). Mary of Bethany is not the same person as Mary Magdalene, and she is not the sinful woman of Luke 7.

In the first century a woman who sat at the feet of a teacher was taking the place of a disciple, which was normally a man’s. Jesus welcomes this. At the same time he does not despise Martha’s service; he loves her too and calls her by name twice.
str: v. 38: Martha welcomes Jesus into her home.
v. 39: Mary sits at his feet and listens.
v. 40: Martha, distracted by many tasks, complains.
vv. 41–42: Jesus: Martha, Martha, there is need of only one thing; Mary has chosen the better part.
kw: The word for ministry in the Church. Martha’s work is real service. The trouble is not the service but the distraction that has taken her away from the guest.
you are worried … you are troubled
Two words of anxiety. The Lord does not scold her activity but her worry, which divides the heart. Compare Matthew 6:25–34.
A word for a portion or share. The “better part” will not be taken away: it is a share in the Lord himself.
vv: a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home.
Martha is the host. Her welcome is the first act of faith in the story, and the Gospel records it with respect.
Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to what he was saying.
To sit at someone’s feet is the posture of a disciple (Acts 22:3). Mary places herself under the word.
Martha, Martha, you are worried and distracted by many things
The repeated name is a sign of affection. Jesus speaks to her heart, not only to her habits.
there is need of only one thing. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.
The one thing is the Lord himself. Service flows from listening to him and does not replace it. The service of Martha and the listening of Mary belong together.
ch: St Augustine preached on this passage and taught (in substance) that both women are blessed: Martha stands for the service of the present life, Mary for the joy of the life to come, and Martha too must learn to listen, so that her service becomes love and not strain (Sermon 103). In the Church’s tradition active and contemplative life are never opposed. In the West Syriac tradition the whole day is shaped by the prayers of the hours, so that work and prayer support each other, as at Bethany, where the Lord loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:5).

qa: Is Jesus saying that prayer is better than work?

No. He is not praising idleness or blaming service. Luke has just told the parable of the Good Samaritan, which praises practical help. What Jesus corrects is the worry and distraction that have taken Martha away from the guest she is serving. Service is the fruit of love, and love is fed by listening to the Lord. The same Martha, in John 11, makes one of the great confessions of faith: “I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God” (John 11:27).
study: The author of Hebrews asks us to remember those in prison and to welcome strangers. Whom could I welcome or visit this week, and what stops me?
Jesus tells Martha that only one thing is needed. In the busiest part of my day, where can I sit at his feet for a few minutes and listen?

lead: Both readings are about wakefulness and about the work that cannot wait. Paul tells the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord comes without warning, and that those who belong to the light are to stay awake and sober. In Luke, Jesus rises before dawn to pray alone, and then refuses to stay where he is welcomed because he was sent to proclaim the kingdom to other towns as well. The key words are keep awake and I must proclaim.

r.h: Children of light and of the day
set: First Thessalonians was written by Paul from Corinth, probably around AD 50–51, and is one of the earliest writings of the New Testament. The young church at Thessalonica was anxious about believers who had died (4:13–18) and about when the Lord would return. Paul has comforted them about the first and now turns to the second.

He does not give a timetable. He says that they know very well that the day of the Lord will come “like a thief in the night”, and then tells them how to live in the meantime. Many scholars hear in “peace and security” (v. 3) an echo of the slogans of the Roman Empire; whether or not this is so, the words describe the false calm that comes before a sudden crisis.
str: vv. 1–2: no need to write about times and seasons: the day comes like a thief in the night.
v. 3: those who say “peace and security” will be taken by sudden destruction, like labour pains.
vv. 4–5: but you are not in darkness; you are children of light and of the day.
v. 6: so let us not sleep but keep awake and be sober.
kw: The image comes from Jesus’ own teaching (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39). It is not the picture of a threat to believers but of a surprise for those who do not expect the Lord.
To be spiritually alert. In the Gospels Jesus repeats this call at Gethsemane and in his teaching on the end (Mark 13:35–37).
Literally not drunk. A clear mind, clear of the intoxication of the world’s false promises, is the mark of those who live in the light.
vv: the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
No one knows the day. The right response is not to calculate but to live ready.
you are all children of light and children of the day
Paul reminds them who they are before telling them what to do. Their identity is given by God in Baptism, and their behaviour follows from it.
let us keep awake and be sober
Paul says “let us”, and includes himself. Wakefulness is a task for the whole Church, together.
ch: The Church has always taught that no one knows the time of the end. The Catechism says that we know neither the moment of the consummation of the earth and of humanity nor the way in which the universe will be transformed (CCC 1048). The right reaction to this is the one Paul asks of the Thessalonians: faith, hope and love (5:8), and prayer. The Church’s whole liturgical year is a school of watchfulness, and the call “watch” returns constantly, with the parable of the ten virgins in Matthew 25:13.

r.h: I must proclaim the good news
set: The passage closes Luke’s first day of ministry at Capernaum: Jesus has taught in the synagogue, driven out a demon and healed Simon’s mother-in-law and many others (4:31–41). The crowds are now at his door. In the morning he goes alone to a deserted place, as he does at other key moments in Luke (5:16; 6:12; 9:18, 28).

The crowds find him and want to keep him. Jesus answers that his mission is larger than one town. A textual note: many manuscripts read “synagogues of Galilee” in verse 44 (as in Mark 1:39), but the NRSV text has “Judea”, and Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the land of the Jews as a whole.
str: v. 42: at daybreak Jesus goes to a deserted place; the crowds seek him and try to keep him.
v. 43: “I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also”.
v. 44: he continues preaching in the synagogues.
kw: A place of prayer, silence and meeting with God, as in the story of Moses and Elijah. Jesus’ own source of strength is in this solitude.
A word Luke uses of God’s plan. Jesus does not follow popularity but the Father’s will.
Jesus knows that he is sent. The mission precedes the crowds’ desires.
vv: At daybreak he departed and went into a deserted place.
After a day of healing, Jesus goes to pray. His public work comes out of a hidden life with the Father.
the crowds were looking for him
The crowds are not wrong to want him; they are right to seek him. But they would keep him for themselves.
I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose.
Jesus’ mission is for everyone. He cannot be kept in one place, however much he is loved there.
ch: The Catechism points to the prayer of Jesus before decisive moments in his ministry, as Luke’s Gospel stresses (CCC 2602), and to his proclamation of the kingdom as the centre of his mission (CCC 541–542). The Church sees in this passage the rhythm of her own life: prayer first, then mission. A parish that wishes to proclaim the Gospel to the other “cities” must also keep its deserted places of prayer. The sentence “I was sent” is repeated in the Church’s own sending: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21).

rite: In the West Syriac tradition the Church keeps vigil in the night hours of prayer, the Lilyo, as well as the morning hours of the Sapro. Paul’s words about being awake and sober are lived each time the faithful rise to pray while others sleep, and Jesus’ early morning prayer in the deserted place is the model of these hours.
study: Paul says that we are children of light and of the day. What is one way in which I can live as one who is awake this week, and not as one who sleeps?
Jesus withdrew to pray before going on to other towns. Where is my own “deserted place”, and what mission might come out of it?

lead: Both readings are about the single aim that gives order to the whole of life. Paul says that whatever we do, we should do it for the glory of God, and that he himself imitates Christ. In Luke, Jesus speaks to large crowds and says that to follow him costs everything, as a builder or a king must count the cost before beginning. The day also names St Ignatius of Loyola, whose motto was the greater glory of God. The key words are for the glory of God and count the cost.

r.h: Do everything for the glory of God
set: Paul closes a long answer (8:1–11:1) to the Corinthians’ question about eating meat that has been offered to idols. His answer is balanced: idols are nothing, but the weak may be hurt if the strong use their freedom without love. Many in the city bought meat from temple markets, and a meal in a friend’s house could easily raise the question.

Our verses give the summary. All of life, the plainest acts such as eating and drinking, is to be offered to God, and in whatever he does Paul seeks the good of others so that they may be saved. The chapter division is unfortunate: the first verse of chapter 11 belongs to the argument of chapter 10.
str: v. 31: whether you eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God.
v. 32: give no offense to Jews, to Greeks or to the church of God.
v. 33: Paul’s own practice: not seeking his own advantage but that of many.
11:1: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
kw: The weight and radiance of God. To do something “for the glory of God” is to let his goodness show in it.
Literally “not causing to stumble”. The word recalls the stumbling block that Paul fears to put before a weaker believer (8:9).
Paul asks to be imitated only as he imitates Christ. The standard is Christ, and the apostle is a pointer.
vv: do everything for the glory of God.
Nothing is too small. Eating, drinking and the ordinary acts of the day can be given to God.
Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God
Paul names the three groups of his world: Jews, Gentiles and the Church. He wants to cause no needless stumbling to any.
Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
Christianity is learned by following people who follow Christ. Parents, catechists and pastors are all asked to be this kind of example.
ch: The Church takes up Paul’s verse as the principle of the whole Christian life: every act, offered to God, becomes prayer. The Catechism teaches that the glory of God consists in the manifestation and communication of his goodness, for which the world was created (CCC 294). It also puts before us the saints as models and intercessors (CCC 828). In the Eastern tradition, the whole day, with its meals and its work, is surrounded with the prayers of the hours.

set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, and large crowds travel with him (14:25). He turns and tells them what following him means. The language is deliberately sharp. Just before this he has told of the great banquet to which many make excuses (14:15–24), and now he warns those who join the journey that it is not a casual walk.

“Hate” in verse 26 is Semitic speech: to love less by comparison. Matthew gives the sense: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (10:37). Jesus does not teach contempt for family, which the fourth commandment honours. He asks that no bond come before him. Then come two small parables, the builder and the king, both about thinking ahead before starting.
str: v. 25: large crowds with him on the road.
vv. 26–27: no one can be a disciple who puts even family or life before him, or who will not carry the cross.
vv. 28–30: the tower builder: count the cost first.
vv. 31–32: the king: weigh your strength before going to war.
v. 33: so none can be a disciple who does not give up all possessions.
kw: In biblical Hebrew and Aramaic “hate” can mean “love less” or “prefer something else”, as in Genesis 29:30–31 where Leah is “hated” in comparison with Rachel.
Literally to count with pebbles. The builder sits down and reckons honestly. Discipleship is not an impulse; it is a considered, lasting decision.
to say farewell, to give up
A word used for taking leave of someone. Disciples take leave of everything that would rule them.
vv: Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple.
The sentence is shocking on purpose, to show the place of Christ. Those who love him most also love their families best, because they love them in him.
Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
Every disciple has a cross. Jesus does not hide it. It is carried behind him, never alone.
which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost
Jesus encourages planning. A well-built life asks for clear thought and honest prayer.
none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.
To give up is to hold nothing as one’s own security. Some are called to leave everything; all are called to hold everything lightly.
ch: The Catechism teaches that detachment from riches is necessary for entering the kingdom of heaven (CCC 2544), and that the bonds of the family are not absolute, for the child’s first loyalty is to God (CCC 2232). The tradition has understood the words as the call of every Christian, and as the source of the counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience in the religious life. The two parables remind us that the response to Christ is made with open eyes. The cross that Jesus asks us to carry is in the end the road to joy.

qa: Does Jesus really ask us to hate our families?

No. The word is a Semitic way of saying “love less than”, as Matthew’s parallel shows (10:37). Jesus himself honoured his mother and gave her to the beloved disciple from the cross (John 19:26–27). What he asks is that no loyalty, even the dearest, stand in the way of following him. In practice, those who put Christ first become better sons, daughters, spouses and parents.
rite: The day also names St Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), a Basque soldier who was wounded in battle, read the lives of Christ and the saints during his recovery, and gave his life to God. He founded the Society of Jesus, whose motto is “for the greater glory of God”. His own life shows both of today’s readings: the call to do everything for God’s glory and the cost of leaving the old way of living for Christ. Many Jesuit missionaries, among them St Francis Xavier, a companion of Ignatius, came to India.
study: Paul asks us to do everything for the glory of God, even eating and drinking. What ordinary part of my day could I deliberately offer to God this week?
Jesus asks the builder to count the cost. What might I need to give up or hold more lightly so that I can follow him more fully and with an undivided heart?
